117314.q: A solid sphere and a thin-walled hollow cylinder with the same mass and radius roll down a slope at the same time. Which one reaches the bottom first?
a: It depends only on the mass
117314.e: In the hollow cylinder all the mass is on the outside, so it has the larger moment of inertia. It needs more energy for rotation and therefore rolls more slowly.
117314.m: The smaller the moment of inertia, the faster a body rolls.

117315.q: A thin rod of 6 kg and 2 m in length rotates about an axis through its centre. Its moment of inertia is J = m · l² / 12. How large is J?
117315.e: Putting in the values gives J = 6 kg · 4 m² / 12 = 2 kg·m².
117315.m: A rod about its centre has one twelfth m l squared.

117316.q: A torque of 10 N·m acts on a body with a moment of inertia of 2 kg·m². What is the angular acceleration?
117316.e: The basic equation of rotation is M = J · α. So α = 10 N·m / 2 kg·m² = 5 rad/s².
117316.m: Torque is moment of inertia times angular acceleration.

117317.q: What is the SI unit of the moment of inertia?
117317.e: The moment of inertia is a sum of masses times squared distances. This gives the unit kilogram times square metre.
117317.m: The moment of inertia has the unit kilogram times square metre.

117318.q: Which physicist proposed a model of the atom in 1913 in which the angular momentum of electrons can only take certain values?
117318.e: In Bohr's model of 1913, electrons may only orbit on paths whose angular momentum is a whole-number multiple of h / 2π. This is how Bohr explained the spectral lines of hydrogen.
117318.m: Niels Bohr introduced quantised electron orbits.

117319.q: A wheel with a moment of inertia of 0.4 kg·m² rotates at 10 rad/s. What is its angular momentum?
117319.e: L = J · ω = 0.4 kg·m² · 10 rad/s = 4 kg·m²/s.
117319.m: Faster rotation means more angular momentum.

117320.q: A mass of 0.2 kg moves at 3 m/s on a circle with a radius of 0.5 m. What is its angular momentum about the centre of the circle?
117320.e: For a point mass on a circular path, L = r · m · v. 0.5 m · 0.2 kg · 3 m/s gives 0.3 kg·m²/s.
117320.m: A point mass on a circular path also has angular momentum.

117321.q: A constant torque of 2 N·m acts on a wheel for 3 seconds. By how much does its angular momentum change?
117321.e: Torque is the rate of change of angular momentum. ΔL = M · Δt = 2 N·m · 3 s = 6 kg·m²/s.

117322.q: Which constant of nature has the same unit as angular momentum?
117322.e: The Planck constant has the unit joule second, which equals kg·m²/s. In quantum mechanics, angular momenta occur in multiples of it.
117322.m: Angular momenta in atoms are quantised.

117323.q: What is the intrinsic angular momentum of elementary particles such as the electron called?
117323.e: Spin is an internal angular momentum that particles have without any classical rotation. For the electron it is ½ in units of ħ.
117323.m: Spin is the intrinsic angular momentum of a particle.

117324.q: How do you find the direction of the angular momentum vector of a spinning wheel?
a: With the right-hand rule along the axis
It always points to the centre of the Earth
It points in the direction the rim moves
117324.e: If you curl the fingers of your right hand in the direction of rotation, your thumb points in the direction of the angular momentum. It lies on the axis of rotation.
117324.m: Angular momentum points along the axis of rotation.

117325.q: Why does a fast-spinning top not fall over straight away?
a: Its angular momentum stabilises the direction of its axis
It is lighter than a top at rest
The air holds it up from below
The Earth pulls on it less strongly
117325.e: A large angular momentum can only be changed by a torque. So gravity does not tip the top over but makes its axis slowly circle around.
117325.m: Angular momentum stabilises the axis of rotation.

117326.q: Under what condition is the angular momentum of a system conserved?
a: When there is no internal friction
When the mass does not move
117326.e: Only an external torque can change the total angular momentum. The effects of internal forces cancel out.
117326.m: Without an external torque, angular momentum stays the same.

117327.q: Why does a figure skater spin faster when she pulls her arms in to her body?
a: Her moment of inertia falls while her angular momentum stays the same
117327.e: With her arms pulled in, her mass is closer to the axis of rotation, so the moment of inertia gets smaller. Since J · ω stays constant, the angular velocity rises.
117327.m: Pulling in your arms makes a pirouette faster.

117328.q: A skater spins at 2 revolutions per second and reduces her moment of inertia from 4 to 1.6 kg·m². How fast does she spin afterwards?
117328.e: From J₁ · ω₁ = J₂ · ω₂ it follows that ω₂ = 4 · 2 / 1.6 = 5 revolutions per second.
117328.m: Halving the moment of inertia doubles the rate of spin.

117329.q: Where does the extra rotational energy come from when a figure skater pulls in her arms during a pirouette?
a: From the work done by her muscles
117329.e: The angular momentum stays the same, but the rotational energy L² / (2J) increases. The skater supplies the difference by pulling her arms inwards against the centrifugal force.
117329.m: Pulling in your arms means doing work.

117330.q: Which of Kepler's laws follows directly from the conservation of angular momentum?
a: The second, the law of equal areas
117330.e: The Sun's gravity acts towards the centre and produces no torque. So the line from the Sun to the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times.
117330.m: The law of equal areas is conservation of angular momentum.

117331.q: Why do neutron stars often rotate extremely fast?
a: Their radius shrinks hugely when they collapse
117331.e: When a star's core collapses, its radius becomes enormously smaller. With angular momentum conserved, the rate of spin rises, up to hundreds of revolutions per second.

117332.q: What is the tail rotor of a helicopter with one main rotor for?
a: It stops the body from turning against the rotor
117332.e: When the engine drives the main rotor, an equal counter-torque acts on the body. The tail rotor produces an opposing torque and keeps the body steady.
117332.m: The tail rotor balances the counter-torque.

117333.q: A person sits on a swivel chair holding a spinning wheel with a vertical axis. What happens when they turn the wheel upside down?
117333.e: The wheel's angular momentum is reversed. To keep the total angular momentum the same, the person and chair must turn in the direction the wheel was originally spinning.
117333.m: Turning a wheel over sets the swivel chair spinning.

117334.q: How can a falling cat turn in the air to land on its feet, even though its total angular momentum stays zero?
a: It twists its front and back body against each other
It pushes off against the air
117334.e: The cat twists its front and back body in turn and changes the moments of inertia as it does so. This lets it change its position without the total angular momentum moving away from zero.
117334.m: Internal movements let you turn without gaining angular momentum.

117335.q: What is Steiner's theorem (the parallel axis theorem) for an axis at distance d parallel to the axis through the centre of mass?
117335.e: The moment of inertia about the shifted axis is the moment of inertia about the centre of mass plus mass times distance squared. Both axes must be parallel.
117335.m: Steiner's theorem adds mass times distance squared.

117336.q: From which present-day Swiss canton did the mathematician Jakob Steiner, after whom the theorem is named, come?
117336.e: Jakob Steiner was born in 1796 in Utzenstorf in the canton of Bern. He later became a professor in Berlin and is known above all for his geometry.
117336.m: Jakob Steiner was a mathematician from Bern.

117337.q: A thin rod of 3 kg and 2 m in length rotates about an axis through one end, at right angles to the rod. What is its moment of inertia?
117337.e: About the centre, J_S = 3 · 4 / 12 = 1 kg·m². The distance to the end is 1 m, so J = 1 + 3 · 1² = 4 kg·m².
117337.m: A rod is harder to turn about its end than about its centre.

117338.q: For which position of the axis of rotation is the moment of inertia smallest among all parallel axes?
a: For the axis through the centre of mass
For the axis at the edge of the body
It is the same for all axes
117338.e: According to Steiner's theorem, m · d² is always added to the value for the centre of mass. This addition is only zero when d = 0.
117338.m: The moment of inertia is smallest through the centre of mass.

117339.q: A solid cylinder of 2 kg with a radius of 0.1 m rotates about an axis on its curved surface, parallel to its axis of symmetry. What is its moment of inertia?
117339.e: J_S = ½ · 2 · 0.01 = 0.01 kg·m². Steiner adds 2 · 0.1² = 0.02 kg·m², making 0.03 kg·m² in total.
117339.m: A rolling cylinder momentarily turns about the line where it touches the ground.

117340.q: A solid sphere of 1 kg with a radius of 0.1 m has a moment of inertia of 0.004 kg·m² about its centre. What is it about a tangent to its surface?
117340.e: Steiner adds m · d² = 1 · 0.1² = 0.01 kg·m². Together that gives 0.004 + 0.01 = 0.014 kg·m².
117340.m: Steiner's theorem also works for spheres.

117341.q: A body of 2 kg has a moment of inertia of 0.1 kg·m² about the axis through its centre of mass. What is it about a parallel axis 0.3 m away?
117341.e: According to Steiner, J = J_S + m · d². 0.1 + 2 · 0.3² = 0.1 + 0.18 gives 0.28 kg·m².
117341.m: The Steiner part grows with the square of the distance.

117342.q: Which condition must be met to apply Steiner's theorem?
a: One of the axes passes through the centre of mass
Both axes are at right angles to each other
The body must be at rest
117342.e: The theorem links any axis with the parallel axis through the centre of mass. It does not apply directly between two arbitrary parallel axes.
117342.m: Steiner's theorem needs an axis through the centre of mass.

117343.q: How did the gyrobus made by Maschinenfabrik Oerlikon store its driving energy?
117343.e: At charging stations an electric motor sped up the flywheel. While driving, it gave its rotational energy back as electrical energy to the traction motor.
117343.m: The gyrobus ran on the rotational energy of a flywheel.

117344.q: A body with J = 2 kg·m² rotates at 3 rad/s. What is its rotational energy?
117344.m: For rotational energy you square the angular velocity.

117345.q: How does rotational energy change when the angular velocity doubles?
117345.e: Since ω is squared, doubling it gives a factor of 2² = 4.
117345.m: Twice the rate of spin means four times the rotational energy.

117346.q: What do you call a rotating mass that is used to store energy?
117346.e: A flywheel stores energy as rotational energy and releases it again when it slows down. It smooths the running of engines, for example.
117346.m: A flywheel stores energy in its rotation.

117347.q: What fraction of the total kinetic energy of a rolling solid cylinder is rotational energy?
117347.e: Translation: ½ · m · v². Rotation: ½ · ½ · m · r² · (v/r)² = ¼ · m · v². So of the total ¾ · m · v², one third is rotational energy.
117347.m: In a rolling solid cylinder, one third of the energy is in the rotation.

117348.q: A solid sphere and a thin-walled hollow sphere of the same mass and size roll down the same slope. Which reaches the bottom first?
117348.e: The hollow sphere has a larger moment of inertia and puts more energy into rotation. So the solid sphere becomes faster.
117348.m: The solid sphere wins the rolling race against the hollow sphere.

117349.q: A solid cylinder starts from rest and rolls without slipping down a height of 0.3 m. Roughly how fast is it at the bottom (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
117349.e: From m · g · h = ¾ · m · v² it follows that v = √(4 · g · h / 3) = √(3.92) ≈ 2.0 m/s. A body sliding without friction would be faster, at about 2.4 m/s.
117349.m: Rolling bodies are slower than sliding ones.

117350.q: A disc with J = 0.5 kg·m² rotates at 600 revolutions per minute. Roughly what is its rotational energy?
117350.e: 600 per minute is 10 per second, so ω = 2π · 10 ≈ 62.8 rad/s. E = ½ · 0.5 · 62.8² ≈ 990 J.
117350.m: First convert rates of rotation into radians per second.

117351.q: Why is the Earth's rotational energy slowly decreasing?
117351.e: The tides caused by the Moon rub against the sea floor and slow the Earth's rotation. As a result, the days are getting longer very slowly.
117351.m: The tides slow the Earth down.

117352.q: In physics, what is meant by a top (gyroscope)?
a: A rigid body rotating about a fixed point
Any body on a circular path
117352.e: A top is a rigid body that can turn about a fixed point. Toy spinning tops are just one example.
117352.m: A top rotates about a fixed point.

117353.q: What is the slow circling movement of the axis of a tilted toy top called?
117353.e: Gravity exerts a torque on the tilted top. Instead of falling over, its axis slowly moves round in a circle. The Earth's axis also precesses, once in about 26,000 years.
117353.m: Precession is the slow circling of a top's axis.

117354.q: Why does a fast-spinning top not fall over straight away?
a: Gravity only changes the direction of its angular momentum
Gravity does not act on it
It floats on the air pressure
It is magnetically fixed to the floor
117354.e: The torque from gravity is perpendicular to the angular momentum. It turns the axis sideways instead of tipping the top over.
117354.m: A fast top moves sideways instead of falling over.

117355.q: In space, a cosmonaut watched a spinning wing nut flip over again and again. What is this effect called?
117355.e: In 1985, Vladimir Dzhanibekov saw in weightlessness that rotation about a certain axis is unstable. The body flips over at regular intervals.
117355.m: The Dzhanibekov effect shows unstable rotation in weightlessness.

117356.q: Which device uses the Earth's rotation and a gyroscope to find north without a magnetic field?
117356.e: In a gyrocompass, the Earth's rotation turns the gyroscope's axis into the north-south direction, that is, into the plane of the meridian. It shows geographic north and is not disturbed by iron.

117357.q: Why are bullets from rifled gun barrels given a spin?
a: The rotation stabilises their direction of flight
117357.e: By spinning about its long axis, the bullet acts like a gyroscope. Its angular momentum stops it from tumbling in flight.

117358.q: After which mathematician from Basel are the equations of motion of a rigid spinning body named?
117358.e: In the 18th century, Leonhard Euler set up Euler's equations for rotating bodies. They describe rotation in a frame of reference that moves with the body.
117358.m: The equations for spinning bodies come from Leonhard Euler.

117359.q: What do you call a top in which two of the three principal moments of inertia are equal?
117359.e: In a symmetric top, two principal moments of inertia are equal and the figure axis is an axis of symmetry. If all three are equal, it is called a spherical top.
117359.m: A symmetric top has two equal principal moments of inertia.

a: The change in direction of an axis of rotation under a torque
A top slowing down because of friction
An increase in the rate of spin
117360.e: If a torque acts on a rotating body at right angles to its angular momentum, the axis traces out the surface of a cone. This movement is called precession.
117360.m: Precession is the wandering of the axis of rotation.

117361.q: Roughly how long does one cycle of the precession of the Earth's axis take?
117361.e: The Earth's axis traces a cone with a period of about 26,000 years. This is also called the Platonic year.
117361.m: The Earth's axis precesses once in about 26,000 years.

117362.q: What effect does the precession of the Earth's axis have on the sky?
a: The pole star changes over thousands of years
The phases of the Moon disappear
The Sun rises in the west
117362.e: The celestial poles slowly move along a circle. In a few thousand years a different bright star will be near the north celestial pole.

117363.q: A tilted top is spinning fast. Why does it not simply tip over, but its axis moves round in a circle instead?
a: The torque from gravity only changes the direction of the angular momentum
The air holds the top up
Gravity does not act on spinning bodies
Friction with the floor lifts it
117363.e: Gravity produces a torque at right angles to the angular momentum. It does not change its size, only its direction, and the axis traces out a cone.
117363.m: A torque pushes the axis of a top sideways.

117364.q: How does the rate of precession of a top change when it spins faster?
117364.e: The rate of precession is inversely proportional to the angular momentum. So a fast top precesses slowly.
117364.m: The faster the top, the slower the precession.

117365.q: Which medical imaging method is based on the precession of nuclear spins in a magnetic field?
117365.e: In a strong magnetic field, the nuclear spins of hydrogen atoms precess at the Larmor frequency. MRI uses the signals from these spins.
117365.m: MRI uses the precession of nuclear spins.

117366.q: Which theory was the first to fully explain the observed precession of Mercury's perihelion?
117366.e: Part of the perihelion precession, about 43 arcseconds per century, could not be explained with Newton. In 1915 Einstein explained it with the general theory of relativity.
117366.m: Mercury's perihelion precession confirmed Einstein's theory.

117367.q: Which two conditions must be met for a rigid body to be in equilibrium?
a: The sum of forces and the sum of torques are zero
Only the sum of forces is zero
117367.e: For a rigid body to be neither shifted nor turned, all forces and all torques must cancel each other out.
117367.m: In equilibrium, forces and torques cancel out.

117368.q: What kind of equilibrium does a ball at the bottom of a bowl have?
117368.e: If the ball is pushed aside, its centre of mass rises. Gravity drives it back to its starting position.
117368.m: In stable equilibrium a body returns to its position.

117369.q: How many independent equilibrium conditions must a freely movable rigid body in space meet?
117369.e: In space there are three components of force and three components of torque. All six sums must be zero.
117369.m: In space a rigid body has six equilibrium conditions.

117370.q: On a mobile rod, a figure of 0.2 kg hangs on the left, 0.3 m from the suspension point. Where must a figure of 0.3 kg hang on the right so that the rod stays level?
117370.e: The torques must be equal: 0.2 · 0.3 = 0.3 · x. It follows that x = 0.06 / 0.3 = 0.2 m.
117370.m: In a mobile the torques balance each other.

117371.q: A child of 30 kg sits on a seesaw 2 m from the pivot. Where must a child of 40 kg sit on the other side for it to balance?
117371.e: The torques must be equal: 30 · 2 = 40 · x. It follows that x = 60 / 40 = 1.5 m.
117371.m: The heavier child sits closer to the pivot.

117372.q: A beam 4 m long weighing 200 N rests on supports at both ends. A load of 600 N hangs 1 m from the left end. What force does the left support carry?
117372.e: Moments about the right support: 200 N · 2 m + 600 N · 3 m = F_L · 4 m. So F_L = 2200 / 4 = 550 N.
117372.m: The support closer to the load carries more.

117373.q: Why does a construction crane carry a heavy counterweight on its short jib?
a: To balance the torque of the load
To make the crane turn faster
117373.e: The load on the long jib produces a large torque about the tower. The counterweight acts on the other side and keeps the overall centre of mass above the base.
117373.m: A counterweight stops the crane from tipping over.

117374.q: Where is a hanging body positioned when it is in stable equilibrium?
a: Its centre of mass is directly below the point of suspension
Its centre of mass is above the point of suspension
Its centre of mass is beside the point of suspension
Its centre of mass is at the point of suspension
117374.e: If the centre of mass hangs below the point of suspension, any displacement lifts it. The weight turns the body back.
117374.m: Hanging bodies come to rest with their centre of mass at the bottom.

117375.q: What does statics, a branch of mechanics, deal with?
117375.e: Statics studies how forces act on bodies and structures at rest. It is the basis for calculating bridges and buildings.
117375.m: Statics studies forces on bodies at rest.

117376.q: Which ancient scholar is said to have said “Give me a place to stand, and I will move the world”?
117376.e: Archimedes formulated the law of the lever. The saying shows that with a long enough lever you could move any load.
117376.m: Archimedes formulated the law of the lever.

117377.q: How many independent equilibrium conditions does a rigid body in a plane have?
117377.e: In a plane there are two force equations, horizontal and vertical, and one moment equation. This lets you work out at most three unknown support forces.
117377.m: In a plane there are three equilibrium conditions.

117378.q: What force can a roller support take in a plane?
a: Only a force perpendicular to the direction it can slide
117378.e: A roller support can move along its track. So it only transmits a force perpendicular to it, for example so that a bridge can expand in the heat.
117378.m: A roller support allows movement along its track.

117379.q: Which drawing method do you use to add two forces acting at the same point?
117379.e: The two force arrows form two sides of a parallelogram. The diagonal is the resultant force.

117380.q: A 50 N lamp hangs in the middle of a rope whose two halves are each tilted at 30° to the horizontal. What is the force in each half of the rope?
117380.e: The vertical parts of both rope forces carry the lamp: 2 · F · sin(30°) = 50 N. With sin(30°) = 0.5, F = 50 N.
117380.m: Ropes stretched flat carry large forces.

117381.q: Which forces occur in the members of an ideal truss?
117381.e: In an ideal truss, the members are joined by hinges and are only loaded at the joints. So only forces along the direction of each member act in them.
117381.m: Truss members are only loaded in tension or compression.

117382.q: A block weighing 100 N rests on a slope inclined at 30°. How large is the force pulling it down the slope?
117382.e: The force down the slope is F_G · sin(30°) = 100 N · 0.5 = 50 N. Static friction must balance this force for the block to stay at rest.
117382.m: On a slope, part of the weight pulls downhill.

117383.q: What does the centre of mass theorem state?
a: The centre of mass moves as if all external forces acted there
The centre of mass is always in the middle of the body
The centre of mass never moves
The centre of mass always lies inside the body
117383.e: For a system of masses, total mass times the acceleration of the centre of mass equals the sum of the external forces. The centre of mass moves like a point mass.
117383.m: The centre of mass moves like a single point mass.

117384.q: Which forces cannot change the motion of a system's centre of mass?
117384.e: According to Newton's third law, internal forces occur in opposite pairs. They cancel out in total.
117384.m: Internal forces do not move the centre of mass.

117385.q: A firework rocket explodes in the air. How does the centre of mass of all the pieces move as long as none has reached the ground (ignoring air resistance)?
a: It keeps following the original parabolic path
It stays still in the air
117385.e: The explosion is an internal force. Only gravity still acts on the system, so the centre of mass carries on along the parabola.
117385.m: An explosion does not change the path of the centre of mass.

117386.q: A mass of 2 kg is at x = 0 m and one of 6 kg is at x = 4 m. Where is their combined centre of mass?
117386.m: The centre of mass is closer to the larger mass.

117387.q: Where is the combined centre of mass of the Earth and the Moon?
a: On the surface of the Moon
117387.e: The Earth is about 81 times heavier than the Moon. That is why the combined centre of mass is still inside the Earth, about three quarters of the Earth's radius from its centre.
117387.m: The Earth and the Moon circle a point inside the Earth.

117388.q: A 60 kg person walks 3 m forwards in a 120 kg boat at rest. How far does the boat move, ignoring water resistance?
117388.e: The centre of mass stays at rest: 60 · (3 − x) = 120 · x. It follows that x = 1 m; the person moves 2 m relative to the water.
117388.m: If you walk forwards in a boat, the boat slides back.

117389.q: Why can a high jumper using the Fosbury flop clear a bar even though their centre of mass stays below it?
a: The arched body is partly below the bar
Gravity does not act during the flop
117389.e: In the flop, the body arches over the bar. This lets the centre of mass pass just below or at the bar while each part of the body slides over it one after another.
117389.m: In the high jump flop, the centre of mass can stay below the bar.

117390.q: A 1 kg body moves at 4 m/s and a second body of 3 kg is at rest. How fast does their combined centre of mass move?
117390.e: Total momentum divided by total mass: (1 · 4 + 3 · 0) / 4 = 1 m/s.
117390.m: Total momentum is total mass times the velocity of the centre of mass.

a: A fast-spinning top that keeps the direction of its axis
A device for measuring air pressure
117391.e: A gyroscope usually consists of a fast-spinning rotor in a movable mounting. Because of its angular momentum, it keeps its direction in space.
117391.m: A gyroscope holds its axis fixed in space.

117392.q: Which French physicist gave the gyroscope its name in 1852?
117392.e: Léon Foucault wanted to use the device to make the Earth's rotation visible. The name means roughly “rotation viewer”.

117393.q: What is the mounting made of rings turning inside each other that lets a gyroscope point its axis in any direction called?
117393.e: In a gimbal mounting, two or three rings sit inside each other, each able to turn about its own axis. This lets the rotor hold its direction independently of the casing.
117393.m: A gimbal mounting lets a gyroscope move freely.

117394.q: Which aircraft instrument uses a gyroscope to show the plane's position relative to the horizon?
117394.e: In the artificial horizon, a gyroscope keeps its position in space. When the aircraft tilts, you can see the difference from this reference.
117394.m: The artificial horizon uses a gyroscope.

117395.q: Which force do the tiny micromechanical gyroscopes in smartphones use to measure rotation?
117395.e: In MEMS gyroscopes a small mass vibrates. When the device turns, the Coriolis force pushes it sideways, and this is measured electrically.
117395.m: Phone gyroscopes measure rotation using the Coriolis force.

117396.q: In a ring laser gyroscope, what replaces the fast-spinning rotor?
a: Two laser beams travelling in opposite directions around a ring
A vibrating tuning fork made of glass
A pendulum in a vacuum chamber
117396.e: Two laser beams travel in opposite directions around the ring. When the ring turns, their paths around it differ in length, and the rate of rotation follows from the difference.
117396.m: Ring lasers measure rotation with light.

117397.q: How do satellites with reaction wheels change their orientation without using fuel?
a: They change the speed of the wheels
117397.e: When a motor speeds up the wheel in one direction, the satellite turns the opposite way because angular momentum is conserved.
117397.m: Reaction wheels turn satellites without fuel.

117398.q: Which satellite mission used extremely precise gyroscopes to test predictions of the general theory of relativity?
117398.e: Gravity Probe B was launched in 2004 with four almost perfect quartz spheres as gyroscopes. They measured how the Earth curves space-time and drags it along.
117398.m: Gravity Probe B confirmed Einstein with gyroscopes.

117399.q: Which photosynthetic pigments do green algae share with land plants?
117399.e: Green algae and land plants use chlorophyll a and b. Brown algae, by contrast, have chlorophyll c and fucoxanthin, and red algae have phycobilins such as phycoerythrin.
117399.m: Green algae and land plants share the same chlorophylls a and b.

117400.q: Which storage substance do green algae, like land plants, store in their plastids?
117400.e: Like land plants, green algae store starch in their chloroplasts. Glycogen is stored by animals and fungi, laminarin by brown algae.
117400.m: Like land plants, green algae store starch in their chloroplasts.

117401.q: From which group of living things did land plants evolve?
117401.e: Land plants share chlorophyll a and b, starch as a storage substance and cellulose cell walls with green algae. Their closest relatives are the conjugating green algae.
117401.m: Land plants are descended from green algae.

117402.q: Which single-celled green alga with two flagella and a red eyespot is an important model organism?
117402.e: Chlamydomonas swims with two flagella and uses its eyespot to orient itself towards light. It is often studied in genetics and cell biology.
117402.m: Chlamydomonas is a flagellated green alga with an eyespot.

117403.q: Which green alga forms hollow spheres made of hundreds to tens of thousands of flagellated cells?
117403.e: Volvox colonies are hollow spheres whose cells beat their flagella in a coordinated way. They are seen as an example of the transition to multicellular life.
117403.m: Volvox forms spherical colonies of many flagellated cells.

117404.q: Which threadlike freshwater green alga is named after its spirally wound chloroplasts?
117404.e: The name Spirogyra means roughly “twisted circle”. Its ribbon-shaped chloroplasts spiral through the cell.

117405.q: Which marine green alga with a thin, leaf-like thallus is called “sea lettuce”?
117405.e: Ulva forms lettuce-like lobes only two cell layers thick. Fucus and Laminaria are brown algae, Porphyra is a red alga.
117405.m: Sea lettuce, Ulva, is a leaf-like green alga.

117406.q: What is the main building material of the cell wall in most green algae?
117406.e: Like land plants, green algae build their cell walls mainly from cellulose. Chitin is found in fungi, murein in bacteria and silica in diatoms.
117406.m: Like land plants, green algae have cell walls made of cellulose.

117407.q: On which single-celled “mermaid's wineglass” alga did Joachim Hämmerling show that the nucleus controls the shape of the cell?
117407.e: Acetabularia is a single cell several centimetres tall with its nucleus in the base. Using grafting experiments, Hämmerling showed that the shape of the cap is determined by the nucleus.
117407.m: Hämmerling's experiments with Acetabularia showed the controlling role of the nucleus.

117408.q: Roughly how many years ago did plants begin to colonise the land?
117408.e: The oldest spores of land plants date from the Ordovician. Larger plant fossils only follow in the Silurian and Devonian.
117408.m: Plants have colonised the land for around 470 million years.

117409.q: Which waxy layer protects the above-ground parts of land plants from drying out?
117409.e: The cuticle consists of cutin and waxes and lies on top of the epidermis. It greatly reduces evaporation and was a requirement for life on land.
117409.m: The cuticle protects land plants from drying out.

117410.q: Which structures in the epidermis regulate gas exchange in land plants?
117410.e: Stomata consist of two guard cells that open and close. This lets carbon dioxide in without water being lost all the time.
117410.m: Stomata control gas exchange in land plants.

117411.q: Why are pollen grains still well preserved in bogs and lake sediments after thousands of years?
a: Their outer wall is made of an extremely durable substance
Bees have coated them with wax
They go on living in the bog
117411.e: The pollen wall is made of sporopollenin, one of the most durable organic substances. This is why pollen analysis can be used to reconstruct the vegetation of earlier times.
117411.m: Thanks to their tough outer wall, pollen grains survive for a very long time.

117412.q: What do mosses, ferns and seed plants have in common that algae lack?
a: Their embryo develops protected on the parent plant
117412.e: In all land plants the embryo is nourished and protected by the parent plant. This is why together they are called embryophytes.
117412.m: All land plants nourish their embryo on the parent plant.

117413.q: Which living group of land plants has no woody vascular tissue?
117413.e: Mosses have at most simple conducting cells without lignin. That is why they stay small and depend on damp places.
117413.m: Mosses have no woody vascular tissue and therefore stay small.

117414.q: Which of these plants is not a moss at all, despite its name?
117414.e: Iceland moss is a shrubby lichen, a partnership of a fungus and an alga. True mosses include peat moss and haircap moss, as well as liverworts and hornworts.
117414.m: Iceland moss is a lichen, not a moss.

117415.q: Which symbiosis helped even early land plants take up nutrients from the soil?
117415.e: Fossils from the Devonian show fungal structures in plant tissue. The fungi supplied water and minerals and received sugar in return.
117415.m: Mycorrhiza with fungi made it easier for plants to move onto land.

117416.q: In which country is the site after which the early plant Rhynia is named?
117416.e: Rhynia is named after the village of Rhynie in Aberdeenshire. That is where the famous Rhynie chert, a rock layer rich in fossils, is found.
117416.m: Rhynia comes from the Rhynie chert in Scotland.

117417.q: Why is the site where Rhynia was found so valuable for research?
a: It shows one of the oldest known land ecosystems
It contains the oldest dinosaur bones
It is the oldest forest with tall trees
It contains the first flowering plants
117417.e: The Rhynie chert in Scotland is around 400 million years old. It preserves early land plants, fungi and small arthropods together.
117417.m: The Rhynia site shows very early life on land.

117418.q: How were the plants in the Rhynie chert preserved right down to individual cells?
a: By being trapped in tree resin
By being charred in forest fires
117418.e: Silica-rich water from hot springs soaked the plants and quickly turned them to stone. This means even cell walls and stomata are visible.
117418.m: Hot, silica-rich springs preserved the Rhynie plants.

117419.q: Which organs did the early vascular plant Rhynia lack?
117419.e: Rhynia consisted only of leafless stems. Photosynthesis took place in the green surface of the stem.
117419.m: Rhynia had neither leaves nor true roots.

117420.q: Apart from plants, what else is preserved as fossils in the Rhynie chert?
117420.e: Fungi, lichens and small arthropods such as mites and springtails are also fossilised in the Rhynie chert. It therefore shows a whole early community of life on land.
117420.m: The Rhynie chert preserves a whole early land ecosystem.

117421.q: Where did Rhynia form its sporangia?
a: At the tips of the stems
On the undersides of the leaves
117421.e: The elongated sporangia sat singly at the tips of the stems. There were no leaves they could have grown on.
117421.m: Rhynia bore its sporangia at the tips of its stems.

117422.q: Roughly how tall did Rhynia grow?
117422.e: Rhynia was a small herbaceous plant which, depending on the source, grew about 20 to 40 centimetres tall. Tree-like plants only appeared later.
117422.m: Rhynia was only a few decimetres tall.

117423.q: Which feature made Rhynia an early vascular plant?
117423.e: Rhynia had simple conducting strands in its stem that transported water. It did not yet have leaves, flowers or seeds.
117423.m: Rhynia already had conducting tissue, but no leaves yet.

117424.q: What anchored Rhynia in the ground?
117424.e: Rhynia had parts of its stem creeping along the ground (rhizomes). Fine rhizoids took up water and held the plant in place.
117424.m: Rhynia anchored itself with creeping stems and rhizoids.

117425.q: What mainly drives water transport in the xylem of tall trees?
a: The transpiration pull of the leaves
117425.e: When water evaporates from the leaves, it pulls the continuous columns of water upwards. This cohesion-tension theory explains transport to heights of over 100 metres.
117425.m: The transpiration pull draws water up into the tree.

117426.q: Which tissue in vascular plants transports sugar from the leaves to where it is used?
117426.e: In the phloem, sugary sap flows through living sieve cells. In this way it reaches the roots, fruits and buds.
117426.m: The phloem distributes sugar around the plant.

117427.q: Which substance strengthens the cell walls of the water-conducting cells and makes vascular plants sturdy?
117427.e: Lignin is deposited in the cell walls and makes them resistant to pressure. Only then could plants grow tall and upright.
117427.m: Lignin makes cell walls woody and gives stability.

117428.q: What are the long, dead water-conducting cells of ferns and conifers called?
117428.e: Tracheids are dead, lignified cells with pits through which water flows from cell to cell. In conifers they make up almost all of the wood.
117428.m: Tracheids are the water-conducting cells of ferns and conifers.

117429.q: In vascular plants, which generation forms the large, long-lived plant?
117429.e: In ferns, conifers and flowering plants, the visible plant is diploid. The gametophyte is small or greatly reduced.
117429.m: In vascular plants the sporophyte dominates.

117430.q: Roughly when did the first vascular plants appear on land?
117430.e: One of the oldest known vascular plants is Cooksonia from the Silurian, around 430 million years old. It was only a few centimetres tall.
117430.m: The first vascular plants appeared around 430 million years ago.

117431.q: What distinguishes vascular plants from mosses?
a: They have vascular bundles for water and nutrients
They do not carry out photosynthesis
117431.e: Vascular plants have xylem and phloem, which carry water and sugar through the plant. Mosses do not have such vascular bundles and therefore stay small.
117431.m: Vascular plants have vascular bundles, mosses do not.

117432.q: Which vascular plants do not produce seeds and spread by spores?
117432.e: Ferns and horsetails are vascular plants without seeds. Their spores germinate into a small prothallus.
117432.m: Ferns are vascular plants that spread by spores.

117433.q: What advantage did large leaves give early land plants?
117433.e: Large leaves capture more light and so increase photosynthesis. But they also lose more water by evaporation and therefore need good vascular bundles.
117433.m: Large leaves increased the surface area for photosynthesis.

117434.e: Like ferns, clubmosses produce spores, often in spike-like cones. Seeds and fruits only exist in seed plants.

117435.q: Which tree-like clubmoss dominated the coal forests of the Carboniferous?
117435.e: The scale tree grew to over 30 metres tall. The leaf scars on its bark look like scales. Calamites was a relative of horsetails.
117435.m: The scale tree was a giant clubmoss of the Carboniferous forests.

117436.q: What were the spores of the stag's-horn clubmoss once used for?
a: As flash powder for fire effects
117436.e: The spores are fine and rich in oil. Blown into a flame as a cloud of dust, they burn off with a bright flash. They were also called witch's flour.
117436.m: Clubmoss spores were used as flash powder.

117437.q: Roughly how old is the plant group of clubmosses?
117437.e: Clubmosses have existed since the Silurian and Devonian. They are among the oldest groups of vascular plants still alive today.
117437.m: Clubmosses are over 400 million years old.

117438.q: Which plant, despite its name, is not a moss but a relative of the clubmosses?
117438.e: Spikemoss looks moss-like because of its tiny leaves. But it has conducting tissue and belongs to the clubmosses.
117438.m: Spikemoss is a relative of the clubmosses.

117439.q: What does the genus name Lycopodium literally mean?
117439.e: The name comes from the Greek “lykos” for wolf and “pous” for foot. It refers to the furry, leafy tips of the shoots.

117440.q: Which feature do clubmosses share with ferns and seed plants, but not with mosses?
a: Conducting tissue with xylem and phloem
117440.e: Clubmosses are vascular plants. Like ferns and seed plants they have conducting tissue, which mosses lack. They do not have flowers or seeds.
117440.m: Clubmosses belong to the vascular plants.

117441.q: Where do clubmosses typically grow in Switzerland?
a: In conifer forests and on heaths with acidic soil
117441.e: Clubmosses such as stag's-horn clubmoss or fir clubmoss grow in mountain conifer forests, dwarf shrub heaths and bogs. They prefer acidic, nutrient-poor soils.
117441.m: Clubmosses like acidic forest soils and heaths.

a: Embryo, nutritive tissue and seed coat
117442.e: The seed is an organ for spreading and surviving. The embryo is fed by the nutritive tissue and protected by the seed coat.
117442.m: A seed contains an embryo with a food store and a protective coat.

117443.q: In flowering plants, what does the seed develop from after fertilisation?
117443.e: The ovule lies in the ovary. After fertilisation the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.

117444.q: In terms of the alternation of generations, what is a pollen grain?
117444.e: Inside the pollen grain, a microspore develops into a tiny gametophyte of just a few cells. It supplies the sperm cells.
117444.m: A pollen grain is a tiny male gametophyte.

117445.q: Which advantage made seed plants more successful on land than ferns?
a: They only grow in the shade
117445.e: In ferns, sperm have to swim through a film of water. Seed plants get pollen to the egg cell by wind or animals and so are independent of water.
117445.m: Seed plants do not need water for fertilisation.

117446.q: Which plant group existed on Earth before the seed plants?
117446.e: Ferns and their relatives reproduce with spores and are older than the seed plants. Grasses, roses and orchids are much younger flowering plants.
117446.m: Ferns are older than the seed plants.

117447.q: What is the extinct group with fern-like fronds that already bore seeds called?
117447.e: Seed ferns (pteridosperms) were common in the Carboniferous. Despite looking like ferns, they were true seed plants.
117447.m: Seed ferns looked like ferns but bore seeds.

117448.q: What is the scientific name for seed plants?
117448.e: The name comes from the Greek “sperma” for seed. Pteridophyta is the old name for ferns and their relatives.
117448.m: The scientific name for seed plants is Spermatophyta.

117449.q: Which plant produces the heaviest seeds in the world?
117449.e: The coco de mer palm grows naturally only on the Seychelles islands of Praslin and Curieuse. Its seeds weigh around 10 to 25 kilograms.
117449.m: The coco de mer palm has the heaviest seeds.

117450.q: Why are gymnosperms (“naked seeds”) called that?
a: Their ovules lie exposed on scales
They have no nutritive tissue at all
117450.e: In conifers the ovules sit openly on the seed scales of the cones. They are not enclosed in an ovary.
117450.m: Gymnosperms carry their ovules exposed on scales.

117451.q: Which plant group, which looks like palms from the outside, belongs to the gymnosperms?
117451.e: Cycads have a trunk with a crown of feather-like leaves. They form cones and are gymnosperms.
117451.m: Cycads look like palms but are gymnosperms.

117452.q: Which gymnosperm from the Namib Desert produces only two leaves in its whole life?
117452.e: The two strap-shaped leaves of Welwitschia keep growing from the base and fray at the ends. The plant can live for over a thousand years.
117452.m: Welwitschia lives in the desert with just two leaves.

117453.q: Where do the gymnosperms (“naked seeds”), which include the conifers, get their name from?
a: Their ovules lie exposed on scales
Their branches have no needles in winter
117453.e: In gymnosperms the ovules lie openly on the scales of the cones. In angiosperms they are enclosed in an ovary.
117453.m: In gymnosperms the ovules lie exposed and not in an ovary.

117454.q: Which gymnosperm with fan-shaped leaves is known as a “living fossil”?
117454.e: The ginkgo is the last survivor of a plant group that was already widespread in the time of the dinosaurs. Its leaves are fan-shaped rather than needle-shaped.
117454.m: The ginkgo is a living fossil with fan-shaped leaves.

117455.e: Conifers produce huge amounts of pollen, which is blown by the wind. In spring you can see it as yellow dust on puddles.
117455.m: Conifers are mostly pollinated by the wind.

117456.q: Which native conifer is poisonous almost everywhere but has a red seed covering?
117456.e: The needles, wood and seeds of the yew contain poisonous taxines. Only the fleshy red seed covering (aril) is not poisonous.
117456.m: The yew is poisonous apart from its red seed covering.

117457.q: Which Alpine tree has needles in bundles of five and edible seeds?
117457.e: The Swiss stone pine (arolla pine) grows up to the tree line. The spotted nutcracker hides its nuts and so helps to spread them.
117457.m: The Swiss stone pine has five needles per bundle.

117458.q: Which plant group, with around 300,000 species, is the most species-rich on Earth?
117458.e: Angiosperms form flowers and enclose their seeds in an ovary. They make up the great majority of all plant species.
117458.m: Flowering plants are the most species-rich plant group.

117459.q: What distinguishes angiosperms from gymnosperms such as pines and spruces?
a: Their ovules are protected inside an ovary
They produce no seeds at all
117459.e: In angiosperms the ovules are enclosed in the ovary, which later becomes the fruit. In gymnosperms they lie exposed, for example on the scales of a cone.
117459.m: Angiosperms protect their ovules in an ovary.

117460.q: Roughly how many species of angiosperms are known?
117460.e: Angiosperms are the most species-rich plant group. Estimates are around 300,000 described species.
117460.m: Around 300,000 species make flowering plants the largest plant group.

117461.q: Since when have angiosperms been reliably recorded as fossils?
a: Since the Early Cretaceous, around 130 million years ago
Since the Carboniferous, around 330 million years ago
Since the Ordovician, around 460 million years ago
Since the Oligocene, around 30 million years ago
117461.e: The oldest reliable pollen and flower fossils come from the Early Cretaceous. After that, flowering plants spread rapidly.
117461.m: Flowering plants have been recorded as fossils since the Early Cretaceous.

117462.q: What did Charles Darwin call the sudden appearance of flowering plants in the fossil record?
117462.e: In 1879 Darwin wrote to Joseph Hooker of an “abominable mystery”. The rapid diversity did not fit well with his idea of gradual change.
117462.m: Darwin called the rapid spread of flowering plants an abominable mystery.

117463.q: Which water-conducting cells do most angiosperms have in addition to tracheids?
117463.e: Vessels are long tubes made of cells whose end walls have dissolved. They conduct water faster than tracheids.
117463.m: Vessels are the fast water pipes of flowering plants.

117464.q: In angiosperms, what does the fruit develop from?
117464.e: After fertilisation the wall of the ovary becomes the fruit wall. In some fruits other parts of the flower grow into it as well.
117464.m: The fruit develops from the ovary.

117465.q: Which water plant has the largest undivided floating leaves?
117465.e: The leaves of the giant water lilies from South America reach about three metres across. Ribs on the underside make them able to bear a lot of weight.
117465.m: The giant water lily has enormous floating leaves.

117466.q: How do the leaf veins run in most monocots?
117466.e: Grasses, lilies and orchids usually have leaf veins running in parallel. Net-like veins are typical of dicots.
117466.m: Monocots usually have leaves with parallel veins.

117467.q: In what numbers are the flower parts of monocots usually arranged?
117467.e: A tulip, for example, has six petals in two rings of three. The stamens and carpels also follow the pattern of three.
117467.m: Monocot flowers usually have parts in threes.

117468.q: How are the vascular bundles arranged in the stem of a typical monocot?
117468.e: In a cross-section of a maize stem, the vascular bundles are scattered. As there is no ring of cambium, the typical growth in thickness is missing.
117468.m: In monocots the vascular bundles are scattered in the stem.

117469.q: What does the root system of typical monocots look like?
a: Fibrous, the first root dies early
Made of a single swollen root
117469.e: In grasses the first root soon dies. Instead, many roots of equal thickness grow from the base of the shoot.
117469.m: Monocots form a fibrous root system.

117470.q: To which monocot family do wheat, maize and rice belong?
117470.e: The grass family (Poaceae) provides humanity's most important staple foods. Their fruits are cereal grains.
117470.m: Wheat, maize and rice are grasses.

117471.q: Which monocot family, with over 25,000 species, is one of the most species-rich plant families?
117471.e: Orchids are found almost all over the world, especially in the tropics. Around 70 wild orchid species grow in Switzerland too.
117471.m: Orchids are one of the largest plant families.

117472.q: Which of these crops is a monocot?
117472.e: Palms are monocots, even though they grow like trees. Cacao, coffee and olive are dicots.
117472.m: Palms are monocots, even though they look like trees.

117473.q: How do palms get their thick trunk without a cambium?
a: Through primary thickening just below the shoot tip
Through a thick layer of cork
117473.e: In palms the trunk is already laid down near the growing point as thick as it will stay. After that it grows almost only in height.
117473.m: Palms become thick through primary thickening.

117474.q: Which pattern of leaf veins is typical of dicots?
117474.e: In beech, rose or bean, the veins branch out into a network. This distinguishes them from grasses with parallel veins.

117475.q: In what numbers are the flower parts arranged in many dicots?
117475.e: A rose, for example, has five petals, oilseed rape has four. Threes, on the other hand, are typical of monocots.
117475.m: Many dicots have flowers with parts in fours or fives.

117476.q: What is the technical term for seed leaves?
117476.e: Monocots and dicots are distinguished by the number of cotyledons. Bracts are leaves near the flower, stipules are small outgrowths at the base of the leaf stalk.
117476.m: The technical term for seed leaves is cotyledons.

117477.q: Which root system is typical of many dicots?
a: A main root with side roots
Many fibrous roots of equal thickness
Only roots growing from the shoot
117477.e: In dandelions or carrots the first root grows into a taproot. Side roots branch off from it.

117478.q: Which plant group is the counterpart to the dicots?
117478.e: Flowering plants with a closed ovary are traditionally divided into monocots and dicots. Monocots include grasses, lilies and orchids.
117478.m: Monocots are the counterpart to dicots.

117479.q: How can you tell from a seedling whether a plant is a dicot?
117479.e: In dicots such as the bean, two seed leaves unfold when the seed germinates. Monocots such as maize show only a single narrow seed leaf.
117479.m: Dicots germinate with two seed leaves.

117480.q: Which of these plants is a dicot?
117480.e: The dandelion has two seed leaves, net-like veins and a taproot. Maize, tulip and reed are monocots.
117480.m: The dandelion is a dicot plant.

117481.q: What allows many dicots such as beech or oak to grow thicker every year?
a: A ring of cambium between xylem and phloem
A growth tissue in the root tip
117481.e: The cambium produces wood towards the inside and bast towards the outside. This is how the annual rings form.
117481.m: A ring of cambium lets trees grow thicker year after year.

117482.q: What does the abbreviation APG stand for in plant classification?
117482.e: The Angiosperm Phylogeny Group is an international team of researchers. It publishes a shared classification of flowering plants.
117482.m: APG stands for the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group.

117483.q: In which year did the first version of the APG system appear?
117483.e: APG I appeared in 1998, followed by APG II (2003) and APG III (2009). It was the first widely accepted system based on DNA.
117483.m: The first APG system was published in 1998.

117484.q: Why does the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group keep publishing new versions of its system?
a: New DNA data change the picture of how plants are related
Many new plant families appear every year
Old names are no longer valid after ten years
Every country needs its own system
117484.e: APG I (1998) was followed by APG II, III and, in 2016, APG IV. Each new version included more DNA analyses, which rearranged some families and orders.
117484.m: New DNA data lead to new versions of the APG system.

117485.q: What is the APG system mainly based on?
117485.e: Earlier systems relied mainly on shape and structure. The APG arranges the families according to molecular analyses of relationships.
117485.m: The APG system is based mainly on DNA comparisons.

117486.q: What does it mean that the plant Amborella is considered the sister group of all other flowering plants?
a: Its line was the first to split off from the other flowering plants
It is the youngest flowering plant on Earth
It is the only flowering plant that has no flowers
It descends directly from the conifers
117486.e: Amborella grows only on New Caledonia. Its line was the first to branch off the family tree of flowering plants, so it helps us understand what early flowering plants looked like.
117486.m: Amborella stands at the base of the family tree of flowering plants.

117487.q: What does it mean if the sunflower and the potato belong to the same large group in the APG system?
a: They are more closely related to each other than to many other flowering plants
They grow in the same place
They have the same number of chromosomes
They flower at the same time of year
117487.e: The APG system arranges plants by their descent. Sunflower and potato both belong to the asterids, so they share a common ancestor.
117487.m: The same group in the APG system means a close relationship.

117488.q: Which kind of groups does the APG system recognise as taxa?
117488.e: A monophyletic group includes an ancestor and all its descendants. That is why old groups such as the dicots were dropped.
117488.m: The APG system only accepts complete lines of descent.

117489.q: Which pair of plants is most closely related according to DNA comparisons?
117489.e: Tomato and potato belong to the nightshade family and even to the same genus, Solanum. The pea is a legume, wheat and maize are grasses.
117489.m: Tomato and potato are close relatives.

117490.q: Which well-known water plant belongs to the oldest lines of flowering plants?
117490.e: Water lilies branched off the family tree of flowering plants very early. Duckweed, reed and waterweed belong to the much younger monocots.
117490.m: Water lilies are among the most primitive flowering plants.

117491.q: Who first used the expression “living fossil” in 1859?
117491.e: In “On the Origin of Species”, Darwin wrote of “living fossils”. He meant species that have kept ancient forms up to the present day.
117491.m: Darwin coined the expression living fossil in 1859.

117492.q: Which tree is the only living species of a once species-rich class of plants?
117492.e: The ginkgo is the last member of the Ginkgopsida, which were widespread in the Mesozoic. Its fan-shaped leaf has forked veins.
117492.m: The ginkgo is the last survivor of its class.

117493.q: Which trees in Hiroshima became a symbol of hope because they sprouted again after the atomic bombing of 1945?
117493.e: Several ginkgos in Hiroshima survived the explosion and sprouted again. Today they are seen as a symbol of hope.
117493.m: Ginkgos in Hiroshima survived the atomic bomb in 1945.

117494.q: Which conifer was first described as a fossil and then discovered alive in China in the 1940s?
117494.e: Shigeru Miki described the genus Metasequoia from fossils in 1941. Shortly afterwards, living trees were found in central China.
117494.m: The dawn redwood was first known as a fossil and then found alive.

117495.q: Why is the exact location of the wild Wollemi pine in Australia kept secret?
a: To protect the few trees from diseases and collectors
Because the area is a military site
117495.e: The Wollemi pine was only known from similar fossils until just under a hundred wild trees were found in a gorge in 1994. Visitors could bring in fungal diseases, for example.
117495.m: The rare Wollemi pine is protected by keeping its location secret.

117496.q: Which genus is the only survivor of a plant line that had tree-sized members in the Carboniferous?
117496.e: In the Carboniferous the horsetail family included Calamites up to 20 metres tall. Today only the herbaceous genus Equisetum remains.
117496.m: Horsetails are the last members of an ancient plant line.

117497.q: Why is the term “living fossil” controversial in biology?
a: These species have also continued to evolve genetically
There are no ancient plant lines
The term only applies to animals
117497.e: The shape can stay similar over a long time, but the genes and adaptations keep changing. Today such species are often called relict species.

117498.q: Since which geological period have fossil ginkgo leaves that closely resemble today's ginkgo been recorded?
117498.e: Fossil ginkgo species from the Jurassic are very similar to today's Ginkgo biloba. The genus has therefore survived for well over 150 million years.
117498.m: Ginkgos have existed since the Jurassic.

117499.q: Around what time did Louis Pasteur carry out his experiments with swan-neck flasks?
117499.e: Pasteur published the results in the early 1860s. They settled a years-long dispute in the Paris Academy of Sciences.
117499.m: Pasteur’s swan-neck flask experiments date from around 1860.

117500.q: Why did the boiled nutrient solution in the swan-neck flask stay free of germs even though the flask was open?
a: Dust and germs were caught in the curved neck
The neck was sealed with wax
There was a vacuum in the flask
117500.e: Air could flow in freely through the S-shaped neck. But dust particles with germs settled in the damp bend and did not reach the solution.
117500.m: The curved neck let air in but held the germs back.

117501.q: What happened when Pasteur broke off the neck of a swan-neck flask?
a: The solution soon turned cloudy because of microorganisms
The solution stayed clear for ever
117501.e: Without the neck, dust and germs fell straight into the nutrient solution. After only a short time microorganisms grew in it.
117501.m: Without the swan neck, germs got in and the solution spoiled.

117502.q: Which objection from his opponents did Pasteur dispose of by leaving his flasks open?
a: That fresh air was needed for new life
117502.e: The supporters of spontaneous generation believed that a life force in the air was missing in sealed vessels. In Pasteur’s flasks the air had free access, yet no life appeared.
117502.m: Pasteur’s open flasks showed that air alone does not produce life.

117503.q: Which idea did Pasteur refute with his swan-neck flasks?
117503.e: Supporters of spontaneous generation such as Félix-Archimède Pouchet believed that microorganisms arose by themselves in nutrient solutions. Pasteur showed that they are carried in from the air.

117504.q: What did Pasteur do with the nutrient solution in the flask at the start of the experiment?
a: He cooled it to zero degrees
117504.e: Boiling killed all the germs present. After that only life entering anew could cloud the solution.
117504.m: Pasteur first boiled the nutrient solution.

117505.q: What did Pasteur observe when he briefly opened germ-free flasks on a glacier near Chamonix?
a: Fewer flasks turned cloudy than in the valley
All the flasks turned cloudy at once
117505.e: In the clean high-mountain air far fewer germs floated than in the town. This showed that the cloudiness depends on germs in the air.
117505.m: In pure mountain air there are fewer germs than in a town.

117506.q: Which philosopher of antiquity held the doctrine that some animals arise from mud or rot?
117506.e: Aristotle described, for example, that eels and insects arose from mud and rotting material. His authority kept the idea alive for almost 2000 years.
117506.m: Even Aristotle believed in spontaneous generation.

117507.q: Who showed in 1668, using covered meat, that maggots hatch from fly eggs?
117507.e: Redi put meat in open vessels and in vessels covered with gauze. Maggots appeared only where flies could lay their eggs.
117507.m: Redi proved that maggots come from fly eggs.

117508.q: Which Italian researcher showed in the 18th century that broths boiled for a long time and sealed by melting stay free of germs?
117508.e: Spallanzani boiled broths for a long time and sealed the vessels airtight. Opponents objected that he had thereby destroyed the life force of the air.
117508.m: Spallanzani kept broths free of germs by long boiling and tight sealing.

117509.q: In 1748 John Needham believed he had proved spontaneous generation with boiled mutton broth. What was his mistake?
a: He boiled the broth too briefly, so germs survived
He used too little meat for the broth
He kept the broth too cold
He sealed the vessels too early
117509.e: Needham boiled the broth only briefly and sealed it with corks. Surviving germs multiplied, which he took for spontaneous generation.
117509.m: Needham’s experiments seemed to support spontaneous generation, but were imprecise.

117510.q: In the 17th century it was said that mice arose from dirty laundry and wheat in 21 days. What actually happened?
a: Mice were attracted by the wheat
The sweat in the laundry produced life
Warmth made mice arise from dust
117510.e: The recipe comes from the scholar Jan Baptist van Helmont. The mice in fact came from outside and were attracted by the food.
117510.m: Van Helmont’s mouse recipe shows the old belief in spontaneous generation.

117511.q: What is the principle called that living things arise only from living things?
117511.e: Biogenesis is the opposite of spontaneous generation. Abiogenesis refers to the origin of life from non-living matter.
117511.m: According to biogenesis, life arises only from life.

117512.q: Why did some hay infusions turn cloudy despite boiling?
a: Heat-resistant bacterial spores survived the boiling
The hay contained sugar, which turned cloudy
The steam brought germs along from the water
117512.e: In the 1870s John Tyndall recognised heat-resistant resting forms of bacteria. He developed repeated heating with pauses in between, called tyndallisation.

117513.q: What is the Latin technical term for spontaneous generation?
117513.e: Generatio spontanea means “spontaneous origin”. The term refers to the idea that life arises by itself from non-living matter.
117513.m: Spontaneous generation is called generatio spontanea in Latin.

117514.q: With which solution did Semmelweis have hands disinfected?
117514.e: Semmelweis chose chlorinated lime because it removed the smell of corpses from the hands. Carbolic acid was introduced later by Joseph Lister.
117514.m: Semmelweis relied on washing hands with chlorinated lime.

117515.q: Which event gave Semmelweis the decisive idea in 1847?
a: The death of his colleague Kolletschka
A fire in the Vienna hospital
117515.e: Jakob Kolletschka injured himself during a post-mortem and died of blood poisoning. His illness resembled childbed fever, which led Semmelweis to conclude that it was transmitted.
117515.m: Kolletschka’s death put Semmelweis on the right track.

117516.q: What did Semmelweis notice when he compared the two maternity wards in the Vienna hospital?
a: Far more women died in the doctors’ ward than in the midwives’ ward
The same number of women died in both
More women died in the midwives’ ward
117516.e: In the first ward worked doctors and students who also dissected corpses. The death rate there was several times higher than in the midwives’ ward.
117516.m: The comparison of two wards gave Semmelweis his most important clue.

117517.q: What honorary name did Semmelweis later receive?
117517.e: His hygiene rules greatly reduced the number of deaths from childbed fever. But this was recognised only after his death.
117517.m: Semmelweis is called the saviour of mothers.

117518.q: In which city was Ignaz Semmelweis born in 1818?
117518.e: Semmelweis was born in the Tabán district of Ofen. Ofen is today part of Budapest.
117518.m: Semmelweis came from Ofen, today’s Budapest.

117519.q: What does the “Semmelweis reflex” refer to?
a: The reflex rejection of new findings
Pulling the hand back at pain
117519.e: The term recalls that many doctors rejected Semmelweis’s findings because they did not fit their teachings. It describes in general the fending off of inconvenient evidence.
117519.m: The Semmelweis reflex is the rejection of new, inconvenient findings.

117520.q: How did Ignaz Semmelweis die in 1865?
a: In a mental hospital, of blood poisoning
117520.e: Semmelweis was committed to an institution near Vienna and died there after a few days. The cause was probably an infected wound.
117520.m: Semmelweis probably died in 1865 of blood poisoning.

117521.q: To roughly what value did the death rate in Semmelweis’s ward fall after his rule was introduced?
117521.e: Before the measure, over 10 per cent of the women died in some months. Afterwards the rate fell to about the level of the midwives’ ward.
117521.m: Disinfecting the hands lowered the death rate drastically.

117522.q: Which teacher of Robert Koch formulated basic ideas about pathogens as early as 1840?
117522.e: In a work on miasmas and contagia, Henle demanded that living pathogens be demonstrated as the cause. Koch, his student in Göttingen, put this into practice experimentally.
117522.m: Henle laid the foundation for Koch’s postulates.

117523.q: What does the first Henle-Koch postulate demand?
a: The pathogen can be found in every case of the disease
The pathogen lives only in animals
The pathogen is visible to the naked eye
117523.e: The suspected pathogen must be present in all people who have this disease. Only then does it come into question as the cause.
117523.m: A pathogen must be found in every sick person.

117524.q: What does the second Henle-Koch postulate demand?
a: The pathogen is isolated and grown in pure culture
The pathogen is counted in the blood
The pathogen is killed with antibiotics
117524.e: The pathogen must be able to multiply on a culture medium, separate from the sick person. This rules out other microbes as the cause.
117524.m: The pathogen must be able to be grown in pure culture.

117525.q: What does the third Henle-Koch postulate demand?
a: The pure culture causes the same disease in a healthy test animal
The sick person recovers at once
The pathogen is found in water
117525.e: If the pure culture is transferred to a healthy, susceptible animal, the same disease must arise. This proves the causal link.
117525.m: The pure culture must cause the disease again.

117526.q: Which demand was later often added as a fourth postulate?
a: The pathogen is isolated again from the infected animal
The pathogen is described in a book
The disease occurs only in winter
The pathogen has a cell nucleus
117526.e: The same pathogen must be recovered from the artificially infected animal. This closes the circle of proof.
117526.m: The pathogen must be isolated again from the test animal.

117527.q: Which observation contradicts the first postulate in its strict form?
a: There are healthy carriers of a pathogen
Some diseases run a quick course
117527.e: With cholera or typhoid there are people who carry the pathogen without becoming ill. Koch himself therefore had to relax his demand.
117527.m: Healthy carriers show the limits of the postulates.

117528.q: Why can the postulates not be applied literally to viruses?
a: Viruses multiply only in living cells
Viruses die at once in the air
117528.e: Viruses cannot be grown on artificial culture media. Adapted criteria were therefore developed for them.
117528.m: Viruses need living cells and do not fit the postulates exactly.

117529.q: Which bacterial pathogen does not fully meet the postulates because it cannot be grown on an artificial culture medium?
117529.e: Mycobacterium leprae was discovered in 1873 by Gerhard Armauer Hansen. To this day it cannot be cultivated on culture media.
117529.m: The leprosy pathogen does not grow on artificial culture media.

117530.q: Which Latin motto is linked with Rudolf Virchow?
117530.e: Virchow popularised the saying in 1855: every cell comes from a cell. In doing so he contradicted the idea that cells arise from a formless mass.
117530.m: Every cell comes from a cell.

117531.q: What is the title of Virchow’s main work of 1858, which traces diseases back to disturbances of cells?
117531.e: Virchow explained diseases as changes in the cells. In doing so he replaced the old doctrine of the humours.

117532.q: Virchow described how a clot of blood carried along blocks a blood vessel. What is this process called?
117532.e: In an embolism a clot is carried along with the blood and blocks a vessel at another place. The term was coined by Rudolf Virchow.
117532.m: The term embolism goes back to Virchow.

117533.q: Which three factors for the formation of blood clots does the “Virchow’s triad” sum up?
a: Vessel wall, blood flow, blood composition
117533.e: Damage to the vessel wall, slowed blood flow and altered clotting favour thrombosis. The triad is still used in medicine today.
117533.m: Virchow’s triad explains how blood clots form.

117534.q: Which political term did Virchow coin in 1873 as a member of parliament?
117534.e: Virchow called the conflict between the Prussian state and the Catholic Church a “Kulturkampf”. He was a liberal member of parliament and an opponent of Bismarck.
117534.m: The word Kulturkampf comes from Virchow.

117535.q: What cause did Virchow see in 1848 for a typhus epidemic in Upper Silesia?
117535.e: In his report Virchow demanded education, freedom and prosperity for the population. He is therefore regarded as the founder of social medicine.
117535.m: Virchow recognised social causes of epidemics.

117536.q: Which meat inspection was introduced in Prussia at Virchow’s urging?
117536.e: Virchow studied trichinae, roundworms in pork. The compulsory inspection of meat reduced the number of cases of illness.
117536.m: Trichinae inspection goes back to Virchow’s efforts.

117537.q: Which building project in Berlin did Virchow promote as a city councillor?
117537.e: Together with James Hobrecht, Virchow pressed for a sewage system with sewage fields. This clearly improved the hygiene of the growing city.
117537.m: Virchow fought for a sewer system in Berlin.

117538.q: How did Virchow interpret the bones of the Neanderthal?
a: As the diseased bones of a modern human
As the bones of an ape
As the bones of a bear
As a forgery made of plaster
117538.e: Virchow explained the striking features by diseases such as rickets. Today the Neanderthal is regarded as a human form of its own.
117538.m: Virchow wrongly took the Neanderthal for a sick modern human.

117539.q: What term did Claude Bernard coin for the stable environment of the body’s cells?
117539.e: Bernard recognised that the body keeps blood and tissue fluid constant despite outside fluctuations. This idea was later called homeostasis.
117539.m: The inner environment of the body stays remarkably constant.

117540.q: What is the ability of the body to keep internal conditions such as temperature and blood sugar constant called?
117540.e: The term homeostasis was coined in the 1920s by Walter Cannon. He built on Claude Bernard’s idea of the inner environment.
117540.m: Homeostasis means that the body keeps its inside constant.

117541.q: Which storage substance did Claude Bernard discover in the liver?
117541.e: Bernard showed that the liver stores sugar as glycogen and releases it to the blood when needed. In doing so he refuted the view that only plants could form sugar.
117541.m: The liver stores sugar as glycogen.

117542.q: Which way of working did Claude Bernard put at the centre of medicine?
a: The experiment with hypothesis and testing
117542.e: In his work of 1865 Bernard describes how to set up a hypothesis and test it with experiments. He is regarded as the founder of experimental medicine.

117543.q: What did Bernard show about the arrow poison curare?
a: It blocks the transmission from nerve to muscle
It destroys the red blood cells
117543.e: In poisoned animals the nerves and the muscles could each still be excited on their own. Only the junction between the two was disturbed.
117543.m: Curare interrupts the connection between nerve and muscle.

117544.q: Which task of pancreatic juice did Bernard demonstrate?
117544.e: Bernard showed that the juice of the pancreas breaks down fats. It also helps in the digestion of starch and protein.

117545.q: How does carbon monoxide act according to Bernard’s investigations?
a: It displaces oxygen from the blood pigment
It blocks the air sacs of the lungs
117545.e: Carbon monoxide binds much more strongly to haemoglobin than oxygen does. The blood can then hardly transport any oxygen.
117545.m: Carbon monoxide blocks the transport of oxygen in the blood.

117546.q: In which century did the French physiologist Claude Bernard work?
117546.e: Claude Bernard lived from 1813 to 1878. He worked at the Collège de France in Paris, at first as an assistant to François Magendie.
117546.m: Claude Bernard worked in the 19th century.

117547.q: What did Bernard discover about the regulation of blood vessels?
a: Nerves control the width of the blood vessels
The heart alone determines the width of the vessels
117547.e: Bernard showed that cutting certain nerves widens vessels and warms the skin. In this way he discovered the vasomotor nerves.
117547.m: Vessel nerves regulate how wide the blood vessels are.

117548.q: Which principle did Helmholtz formulate in 1847 in his work “On the Conservation of Force”?
117548.e: Helmholtz showed mathematically that energy is only converted, but not created or destroyed. By “force” he meant what we call energy today.
117548.m: Helmholtz formulated the law of the conservation of energy.

117549.q: Which instrument did Helmholtz invent in 1850 for examining the back of the eye?
117549.e: With the ophthalmoscope the retina of a living person became visible for the first time. Eye medicine took a great leap forward.
117549.m: The ophthalmoscope makes the retina visible.

117550.q: Roughly how fast does a frog’s nerve conduct signals according to Helmholtz’s measurements around 1850?
117550.e: It had been assumed that nerve signals were too fast to measure. Helmholtz determined about 25 to 40 metres per second in a frog’s nerve.
117550.m: Nerve signals are much slower than light.

117551.q: What does the Young-Helmholtz theory state?
a: Colour vision is based on three kinds of receptors
117551.e: Thomas Young and Helmholtz assumed three types of receptor for red, green and blue. Today we know the three types of cone in the retina.
117551.m: Colour vision is based on three types of receptor.

117552.q: What is Helmholtz’s work “On the Sensations of Tone” of 1863 about?
117552.e: Helmholtz explained timbre through overtones and hearing through resonance in the cochlea of the inner ear. The work founded physiological acoustics.
117552.m: Helmholtz researched how we perceive sounds.

117553.q: In which subjects did Hermann von Helmholtz carry out successful research?
117553.e: Helmholtz studied energy, electricity and acoustics, but also seeing, hearing and nerve conduction. He is regarded as one of the most many-sided researchers of the 19th century.

117554.q: What did Helmholtz first work as, because it paid for his medical studies?
117554.e: Studying at a military medical school in Berlin was free. In return Helmholtz then had to serve for some years as a doctor in the Prussian army.
117554.m: Helmholtz began his career as a military doctor.

117555.q: How did Helmholtz explain the focusing of the eye on near objects?
117555.e: In near vision the fibres that hold the lens relax and it becomes rounder. This adjustment is called accommodation.
117555.m: In near vision the lens of the eye becomes more curved.

117556.q: Which law of plant growth is linked with Liebig?
117556.e: The scarcest nutrient limits growth, even if others are present in plenty. Carl Sprengel had formulated the idea earlier, and Liebig made it known.

117557.q: Which view of plant nutrition did Liebig hold against the humus theory?
117557.e: Liebig showed that plants take up inorganic substances such as potassium, phosphorus and nitrogen compounds. Mineral fertiliser is based on this.

117558.q: Which food product did Justus von Liebig bring onto the market in the 19th century?
117558.e: Liebig’s meat extract was made from 1865 in Fray Bentos in Uruguay, where there were very many cattle. It served as a strong broth that keeps.
117558.m: Liebig developed a meat extract that keeps.

117559.q: Which piece of laboratory equipment bears Liebig’s name although he did not invent it?
117559.e: The condenser with a water-cooled jacket was already known earlier. Liebig popularised it so strongly that it is named after him today.
117559.m: The Liebig condenser became famous through Liebig.

117560.q: At which university did Liebig set up a pioneering teaching laboratory from 1824?
117560.e: In Giessen Liebig let students experiment themselves. The model was copied all over the world.
117560.m: Liebig’s laboratory in Giessen became a model.

117561.q: What is Justus von Liebig especially important for in organic chemistry?
a: He made the determination of the elements in organic substances precise and quick
He drew up the periodic table
He was the first to make plastic
117561.e: With his potash bulb apparatus Liebig determined the carbon content of a sample very precisely. This made it possible to establish the composition of organic compounds reliably.

117562.q: What does the law of the minimum, named after Liebig, state?
a: The nutrient that is scarcest limits growth
Plants grow best with as little fertiliser as possible
The most common nutrient determines growth
Plants need only a single nutrient
117562.e: If phosphorus, for example, is missing, even plenty of nitrogen does not help. This is often compared with a barrel whose shortest stave determines how high the water stands.

117563.q: Which substance did Liebig discover in 1831, at about the same time as other chemists?
117563.e: Eugène Soubeiran and Samuel Guthrie also made chloroform in 1831. Later it was used as an anaesthetic.
117563.m: Chloroform was discovered several times independently in 1831.

117564.q: What does the “von” in the name Justus von Liebig mean?
a: He was raised to the nobility for his services
He came from a place called Liebig
He was the son of a prince
117564.e: The Grand Duke of Hesse made Liebig a baron in 1845. He was born the son of a Darmstadt druggist and dealer in dyes.
117564.m: Liebig was ennobled for his services.

117565.q: In which year did Friedrich Wöhler make urea artificially?
