117565.e: Wöhler reported the synthesis in 1828. It is regarded as a turning point of organic chemistry.

117566.q: From which salt did urea form in Wöhler’s experiment?
117566.e: Wöhler wanted to make ammonium cyanate and obtained urea on evaporating it. Both substances have the same molecular formula.
117566.m: Urea was formed from ammonium cyanate.

117567.q: Which doctrine was shaken by the synthesis of urea?
117567.e: According to vitalism, organic substances could arise only in living things through a life force. Wöhler made such a substance in the laboratory.
117567.m: The synthesis of urea shook the belief in a life force.

117568.q: To which chemist did Wöhler write that he could make urea “without needing a kidney for it”?
117568.e: Berzelius was Wöhler’s teacher in Stockholm and the leading authority in chemistry. The letter of 1828 became famous.
117568.m: Wöhler reported his success to Berzelius.

117569.q: What is the chemical formula of urea?
117569.e: Urea consists of a carbonyl group with two amino groups. It is the most important end product of the breakdown of nitrogen in mammals.

117570.q: What is urea made from industrially today?
117570.e: Ammonia and carbon dioxide react under pressure and heat to form urea. It is one of the most important nitrogen fertilisers in the world.
117570.m: Urea is made industrially from ammonia and carbon dioxide.

117571.q: What was special about Wöhler’s synthesis of urea?
a: A substance from living things was made from non-living starting materials
Urea was found in urine for the first time
It was the first explosion in a laboratory
Urea was turned into a metal
117571.e: Urea was known only from the urine of living things. In 1828 Wöhler made it from an inorganic salt.
117571.m: Wöhler made an organic substance in the laboratory.

117572.q: What is urea used for today in large quantities?
a: As a building material for houses
117572.e: Urea contains a lot of nitrogen, which plants need in order to grow. It is one of the most important fertilisers in the world and is also found in skin creams and AdBlue.
117572.m: Urea is an important nitrogen fertiliser.

117573.q: Which botanist explained in 1838 that all plants are made up of cells?
117573.e: Schleiden published “Contributions to Phytogenesis” in 1838. He saw the cell as the basic building block of the plant.
117573.m: Schleiden recognised cells as the building blocks of plants.

117574.q: Who extended cell theory to animals in 1839?
117574.e: In his “Microscopical Researches”, Schwann showed that animal tissues too consist of cells. This made the cell the unit of all life.
117574.m: Schwann showed that animals too are made of cells.

117575.q: What error was there in Schleiden and Schwann’s cell theory?
a: That cells arose from a formless mass
117575.e: Both assumed that new cells formed from a cytoblastema, similar to crystals. That cells arise by division was recognised only later.
117575.m: Schleiden and Schwann were wrong about how new cells arise.

117576.q: Which principle describes how new cells arise?
a: Every cell arises from a cell
Cells grow like crystals out of a liquid
117576.e: In 1855 Rudolf Virchow made the saying “Omnis cellula e cellula” known. New cells arise by the division of existing cells and not from a formless mass.
117576.m: Every cell descends from another cell.

117577.q: Who described the cell nucleus in 1831 as a regular component of plant cells?
117577.e: The Scottish botanist Robert Brown examined orchid cells. He gave the nucleus its name.
117577.m: Robert Brown named the cell nucleus in 1831.

117578.q: Which cells are named after Theodor Schwann?
117578.e: Schwann cells surround the nerve fibres in the peripheral nervous system. Many form an insulating myelin sheath.
117578.m: Schwann cells wrap around nerve fibres.

117579.q: In 1836 Theodor Schwann discovered an enzyme in gastric juice that breaks down proteins. What is it called?
117579.e: Pepsin breaks down proteins in the acidic stomach. Amylase breaks down starch, lipase fats, and insulin is a hormone.
117579.m: Schwann discovered the stomach enzyme pepsin.

117580.q: Who gave cells their name in 1665 when he looked at cork under the microscope?
117580.e: Robert Hooke saw many small chambers in a thin slice of cork and called them “cells”. Only almost 200 years later did cell theory arise from this.
117580.m: Robert Hooke coined the term cell in 1665.

117581.q: At which water pump in London did John Snow identify the source of a cholera outbreak in 1854?
a: At the pump in Broad Street
At the pump by the Tower
At the pump in Trafalgar Square
117581.e: Most of the deaths in the district of Soho were around this pump. Its water had been contaminated by a nearby cesspit.
117581.m: The Broad Street pump was the source of the cholera outbreak of 1854.

117582.q: What did John Snow have removed from the suspect pump in 1854?
a: The stone cover of the well
117582.e: Without the handle nobody could pump water any more. By this time, however, the outbreak was already dying down.
117582.m: Snow had the pump handle taken off.

117583.q: By which method did Snow show the connection between the pump and the disease?
a: With a map of the deaths
117583.e: Snow marked each death as a stroke on a map of the town. The clustering around the pump was clearly visible.
117583.m: Snow’s map is regarded as a milestone of epidemiology.

117584.q: Which explanation of cholera was prevalent in Snow’s time?
117584.e: According to the miasma theory, epidemics spread through foul, bad air. Snow, by contrast, suspected transmission through water.
117584.m: In Snow’s time people believed in bad air that made people ill.

117585.q: What difference did Snow compare between two London water companies?
a: Where they took their Thames water from
117585.e: One company pumped water from a polluted stretch of the Thames, the other from further upstream. Far more people died among the customers of the first.
117585.m: Snow compared households with different sources of water.

117586.q: In which other field of medicine was John Snow a pioneer?
117586.e: Snow studied the dosage of ether and chloroform. He became one of the best-known anaesthetists in England.
117586.m: Snow was also a pioneer of anaesthesia.

117587.q: Which researcher made the cholera pathogen world-famous in 1883 and 1884?
117587.e: Robert Koch demonstrated the comma-shaped pathogen in Egypt and India. Filippo Pacini had already described it in 1854, but that went unnoticed.
117587.m: Robert Koch made the cholera pathogen known.

117588.q: By which route does cholera mainly spread?
117588.e: The bacteria are passed out in the stool and get into drinking water. A clean water supply is therefore the best protection.
117588.m: Cholera is transmitted mainly through polluted water.

117589.q: Why did the workers of a brewery near Broad Street hardly fall ill?
a: They drank beer or water from their own well
117589.e: The brewery had its own well and the workers were given beer. So they did not drink water from the contaminated pump.
117589.m: Anyone who did not drink the pump water stayed healthy.

117590.q: Who was the captain of HMS Beagle on Darwin’s voyage?
117590.e: FitzRoy was looking for an educated companion for the long voyage and took Darwin along. Later he became a pioneer of weather forecasting.

117591.q: Which birds of the Galápagos are today regarded as a prime example of the origin of new species?
117591.e: Darwin’s finches descend from a common ancestor species. On the islands they developed different beak shapes, depending on food.
117591.m: Darwin’s finches show how one species becomes many.

117592.q: What was the main task of the Beagle on this voyage?
a: To survey the coasts of South America
117592.e: The British Navy needed accurate sea charts for trade and navigation. Darwin accompanied the survey as a naturalist.
117592.m: The Beagle was meant above all to survey coasts.

117593.q: Which main work did Darwin publish in 1859, a good twenty years after the Beagle voyage?
117593.e: In “On the Origin of Species” Darwin set out his theory of natural selection. He collected many of the ideas for it on the voyage with the Beagle.
117593.m: Darwin’s “On the Origin of Species” appeared in 1859.

117594.q: Which geological work by Charles Lyell did Darwin read during the voyage?
117594.e: Lyell explained the shape of the Earth through slow processes that are still at work today. This sharpened Darwin’s eye for very long periods of time.
117594.m: Lyell’s Principles of Geology shaped Darwin’s thinking on the voyage.

117595.q: Which fossil giant animals did Darwin find in Argentina?
117595.e: At Punta Alta Darwin dug out the bones of large extinct mammals. He noticed their similarity to present-day sloths and armadillos.
117595.m: In Argentina Darwin found fossils of giant sloths.

117596.q: What did Darwin observe in 1835 after the earthquake of Concepción in Chile?
117596.e: Beds of mussels lay above the waterline after the quake. Darwin concluded that mountains can arise through many such upheavals.

117597.q: How did Darwin explain the origin of atolls?
a: Corals grow upwards while a volcanic island sinks
Atolls are the craters of extinct volcanoes
Waves heap up sand in a ring
Meteorites punched rings into the seabed
117597.e: A coral reef grows around a volcanic island. If the island slowly sinks, the corals keep growing upwards until only a ring with a lagoon remains.
117597.m: Darwin explained atolls through sinking islands and growing corals.

117598.q: Roughly how long did the voyage of HMS Beagle with Darwin on board last?
117598.e: The Beagle set out at the end of 1831 and returned to England in October 1836. Darwin spent a large part of the time on land in South America.
117598.m: Darwin’s voyage with the Beagle lasted about five years.

117599.q: Where does blood formation mainly take place in adults?
117599.e: In adults the red bone marrow of flat bones such as the pelvis, breastbone and vertebral bodies forms the blood cells.
117599.m: Adults make their blood cells in the red bone marrow.

117600.q: In the middle of pregnancy, which organ is the most important site of blood formation in the foetus?
117600.e: After the yolk sac, the foetal liver (together with the spleen) takes over blood formation, before the bone marrow dominates towards the end of pregnancy.
117600.m: In the foetus, for a time it is mainly the liver that makes blood.

117601.q: Which two vitamins does the bone marrow especially need for DNA synthesis during blood formation?
117601.e: Without vitamin B12 or folic acid the precursor cells cannot divide properly; this causes anaemia with oversized red blood cells.
117601.m: Blood formation needs vitamin B12 and folic acid.

117602.q: Which group of blood cells do B cells and T cells belong to?
117602.e: B and T cells are lymphocytes, a subgroup of the white blood cells. They come from the lymphoid line of the blood stem cells.
117602.m: B and T cells are lymphocytes.

117603.q: What are blood stem cells mainly collected for in medicine?
a: For stem cell transplants, for example for leukaemia
117603.e: Blood stem cells can rebuild destroyed bone marrow. In the lab they are recognised by surface markers such as CD34.
117603.m: Blood stem cells can rebuild a whole bone marrow.

117604.q: Why do people sometimes receive a growth factor such as G-CSF after chemotherapy?
a: So that the white blood cells recover faster
So that the hair grows back faster
So that the tumour shrinks faster
So that the blood clots less
117604.e: Chemotherapy damages the bone marrow. G-CSF stimulates the formation of neutrophil granulocytes, an important group of white blood cells, and so lowers the risk of infection.
117604.m: G-CSF increases the formation of neutrophil granulocytes.

117605.q: Which hormone mainly controls the formation of platelets?
117605.e: Thrombopoietin is made mainly in the liver and stimulates the megakaryocytes to form platelets.
117605.m: Thrombopoietin stimulates the formation of platelets.

117606.q: During childhood, what happens to the blood-forming marrow in the shafts of the long bones?
a: It is mostly replaced by fatty marrow
117606.e: In newborns almost all bone marrow is red; later, in the long bones, it largely turns into yellow fatty marrow.
117606.m: During childhood, red marrow in long bones turns into fatty marrow.

117607.q: In which organ is erythropoietin mainly made in adults?
117607.e: Specialised cells in the renal cortex make about 90 per cent of erythropoietin; only a small part comes from the liver.
117607.m: In adults, erythropoietin comes mainly from the kidney.

117608.q: Which stimulus increases the release of erythropoietin?
a: Lack of oxygen in the tissue
117608.e: In hypoxia the transcription factor HIF is stabilised, and it activates the erythropoietin gene.
117608.m: Lack of oxygen increases erythropoietin release.

117609.q: What did Kaelin, Ratcliffe and Semenza receive the 2019 Nobel Prize in Medicine for?
117609.e: They worked out the HIF signalling pathway, which cells use to measure oxygen levels and, among other things, control erythropoietin production.
117609.m: The 2019 Nobel Prize honoured research into how cells sense oxygen.

117610.q: How is erythropoietin for medicines mainly produced today?
a: By genetic engineering with cell cultures
From the kidneys of slaughtered animals
117610.e: Since the EPO gene was decoded in the 1980s, cell cultures have produced the hormone by genetic engineering. It is used mainly for anaemia caused by kidney failure.
117610.m: Medical EPO is produced by genetic engineering.

117611.q: Why is erythropoietin misused as a doping substance in endurance sport?
a: It increases the number of red blood cells and so oxygen transport
It reduces the feeling of pain
It directly speeds up fat burning
117611.e: More red blood cells carry more oxygen to the muscles, which increases endurance performance.
117611.m: EPO doping increases the blood's capacity to carry oxygen.

117612.q: Which class of substances does erythropoietin belong to?
117612.e: Erythropoietin is a protein of 165 amino acids with sugar chains attached, so it is a glycoprotein.

117613.q: Why does erythropoietin production increase during a stay high in the mountains?
a: Because of the lower partial pressure of oxygen
Because of the stronger UV radiation
117613.e: At altitude the partial pressure of oxygen is lower; the body registers the shortage and releases more erythropoietin.
117613.m: High in the mountains, the low oxygen pressure stimulates EPO production.

117614.q: Which serious side effect can too great a rise in red blood cells from erythropoietin have?
a: Thrombosis because the blood is thick
117614.e: Many red blood cells increase the viscosity of the blood, which can encourage thrombosis, heart attacks and strokes.
117614.m: Too many red blood cells make the blood thick and encourage thrombosis.

117615.q: Why is the haematocrit often hardly changed immediately after acute heavy bleeding?
a: Cells and plasma are lost in the same proportion
The bone marrow replaces the cells immediately
The spleen stores all the red blood cells
The haematocrit only measures the platelets
117615.e: Only when tissue fluid flows in or infusions are given is the blood diluted and the haematocrit falls.
117615.m: After acute bleeding the haematocrit only falls after a delay.

117616.q: Roughly in what range is the haematocrit in healthy adult men?
117616.e: In men it is typically around 40 to 50 per cent, in women somewhat lower.
117616.m: In men, cells make up about 40 to 50 per cent of the blood.

117617.q: How is the haematocrit classically measured in the lab?
a: By spinning blood in a tube in a centrifuge
By weighing a drop of blood
117617.e: When centrifuged, the cells settle at the bottom; the ratio of the cell column to the total height gives the haematocrit.
117617.m: Centrifuged blood shows the haematocrit as the height of the cell column.

117618.q: How does the haematocrit change with severe lack of fluid?
117618.e: If plasma water is lost, the cells remain and their share of the volume increases.
117618.m: When the body lacks water, the haematocrit rises.

117619.q: Which haematocrit limit did the cycling federation UCI introduce in 1997?
117619.e: Because of EPO misuse, riders with a haematocrit over 50 per cent were not allowed to start, to protect their health.
117619.m: From 1997, cycling barred riders with a haematocrit over 50 per cent.

117620.q: As a rule of thumb, the haematocrit in per cent is about three times the haemoglobin value in g/dl. Which haematocrit fits 14 g/dl of haemoglobin?
117620.e: 3 · 14 makes 42, so the haematocrit is about 42 per cent.
117620.m: The haematocrit is roughly three times the haemoglobin value in g/dl.

117621.q: Which blood components practically alone determine the haematocrit?
117621.e: Red blood cells make up well over 99 per cent of the cell volume in the blood; white blood cells and platelets hardly count.
117621.m: The haematocrit mainly reflects the share of red blood cells.

117622.q: How does the blood change if the bone marrow abnormally makes too many red blood cells?
a: It no longer clots at all
117622.e: In diseases such as polycythaemia vera the haematocrit rises sharply. The thicker blood flows more slowly and the risk of blood clots rises.
117622.m: Too many red blood cells make the blood thick.

a: A young red blood cell without a nucleus
117623.e: Reticulocytes are young red blood cells that have already lost their nucleus but still contain remains of RNA.
117623.m: Reticulocytes are young red blood cells without a nucleus.

117624.q: Which component is still present in the reticulocyte but no longer in the mature red blood cell?
117624.e: After staining, the RNA remains form a net-like pattern that gives the reticulocyte its name.
117624.m: Reticulocytes still contain remains of ribosomal RNA.

117625.q: Where are reticulocytes, that is young red blood cells, formed?
117625.e: In adults, red blood cells form in the red bone marrow. As reticulocytes they pass into the blood and finish maturing there.
117625.m: Red blood cells form in the bone marrow.

117626.q: Roughly how long does a red blood cell live in the blood?
117626.e: Red blood cells live about 120 days and are then broken down, mainly in the spleen. That is why the bone marrow must constantly make new ones.
117626.m: Red blood cells live about four months.

117627.q: What does a clearly raised reticulocyte count after blood loss show?
a: That the bone marrow is increasing blood formation
That the bone marrow is failing
That too little erythropoietin is being made
117627.e: If reticulocytes rise, the bone marrow is reacting to the loss by forming more new red blood cells.
117627.m: Many reticulocytes show active new blood formation.

117628.q: What does a very low reticulocyte count in anaemia show?
a: The bone marrow is making too few new red blood cells
The bone marrow is working especially hard
The body has just lost a lot of blood
The red blood cells are living longer than normal
117628.e: Reticulocytes are freshly made red blood cells. If there are hardly any, the bone marrow is not making enough new ones.
117628.m: Few reticulocytes mean little new blood formation.

117629.q: Which hormone from the kidney stimulates the formation of new red blood cells?
117629.e: When oxygen is short, the kidney makes more erythropoietin. The bone marrow then produces more reticulocytes. EPO is also known as a doping substance.
117629.m: EPO from the kidney promotes blood formation.

117630.q: What do human red blood cells lose as they mature?
117630.e: The precursors of red blood cells push out their nucleus. This leaves more room for haemoglobin, which carries oxygen.
117630.m: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus.

117631.q: Which mutation causes sickle cell anaemia?
a: Valine replaces glutamic acid in the beta globin chain
A missing gene for the alpha chain
A doubling of the iron atom in haem
A defect in the erythropoietin receptor
117631.e: A point mutation leads to glutamic acid being swapped for valine at position 6 of the beta globin chain; this produces haemoglobin S.
117631.m: In sickle cell anaemia, valine replaces glutamic acid in the beta chain.

117632.q: Under which condition do sickle cells become particularly deformed?
117632.e: Deoxygenated haemoglobin S clumps together into long fibres that bend the cell into a sickle shape.
117632.m: Lack of oxygen makes sickle cells deform.

117633.q: How is sickle cell anaemia inherited?
117633.e: Usually only people with two altered copies of the gene are ill; carriers with one copy usually have no symptoms.
117633.m: Sickle cell anaemia is inherited in an autosomal recessive way.

117634.q: Against which disease does carrying the sickle cell gene give partial protection?
117634.e: Heterozygous carriers less often become seriously ill with malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum, which is why the gene is common in malaria regions.
117634.m: The sickle cell gene partly protects carriers against severe malaria.

117635.q: What is a typical acute complication of sickle cell anaemia?
a: Painful crises caused by blocked vessels
117635.e: Deformed cells block small vessels, which can cause severe pain and organ damage.
117635.m: Sickle cells block small vessels and trigger pain crises.

117636.q: Why should people with sickle cell anaemia drink plenty and avoid severe cold?
a: So that fewer cells deform and block vessels
Because otherwise they will definitely get malaria
So that more white blood cells form
117636.e: Lack of fluid and cold encourage sickle cells to deform and block small vessels. Drinking plenty and keeping warm can prevent painful crises.
117636.m: Drinking enough and staying warm help prevent sickle cell crises.

117637.q: Which chemist described sickle cell anaemia as a “molecular disease” in 1949?
117637.e: In 1949 Pauling and colleagues showed that haemoglobin S differs from normal haemoglobin in electrophoresis.
117637.m: Linus Pauling called sickle cell anaemia a molecular disease.

117638.q: Which technique does Casgevy, the gene therapy for sickle cell anaemia first approved in 2023, use?
117638.e: With Casgevy, the patient's own blood stem cells are altered with CRISPR-Cas9 so that they make foetal haemoglobin again.
117638.m: Casgevy was the first approved therapy using the CRISPR gene scissors.

117639.q: What is the basic disorder in thalassaemia?
a: Too few globin chains are made
The red blood cells have a nucleus
The haemoglobin no longer binds oxygen
117639.e: In thalassaemias the production of the alpha or beta globin chains is reduced, but their structure is usually normal.
117639.m: In thalassaemia too few globin chains are made.

117640.q: Where does the name “thalassaemia” come from?
a: From the Greek word for sea
From the name of its discoverer, Thalass
From the Latin word for paleness
117640.e: Thalassa means sea; the disease was first described in people from the Mediterranean region.
117640.m: The name thalassaemia is a reminder of the Mediterranean.

117641.q: Which blood picture is typical of thalassaemia?
117641.e: Because there is too little haemoglobin, the red blood cells are microcytic and hypochromic, and target cells are often seen.
117641.m: Thalassaemia shows small, pale red blood cells.

117642.q: What do people with severe beta thalassaemia (thalassaemia major) usually need for their whole life?
117642.e: In the severe form, hardly any working haemoglobin is made. The patients, whose condition used to be called Cooley's anaemia, therefore need donated blood regularly.
117642.m: Severe thalassaemia requires regular blood transfusions.

117643.q: What problem do many blood transfusions cause in thalassaemia patients?
117643.e: Every transfusion brings iron that the body can hardly get rid of; that is why iron chelators such as deferasirox are needed.
117643.m: Many transfusions overload the body with iron.

117644.q: What kind of disease is thalassaemia?
a: A result of too little iron in food
An autoimmune disease of the spleen
117644.e: Thalassaemias are caused by changes in the genes for the globin chains of haemoglobin. They are passed on from parents to children.
117644.m: Thalassaemia is an inherited disorder of haemoglobin production.

117645.q: Which lab value helps to tell mild thalassaemia apart from iron deficiency?
117645.e: Both show small, pale red blood cells, but in thalassaemia the storage iron ferritin is normal or raised, while in iron deficiency it is low.
117645.m: A normal ferritin level argues against iron deficiency.

117646.q: Why is thalassaemia especially common in the Mediterranean region?
a: Carriers are somewhat better protected against malaria
The warm climate damages blood production
The diet contains too little iron
117646.e: People who carry only one altered copy of the gene are hardly ill, but are somewhat better protected against severe malaria. In former malaria areas such as the Mediterranean, the trait therefore spread.
117646.m: Thalassaemia carriers are better protected against malaria.

117647.q: Which protein forms a net of threads at the end of blood clotting that closes the wound?
117647.e: At the end of the clotting cascade, soluble fibrinogen is converted into fibrin. The fibrin threads form a net in which blood cells get caught.
117647.m: Fibrin threads make the blood clot stable.

117648.q: Which blood components are the first to stick to a wound and form a plug?
117648.e: Platelets (thrombocytes) stick to the damaged vessel wall and clump together. Clotting then stabilises the plug with fibrin.
117648.m: Platelets are the first to seal a wound.

117649.q: Which vitamin does the liver need to make several clotting factors?
117649.e: Without vitamin K, the liver cannot finish making several clotting factors. Some blood thinners work by blocking vitamin K.
117649.m: Vitamin K is needed for blood clotting.

117650.q: Which ion is essential for the cascade as clotting factor IV?
117650.e: Calcium ions link clotting factors to phospholipid surfaces, for example on activated platelets; without them the cascade stalls.

117651.q: What is the name of the mostly inherited disease in which blood clots poorly because a clotting factor is missing?
117651.e: In haemophilia, usually factor VIII or IX is missing. Even small injuries can bleed for a long time.

117652.q: Which enzyme dissolves blood clots during fibrinolysis?
117652.e: Plasmin is formed from plasminogen, for example by tissue plasminogen activator, and breaks down fibrin.

117653.q: Why do some people take so-called blood thinners?
a: To prevent blood clots such as thromboses
To make more red blood cells
To make their blood runnier for donating
117653.e: Blood thinners slow down clotting. They prevent dangerous clots from forming in vessels or in the heart, for example after a thrombosis.
117653.m: Blood thinners protect against dangerous blood clots.

117654.q: What happens first to the affected blood vessel when you are injured?
117654.e: The smooth muscle of the vessel wall contracts immediately. That way less blood flows out until platelets and clotting close the wound.

117655.q: What is the main job of thrombin in blood clotting?
117655.e: Thrombin cuts small peptides off fibrinogen, after which the fibrin monomers join together into threads.

117656.q: From which inactive precursor is thrombin formed?
117656.e: Prothrombin (factor II) is split into thrombin (factor IIa) by the prothrombinase complex made of factors Xa and Va.

117657.q: What kind of enzyme is thrombin?
117657.e: Thrombin is a protease: it cuts proteins at specific points, for example fibrinogen. More precisely, it belongs to the serine proteases.

117658.q: Which inhibitor made by the body inactivates thrombin and is strongly boosted by heparin?
117658.e: Antithrombin binds thrombin and factor Xa; heparin speeds up this inhibition many times over.
117658.m: Antithrombin blocks thrombin, and heparin boosts it.

117659.q: Why does the body have, besides thrombin, substances that slow down clotting?
a: So that clots stay limited to the injured spot
So that the blood can carry more oxygen
So that more red blood cells are made
117659.e: Without brakes, clotting would spread through the whole vascular system. Inhibitors such as antithrombin or the protein C system on the vessel wall make sure clots only form where they are needed.
117659.m: Inhibitors keep clotting limited to the wound.

117660.q: Which substance in leech saliva blocks thrombin directly?
117660.e: Hirudin is a strong direct thrombin inhibitor; medicines such as bivalirudin were developed based on it.
117660.m: Hirudin from the leech blocks thrombin.

117661.q: What are medicines that block thrombin used for?
117661.e: Thrombin inhibitors such as dabigatran are among the so-called blood thinners. They protect, for example, against thromboses, pulmonary embolisms or strokes in atrial fibrillation.
117661.m: Thrombin inhibitors protect against dangerous blood clots.

117662.q: Thrombin activates clotting factors, which in turn produce more thrombin. What is such a principle called?
117662.e: Thrombin activates factors V, VIII and XI, among others, which boost its own production. This positive feedback makes clotting start like an avalanche.
117662.m: Thrombin boosts its own production through positive feedback.

117663.q: Which form makes up most cases of haemophilia?
117663.e: Around 80 to 85 per cent of patients have haemophilia A, most of the rest have haemophilia B.
117663.m: Haemophilia A is the most common form.

117664.q: How is bleeding in severe haemophilia usually prevented today?
117664.e: For prevention, factor concentrates are injected into a vein several times a week so that the factor level does not fall too low.
117664.m: Regular factor doses protect people with haemophilia from bleeding.

117665.q: Where does bleeding typically occur in severe haemophilia?
a: In the lens of the eye
117665.e: Repeated bleeding into joints (haemarthrosis), for example in the knee, can permanently damage the joints without treatment.
117665.m: Haemophilia typically leads to bleeding into the joints.

117666.q: Which European queen was a carrier of haemophilia, which spread into several royal houses?
117666.e: Through Queen Victoria's daughters, haemophilia reached the Russian imperial family, among others, where the heir to the throne Alexei had the disease.
117666.m: Queen Victoria spread haemophilia through Europe's royal houses.

117667.q: What is missing from the blood in haemophilia?
117667.e: In haemophilia A, clotting factor VIII is missing; in haemophilia B, factor IX. That is why it takes much longer for bleeding to stop.
117667.m: In haemophilia, a clotting factor is missing.

117668.q: Which new treatment aims to supply people with haemophilia with the missing clotting factor permanently?
117668.e: In gene therapy, a working copy of the gene is placed into liver cells. These cells then make the missing clotting factor themselves.
117668.m: Gene therapy lets the body make the missing clotting factor itself.

117669.q: Why does haemophilia affect almost only males?
a: The gene is on the X chromosome
The gene is on the Y chromosome
117669.e: Males have only one X chromosome. If the gene for the clotting factor on it is altered, there is no healthy backup gene. Females have two X chromosomes and are usually only carriers.
117669.m: Haemophilia is inherited on the X chromosome.

117670.q: Where does the anticoagulant heparin get its name from?
a: From the liver, from which it was first isolated
From the Latin word for blood
117670.e: In 1916 the medical student Jay McLean isolated an anticoagulant substance from dog liver; William Henry Howell named it after the Greek hepar, liver.
117670.m: Heparin is named after the liver.

117671.q: How do vitamin K antagonists such as Marcoumar work?
a: They block the production of clotting factors
They thin the blood with water
They lower the number of red blood cells
117671.e: The liver needs vitamin K to make several clotting factors. Vitamin K antagonists block this step, so the blood clots more slowly.
117671.m: Vitamin K antagonists slow down the production of clotting factors.

117672.q: Which heparins are usually injected under the skin once a day today to prevent thromboses?
117672.e: Low-molecular-weight heparins such as nadroparin or enoxaparin are almost fully absorbed under the skin and work for a long time; they are the treatment of choice for preventing thrombosis.
117672.m: Low-molecular-weight heparins are injected under the skin to prevent thrombosis.

117673.q: What are anticoagulants such as rivaroxaban often prescribed for?
a: Against blood clots, for example in atrial fibrillation
117673.e: In atrial fibrillation or after a thrombosis, clots can form that cause a stroke or a pulmonary embolism. Anticoagulants lower this risk.
117673.m: Anticoagulants protect against dangerous blood clots.

117674.q: Why do people often have to pause an anticoagulant before a planned operation?
a: So that the anaesthetic works better
Because otherwise it causes a fever
So that the wound itches sooner
117674.e: Anticoagulants slow down how fast bleeding stops. During an operation you could therefore lose a dangerous amount of blood.
117674.m: The biggest danger of anticoagulants is bleeding.

117675.q: What was the drug warfarin originally developed from?
a: From a substance in spoiled sweet clover
From the saliva of vampire bats
117675.e: In mouldy sweet clover, dicoumarol forms, which made cattle bleed to death; warfarin was developed from it, first as rat poison.
117675.m: Warfarin comes from a substance in spoiled sweet clover.

117676.q: Why do many blood collection tubes contain citrate or EDTA?
a: They bind calcium and so prevent clotting
They kill bacteria in the blood
They dissolve the red blood cells
117676.e: Without free calcium ions, the clotting cascade cannot run, so the sample stays liquid.
117676.m: Calcium binders keep blood samples liquid.

117677.q: Which antidote reverses the effect of vitamin K antagonists?
117677.e: Vitamin K antagonists block the vitamin K dependent production of clotting factors; added vitamin K reverses this effect within hours.
117677.m: Vitamin K is the antidote to vitamin K antagonists.

117678.q: For which disease is a bone marrow or stem cell transplant used especially often?
117678.e: In leukaemia, the bone marrow makes malignant blood cells. After strong chemotherapy, donated stem cells rebuild a healthy blood system. The pioneer of this method was E. Donnall Thomas, Nobel Prize 1990.
117678.m: Stem cell transplants help especially with leukaemia.

117679.q: Which tissue markers should match as closely as possible in an allogeneic stem cell transplant?
117679.e: HLA molecules decide whether immune cells recognise tissue as foreign; a good match lowers rejection and complications.
117679.m: For stem cell donations, the HLA markers must match.

117680.q: What is the complication called in which the donor's immune cells attack the recipient's body?
117680.e: T cells transferred with the graft recognise the recipient's tissue as foreign and can damage skin, gut and liver.
117680.m: In graft-versus-host disease, the donor's immune system attacks the recipient.

117681.q: What does an autologous stem cell transplant mean?
a: The patient gets their own stem cells back
The stem cells come from a sibling
The stem cells come from an animal
The stem cells come from a cell culture of other donors
117681.e: In an autologous transplant, the patient's own stem cells are collected before high-dose chemotherapy and given back afterwards.
117681.m: Autologous means the stem cells come from the patient themselves.

117682.q: How are blood stem cells for a transplant usually collected today?
117682.e: For a few days the donor receives a medicine (G-CSF) that draws stem cells from the bone marrow into the blood. A machine then collects them from the venous blood. Less often, bone marrow is taken from the hip bone.
117682.m: Stem cells are usually collected from venous blood today.

117683.q: How likely is it that a sibling has the same HLA markers?
117683.e: Each child inherits one of two HLA haplotypes from each parent; the same combination occurs with a probability of 1/2 · 1/2.
117683.m: Siblings are HLA-identical in 25 per cent of cases.

117684.q: Which desired effect can help against leukaemia in an allogeneic transplant?
117684.e: Donor immune cells can recognise remaining leukaemia cells as foreign and destroy them.
117684.m: Donor cells can fight remaining leukaemia cells.

117685.q: Which source of blood stem cells can be collected right after birth?
117685.e: Umbilical cord blood contains many blood stem cells and can be frozen and stored in cord blood banks.
117685.m: Umbilical cord blood is a source of blood stem cells.

117686.q: What requirements does Blood Transfusion SRC Switzerland name for giving blood?
a: Healthy, at least 18 years old and weighing at least 50 kg
At least 16 years old and weighing at least 40 kg
At least 21 years old and weighing at least 60 kg
At least 25 years old, any weight
117686.e: According to Blood Transfusion SRC Switzerland, healthy people aged 18 or over who weigh at least 50 kg may donate (as of 2025).
117686.m: In Switzerland you may give blood from age 18 and 50 kg.

117687.q: How much blood is taken in Switzerland during a whole blood donation?
117687.e: According to Blood Transfusion SRC, 450 ml of blood is taken during a whole blood donation (as of 2025).
117687.m: In a whole blood donation you give 450 ml of blood.

117688.q: How long does a red blood cell concentrate keep, according to Blood Transfusion SRC Switzerland?
117688.e: Red blood cells can be stored chilled for up to 42 days (as of 2025).
117688.m: Red blood cell concentrates keep for up to 42 days.

117689.q: Why do platelet donations have to be replenished especially often?
a: They only keep for about 7 days
They may only be transported frozen
They only suit blood group AB
They are only needed in winter
117689.e: Platelet concentrates are stored at room temperature and, according to Blood Transfusion SRC, only keep for 7 days.
117689.m: Platelets only keep for about a week.

117690.q: How long can frozen blood plasma be stored, according to Blood Transfusion SRC Switzerland?
117690.e: Deep-frozen plasma can be stored for up to 24 months (as of 2025).
117690.m: Frozen plasma keeps for up to two years.

117691.q: Which blood group is the universal donor for blood plasma?
117691.e: Plasma of group AB contains neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies and can therefore be given to all recipients.
117691.m: Plasma of blood group AB suits all recipients.

117693.q: What is the procedure called in which only plasma or platelets are taken and the other components are given back?
117693.e: In apheresis, a cell separator splits the blood and returns the components that are not needed straight back into the vein.
117693.m: In apheresis you get back the blood components that are not needed.

117694.q: Which value is checked before every blood donation to rule out anaemia in the donor?
117694.e: If haemoglobin is too low, the donor is deferred for their own protection.
117694.m: Haemoglobin is measured before a blood donation.

117695.q: Which cells in the bone marrow does erythropoietin mainly act on?
a: Precursor cells of red blood cells
117695.e: Erythropoietin binds to receptors on erythroid precursor cells, prevents them from dying and promotes their division and maturation.
117695.m: Erythropoietin supports the precursors of red blood cells.

117696.q: What happens in a pulmonary embolism?
a: A blood clot carried in the blood blocks a pulmonary artery
The lung fills with air from the abdomen
A lung collapses because of a tear
117696.e: Often a clot breaks loose from a leg vein and is carried with the blood into the lung. There it blocks an artery, and oxygen uptake is disturbed.
117696.m: In a pulmonary embolism, a clot blocks a pulmonary artery.

117697.q: Which well-known painkiller should people with haemophilia avoid?
117697.e: Acetylsalicylic acid inhibits the platelets and so increases the tendency to bleed. Paracetamol, on the other hand, is considered a suitable painkiller in haemophilia.
117697.m: With a tendency to bleed, aspirin is off limits.

117698.q: How is the coefficient of friction μ defined?
a: Friction force divided by normal force
117698.e: μ equals F_R divided by F_N; since the newtons cancel out, μ is a number without a unit.
117698.m: The coefficient of friction is the ratio of friction force to normal force.

117699.q: Which coefficient of static friction is typical for a car tyre on dry tarmac?
117699.e: Rubber grips dry tarmac very well; on a wet road the value falls noticeably, and on ice to below 0.1.
117699.m: Tyres grip dry tarmac very well.

117700.q: How does the coefficient of sliding friction usually compare with the coefficient of static friction for the same pair of materials?
117700.e: Once a body is moving, it usually takes less force to keep it moving than to get it going in the first place.
117700.m: Sliding friction is usually smaller than static friction.

117701.q: A 20 kg crate is pulled across the floor at a constant speed; the coefficient of sliding friction is 0.4. What pulling force is needed (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
117701.e: F = μ · m · g = 0.4 · 20 kg · 9.81 m/s², which gives about 78.5 N.
117701.m: At constant speed, the pulling force exactly balances the friction.

117702.q: To pull a 10 kg block steadily across a table you need 30 N. What is the coefficient of sliding friction (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
117702.e: μ = 30 N divided by (10 kg · 9.81 m/s²) = 30 divided by 98.1, so about 0.31.
117702.m: You get the coefficient of friction from friction force divided by normal force.

117703.q: According to the law of Amontons and Coulomb, what does the sliding friction force roughly not depend on?
a: The size of the contact area
117703.e: A larger area spreads the load, but the real contact area of the tiny rough peaks stays about the same; so only the normal force counts.
117703.m: The friction force hardly depends on the size of the contact area.

117705.q: A car travelling at 25 m/s brakes to a stop on a wet road with a coefficient of friction of 0.5. Roughly how long is the braking distance (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
117705.e: s = v² divided by (2 · μ · g) = 625 divided by 9.81, which gives about 64 m.
117705.m: A smaller coefficient of friction makes the braking distance longer.

117706.q: A crate stands on the back of a braking lorry and does not slide. In which direction does static friction act on the crate?
117706.e: Because of its inertia, the crate tends to keep sliding forwards; static friction acts against this tendency and slows it down together with the lorry.
117706.m: Static friction acts against the sliding that is about to happen.

117707.q: A 50 kg crate stands on the floor; the coefficient of static friction is 0.6. At what horizontal force does it start to slide (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
117707.e: F = 0.6 · 50 kg · 9.81 m/s², which gives about 294 N.
117707.m: A body only starts moving once the maximum static friction is exceeded.

117708.q: Someone pushes with 100 N against a heavy crate that does not move. How large is the static friction force?
117708.e: Static friction adjusts to the applied force as long as its maximum value is not exceeded; since the crate is at rest, the two forces cancel out.
117708.m: Static friction is only as large as needed to prevent movement.

117709.q: Which force pushes a person forwards when walking?
a: Static friction between shoe and ground
The normal force of the ground
117709.e: The foot pushes backwards against the ground, and static friction acts as the opposite force forwards; on black ice it is almost completely missing.
117709.m: When we walk, static friction from the ground pushes us forwards.

117710.q: Why does an anti-lock braking system often shorten the braking distance and keep the car steerable?
a: The wheels keep rolling and use the greater static friction
It increases the weight of the car
117710.e: Skidding wheels transmit less force than rolling ones that grip the ground; ABS keeps the wheels just short of locking.
117710.m: ABS uses static friction instead of sliding friction.

117711.q: What is the highest speed at which a car can go round a flat bend with a radius of 50 m if the coefficient of static friction is 0.8 (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
117711.e: From μ · m · g = m · v² / r it follows that v = √(0.8 · 9.81 · 50), so about 19.8 m/s or about 71 km/h.
117711.m: Static friction limits the speed in a bend.

117712.q: What is the greatest acceleration a four-wheel-drive car can reach with a coefficient of static friction of 0.9 (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
117712.e: The maximum driving force is μ · m · g, so a = μ · g = 0.9 · 9.81 m/s², about 8.8 m/s².
117712.m: Static friction limits how fast a vehicle can accelerate.

117713.q: A crate lies loose on the back of a lorry; the coefficient of static friction is 0.3. What is the greatest acceleration the lorry can have without the crate sliding (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
117713.e: Only static friction accelerates the crate along with the lorry; so a is at most μ · g = 0.3 · 9.81 m/s², about 2.9 m/s².
117713.m: A load slides when the acceleration is more than static friction can provide.

117714.q: At what angle of slope does a block start to slide if the coefficient of static friction is 0.5?
117714.e: Sliding starts when tan α equals μ_H; arctan 0.5 gives about 26.6°.
117714.m: A body slides as soon as the tangent of the angle reaches the coefficient of static friction.

117715.q: What is the normal force on a body with weight F_G on a slope at angle α?
117715.e: Only the component F_G · cos α acts at right angles to the slope; that is why friction on a slope is smaller than on level ground.
117715.m: On a slope the normal force is smaller by a factor of cos α.

117716.q: A block slides down a 30° slope; the coefficient of sliding friction is 0.2. What is its acceleration (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
117716.m: Friction reduces the acceleration on a slope.

117717.q: A block slides down a ramp inclined at 20° at a constant speed. What is the coefficient of sliding friction?
117717.e: At constant speed, the force down the slope and friction balance each other; then μ = tan 20°, so about 0.36.
117717.m: If a body slides steadily, the coefficient of friction equals the tangent of the angle.

117718.q: A 10 kg crate is to be pushed up a 30° ramp at a constant speed; the coefficient of sliding friction is 0.3. What force parallel to the ramp is needed (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
117718.m: When pushing uphill, the force down the slope and friction add up.

117719.q: A 5 kg body rests on a slope inclined at 30°. How large is the static friction force (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
117719.e: Static friction balances the force down the slope: F = m · g · sin 30° = 5 · 9.81 · 0.5, so about 24.5 N.
117719.m: A body at rest on a slope is held against the downhill force by static friction.

117720.q: How does the angle at which a body starts to slide on a slope depend on its mass?
a: It gets larger with greater mass
It gets smaller with greater mass
It is proportional to the mass
117720.e: The force down the slope and static friction are both proportional to the mass, so the mass cancels out in tan α = μ_H.
117720.m: The sliding angle depends only on the coefficient of static friction.

117721.q: A skier glides down a 10° slope without using poles; the coefficient of sliding friction is 0.05. What is the acceleration without air resistance (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
117721.m: Even small friction noticeably slows you down on gentle slopes.

117722.q: With which Latin phrase did Robert Hooke sum up his law in 1678?
117722.e: The phrase means roughly “as the extension, so the force” and describes how force and extension are proportional.
117722.m: Hooke summed up his law with “ut tensio, sic vis”.

117723.q: In which range does Hooke's law apply?
a: Only in the linear elastic range
117723.e: Above the limit of proportionality, the relationship between force and extension is no longer linear.
117723.m: Hooke's law only applies to small, elastic deformations.

117724.q: What is Hooke's law for materials written in terms of stress?
117724.e: The mechanical stress σ is proportional to the strain ε, and the constant of proportionality is Young's modulus E.
117724.m: In the elastic range, stress is proportional to strain.

117725.q: A mass of 0.5 kg hangs from a spring with 200 N/m. By how much is the spring stretched (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
117725.m: The extension is the force divided by the spring constant.

117726.q: What does the minus sign in F = -D · x mean?
a: The spring force acts against the displacement
The spring gets shorter under load
117726.e: The spring force is a restoring force and always points back towards the rest position.
117726.m: The spring force always pulls back towards the rest position.

117727.q: What does the force-extension graph of a spring look like in the range where Hooke's law applies?
a: A straight line through the origin
117727.e: Force and extension are proportional, and the gradient of the line is the spring constant.
117727.m: In the Hooke range, the force-extension graph is a straight line through the origin.

117728.q: Which material clearly departs from Hooke's law even at moderate extension?
117728.e: Rubber behaves in a non-linear way because its molecular chains first have to line up when it is stretched.
117728.m: Rubber does not behave like an ideal Hooke spring.

117729.q: On which physical principle is a spring balance based?
a: The law of conservation of energy alone
117729.e: Since the extension is proportional to the force, the force can be read off a linear scale.
117729.m: A spring balance uses the proportionality of force and extension.

117730.q: In which SI unit is the spring constant given?
117730.e: The spring constant tells you how much force is needed per metre of extension.
117730.m: The spring constant measures force per length.

117731.q: What does a large spring constant tell you about a spring?
a: The spring is stiff and hard to stretch
The spring is soft and easy to stretch
117731.e: The larger D is, the more force is needed for the same extension.
117731.m: A large spring constant means a stiff spring.

117732.q: How long does one oscillation of a spring pendulum with 0.5 kg and 50 N/m take?
117732.m: The period of a spring pendulum depends on the mass and the spring constant.

117733.q: A spring pendulum with 1 kg oscillates with a period of exactly 1 s. What is the spring constant?
117733.e: From T = 2π · √(m / D) it follows that D = 4π² · m / T², so about 39.5 N/m.
117733.m: You can work out the spring constant from the period.

117734.q: A coil spring is cut into two halves of equal length. What is the spring constant of one half?
117734.e: Each coil stretches by the same amount under the same force; with half as many coils, the total extension is halved.

117735.q: How does the spring constant of a coil spring change if it is wound from thicker wire but otherwise has the same shape?
117735.e: Thicker wire is harder to twist. This makes the spring stiffer, so its spring constant gets larger.
117735.m: Thicker wire makes a spring stiffer.

117736.q: How does the period of a spring pendulum change if the spring constant is made four times larger?
117736.e: T is proportional to 1 / √D; the square root of 4 is 2, so T becomes half as large.

117737.q: What effect does a larger number of coils have on the spring constant of an otherwise identical coil spring?
117737.e: Under the same force each coil stretches by the same amount; with more coils the total extension becomes larger and the spring softer.
117737.m: More coils make a spring softer.

117738.q: Roughly what is Young's modulus of steel?
117738.e: For structural steel, about 210,000 N/mm², or 210 GPa, is usually used.
117738.m: Steel has a Young's modulus of about 210 GPa.

117739.q: Roughly what is Young's modulus of aluminium?
117739.e: At about 70 GPa, aluminium gives way about three times more easily than steel.
117739.m: Aluminium has about a third of the Young's modulus of steel.

117740.q: A steel wire 2 m long with a cross-section of 1 mm² is loaded with 210 N. By how much does it lengthen (E = 210 GPa)?
117740.m: The extension is strain times original length.

117741.q: Which of these materials has the smallest Young's modulus?
117741.e: Rubber is typically only in the range of megapascals; the other materials are in the range of gigapascals.
117741.m: Rubber has a very small Young's modulus.

117742.q: Which of these substances has a particularly high Young's modulus of over 1000 GPa?
117742.e: Its strong covalent bonds make diamond the stiffest natural material.

117743.q: How is the strain ε of a rod defined?
a: Change in length divided by original length
Original length times change in length
117743.e: Strain is a relative change in length and so has no unit; it is often given as a percentage.
117743.m: Strain is the relative change in length.

117744.q: After which British scientist is the modulus of elasticity named in English?
117744.e: In English the modulus of elasticity is called “Young's modulus”, after the doctor and physicist Thomas Young.
117744.m: The English name of the modulus honours Thomas Young.

117745.q: What happens to the thickness of a steel rod when it is stretched elastically?
a: The thickness stays exactly the same
117745.e: When a rod is stretched, it contracts slightly across its width. For steel this lateral contraction is about 30 per cent of the lengthwise strain.
117745.m: A stretched rod also gets slightly thinner.

117746.q: What does the tensile strength of a material tell you?
a: The highest stress in a tensile test, based on the original cross-section
The stress at which deformation begins
117746.e: Tensile strength R_m is the maximum tensile force divided by the original cross-section of the sample.
117746.m: Tensile strength is the highest stress in a tensile test.

117747.q: In which unit is the tensile strength of metals often given?
117747.e: One newton per square millimetre equals one megapascal.
117747.m: Tensile strength is usually given in newtons per square millimetre.

117748.q: A steel rod with a cross-section of 50 mm² has a tensile strength of 500 N/mm². At what tensile force does it break?
117748.e: F = R_m · A = 500 N/mm² · 50 mm² = 25,000 N, so 25 kN.
117748.m: The breaking force is tensile strength times cross-section.

117749.q: What does the number in the steel grade S235 tell you?
a: The minimum yield strength in N/mm²
The carbon content in parts per thousand
The melting point in degrees Celsius
117749.e: S stands for structural steel, and 235 for the minimum yield strength of 235 N/mm² for thin products.
117749.m: In S235 the number gives the minimum yield strength.

117750.q: What happens to a ductile tensile sample after its tensile strength has been reached?
a: It returns to its original length
It suddenly becomes harder than diamond
117750.e: After the maximum force, the deformation concentrates at one point and the cross-section there shrinks until the sample breaks.
117750.m: After the tensile strength is reached, a ductile sample forms a neck.

117751.q: Why is concrete reinforced with steel?
a: Concrete has a high compressive strength but low tensile strength
Concrete has a low compressive strength
117751.e: The tensile strength of concrete is only about a tenth of its compressive strength; so the reinforcing steel takes the tensile forces.
117751.m: In reinforced concrete, the steel carries the tensile forces.

117752.q: The breaking length is the length at which a freely hanging wire breaks under its own weight. How long is it for steel with a tensile strength of 500 N/mm² and a density of 7850 kg/m³ (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
117752.m: The breaking length depends on strength and density, not on the cross-section.

117753.q: Why is the practical tensile strength of glass far below the theoretical value?
a: Tiny surface cracks act as notches
117753.e: Stress concentrates at fine cracks, and brittle materials cannot reduce these peaks by flowing.
117753.m: Small cracks greatly reduce the strength of brittle materials.

117754.q: What is typical of plastic deformation?
a: It remains after the load is removed
It disappears completely after the load is removed
117754.e: Unlike with elastic deformation, a plastically deformed body does not return to its original shape.

117755.q: What is the permanent extension of a tensile sample after fracture, relative to its original length, called?
117755.e: Elongation at break is given as a percentage and measures how much a material can be deformed plastically before it breaks.
117755.m: A large elongation at break marks a material that is easy to deform.

117756.q: What happens inside a metal during plastic deformation?
a: Layers of atoms slide past each other
117756.e: Under a large load, whole planes of atoms in the crystal slide past each other. This is made possible by small defects in the lattice, called dislocations, which move through the crystal.
117756.m: Plastic deformation is based on layers of atoms slipping.

117757.q: Why does a copper wire get stiffer when you bend it back and forth several times?
117757.e: The deformation creates many dislocations that get in each other's way; the material becomes stronger but more brittle.

117758.q: In a tensile test, a steel sample is slowly stretched. What does the yield point show?
a: The stress at which the deformation becomes permanent
The stress at which the sample breaks
117758.e: Up to the yield point, the steel springs back after the load is removed. Above it, it starts to flow and stays plastically deformed.
117758.m: Above the yield point a material deforms permanently.

117759.q: Which material breaks at room temperature with practically no plastic deformation?
117759.e: Glass is brittle: it only deforms elastically until it breaks, whereas metals such as copper are ductile.
117759.m: Brittle materials such as glass break without permanent deformation.

117760.q: What is the crumple zone of a car for?
a: It absorbs impact energy through plastic deformation
117760.e: As it crumples, kinetic energy is turned into deformation work and the deceleration of the passengers is softened.
117760.m: The crumple zone uses up energy through plastic deformation.

117761.q: Which heat treatment makes work-hardened metal easy to shape again?
117761.e: During annealing, new grains with few dislocations form, and the material becomes softer and can be shaped again.

117763.q: Two springs of 100 N/m and 400 N/m hang in series and carry a load of 8 N. How far does the lower end drop?
117763.e: Each spring carries the full 8 N: the first stretches by 8 / 100 = 0.08 m, the second by 8 / 400 = 0.02 m, together 0.10 m.
117763.m: In a series arrangement, the extensions of the individual springs add up.

117764.q: Two springs of 200 N/m and 300 N/m are connected in parallel. What is the total spring constant?
117764.e: In parallel, D = 200 N/m + 300 N/m = 500 N/m.
117764.m: In parallel, the spring constants add up.

117765.q: Two springs of 200 N/m and 300 N/m are connected in series. What is the total spring constant?
117765.m: In series, the total spring constant is smaller than each individual one.

117766.q: Two identical springs are connected in series. How does the total spring constant compare with the spring constant of one spring?
a: It is four times as large
117766.m: Two identical springs in series are half as stiff.

117767.q: What force acts in each spring when two springs in series carry a load F?
117767.e: Each spring in the line has to pass on the whole load, like the links of a chain.
117767.m: In a series arrangement, each spring carries the whole load.

117768.q: Two identical springs hang side by side in parallel and together carry a load F. What force does each spring carry?
a: A quarter of the force F
117768.e: Both springs stretch by the same amount and share the load half and half.
117768.m: Identical springs in parallel share the load.

117769.q: Two parallel springs of 100 N/m each are connected in series with a third spring of 200 N/m. What is the total spring constant?
117769.e: The parallel pair gives 200 N/m; in series with 200 N/m, 1 / D = 1/200 + 1/200, so D = 100 N/m.
117769.m: You work out mixed spring arrangements step by step.

117770.q: How is shear stress τ defined?
a: Force parallel to the surface divided by the area
Force perpendicular to the surface divided by the area
117770.e: In shear, the force acts along the surface; τ = F / A.
117770.m: Shear stress is the tangential force per area.

117771.q: What is the material constant that links shear stress and shear angle called?
117771.e: In the elastic range, τ = G · γ, where G is the shear modulus and γ the shear angle.
117771.m: The shear modulus links shear stress and shear angle.

117772.q: What kind of load does a rivet experience when it holds two overlapping metal sheets against sliding sideways?
117772.e: The two sheets tend to slide against each other. The forces act across the rivet and try to shear it off at the joint.
117772.m: Rivets and bolts between sheets are loaded in shear.

117773.q: A bolt with a cross-section of 100 mm² is loaded in shear with 5000 N. What is the shear stress?
117773.e: τ = F / A = 5000 N / 100 mm² = 50 N/mm².
117773.m: Shear stress is shear force divided by cross-section.

117774.q: Why do liquids at rest have no shear modulus?
a: They give way to a shear force by flowing
117774.e: A liquid cannot withstand a static shear stress; it starts to flow under shear.

117775.q: Why do seismic S-waves not pass through the Earth's outer core?
a: It is liquid and does not transmit shear
It is too hot for any wave
117775.e: S-waves are shear waves; since the outer core is liquid, they cannot travel through it.
117775.m: Shear waves need a solid material.

117776.q: What is the job of a shear pin in a drive?
a: It breaks on purpose when overloaded and protects the machine
It increases the speed of rotation
117776.e: The shear pin is deliberately designed as the weakest link; if the torque is too high, it shears off before expensive parts break.
117776.m: A shear pin sacrifices itself when overloaded.

117777.q: What is the angle by which a body deforms under shear called?
117777.e: The shear angle γ describes the change of an originally right angle in the material.
117777.m: The shear angle measures deformation under shear.

117778.q: What does Empa mainly work on?
117778.e: Empa began as a testing institute for building materials. Today it researches new materials and technologies, for example for construction, energy and medicine.

117779.q: What did the abbreviation Empa originally stand for?
a: Federal Museum of Physics and Astronomy
117779.e: Empa began as an institute that tested building materials for strength. Today it is called the Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology.
117779.m: Empa began as a materials testing institute.

117780.q: What can happen to a long, slender rod if you squeeze it hard along its length?
117780.e: Slender parts under compression can suddenly give way sideways. This buckling must be taken into account when building bridges, as the Münchenstein bridge disaster of 1891 showed.
117780.m: Slender rods under compression can buckle.

117781.q: Which three sites does Empa have?
117781.e: St Gallen was added in 1937 when a textile testing institute was incorporated, and Thun in 1994.
117781.m: Empa does research in Dübendorf, St Gallen and Thun.

117782.q: Which group of institutions does Empa belong to?
a: The association of cantonal grammar schools
117782.e: The ETH Domain includes the two Federal Institutes of Technology and the research institutes PSI, WSL, Empa and Eawag.
117782.m: Empa belongs to the ETH Domain.

117783.q: What did the testing institute in St Gallen, which became part of Empa in 1937, specialise in?
117783.e: In keeping with St Gallen's textile tradition, the institute tested fabrics and fibres.
117783.m: Empa's St Gallen site has its roots in textile testing.

117784.e: Tribology studies surfaces that touch and move relative to each other.
117784.m: Tribology is the science of friction, wear and lubrication.

117785.q: What did the British Jost Report of 1966 on friction and wear show?
a: They cost industry a great deal of money
117785.e: Peter Jost showed how much money is lost through friction and wear. After that, the field became known as tribology, from the Greek word for rubbing.
117785.m: Friction and wear cost the economy a lot of money.

117786.q: Why does an engine wear especially quickly right after a cold start?
a: The lubricating film has not fully built up yet
The petrol is still too warm
The engine has the most cooling water then
117786.e: At the start the oil is still cold and thick and does not reach all places at once. Until a load-bearing film of oil separates the parts, the surfaces partly touch directly.
117786.m: Wear is greatest without a complete lubricating film.

117787.q: In which state is the friction of a well-lubricated plain bearing smallest?
a: When the surfaces are completely separated by a lubricating film
117787.e: If a load-bearing lubricating film separates the surfaces completely, almost only the internal friction of the lubricant is left.
117787.m: A complete lubricating film greatly reduces friction.

117788.q: What is wear called when hard particles scratch and remove material from a surface?
117788.e: In abrasion, hard particles or rough peaks plough material out of the softer surface.
117788.m: Abrasion is wear by scratching and grooving.

117789.q: Which substance is often used as a solid lubricant?
117789.e: Graphite consists of layers that slide easily over each other, and it lubricates even where oil is not suitable.
117789.m: Graphite lubricates thanks to its sliding layers.

117790.q: What is the jerky switching between sticking and sliding called, which makes doors squeak, for example?
117790.e: As long as the surface sticks, tension builds up; when it breaks free, it slides on with a jerk until it sticks again. The same effect makes violin strings sound.
117790.m: The stick-slip effect comes from switching between sticking and sliding.

117791.q: Which plastic is known for its particularly low coefficient of friction?
117791.e: Polytetrafluoroethylene is one of the solids with the lowest coefficient of friction and is used for plain bearings and non-stick pan coatings.
117791.m: PTFE slides with particularly little friction.

117792.q: Which pair of materials has a particularly low coefficient of sliding friction of about 0.01?
117792.e: Skate blades glide very easily on ice, so the coefficient of sliding friction there is extremely small.
117792.m: Steel on ice slides with very little friction.

117793.q: Why does a train on steel rails need comparatively little energy to roll?
a: The rolling friction of steel on steel is very small
The rails are built on a downhill slope
The wheels do not touch the rail
Air resistance is zero for trains
117793.e: The hard steel wheels hardly deform, so the coefficient of rolling friction is about 0.001 to 0.002.
117793.m: Steel wheels on steel rails roll especially easily.

117794.q: What is wear called when surfaces briefly weld together at contact points and material is torn out?
117794.e: Under high pressure and without lubrication, rough peaks stick to each other; in extreme cases a bearing “seizes”.
117794.m: Adhesive wear comes from contact points welding together.

117795.q: What is the modular research building of Empa and Eawag in Dübendorf, where new building technologies are tested in everyday use, called?
117795.e: In NEST, opened in 2016, new materials and energy systems are tested under real conditions in exchangeable living and office units.
117795.m: In NEST, Empa tests new building technologies in everyday use.

117796.q: Which order did Gregor Mendel belong to as a monk?
117796.e: Mendel entered the Augustinian Abbey of St Thomas in 1843 and was given the religious name Gregor there.
117796.m: Gregor Mendel was an Augustinian monk.

117797.q: In which city did Gregor Mendel carry out his famous crossing experiments?
117797.e: Mendel experimented in the monastery garden in Brünn, today Brno in the Czech Republic.
117797.m: Mendel's experimental garden was in the monastery in Brno.

117798.q: With which plant did Gregor Mendel carry out his most important experiments on inheritance?
117798.e: For years Mendel crossed varieties of the garden pea (Pisum sativum). Peas have clearly distinguishable traits and are easy to pollinate in a controlled way.
117798.m: Mendel discovered the rules of inheritance using peas.

117799.q: In which year was Mendel's paper “Experiments on Plant Hybrids” published?
117799.e: Mendel presented his results to the Natural History Society in Brno in 1865. The paper was printed in its proceedings in 1866.

117800.q: How many pairs of pea traits did Mendel study in his experiments?
117800.e: Mendel chose seven traits, each with two clear forms, such as seed shape, seed colour and plant height.
117800.m: Mendel followed seven pairs of pea traits.

117801.q: Around which year were Mendel's laws independently rediscovered by several researchers?
117801.e: Around 1900, three botanists came across the same patterns independently of one another and then referred to Mendel.
117801.m: Mendel's work was only rediscovered around 1900.

117802.q: Which researcher was one of those who rediscovered Mendel's laws?
117802.e: Carl Correns published crossing results with peas and maize, among others, which confirmed Mendel's findings. Hugo de Vries and Erich von Tschermak did the same at almost the same time.
117802.m: Carl Correns was one of the rediscoverers of Mendel.

117803.q: Which position did Gregor Mendel take on in the monastery in 1868?
117803.e: In 1868 Mendel was elected abbot of the monastery of St Thomas. After that he had hardly any time left for research.
117803.m: Mendel became abbot of his monastery in 1868.

117804.q: Mendel crossed pure-breeding yellow-seeded peas with pure-breeding green-seeded peas. What did the seeds of the first generation of offspring look like?
117804.e: Yellow is dominant over green. So all offspring of the first generation are yellow. This is Mendel's law of uniformity.
117804.m: In the first generation of offspring, all offspring look the same.

117805.q: Which ratio of phenotypes is expected in the F2 of a monohybrid cross with dominant and recessive alleles?
117805.e: Aa crossed with Aa gives AA, Aa, Aa and aa. Three out of four show the dominant trait, one the recessive trait.
117805.m: A dominant-recessive cross splits three to one in the F2.

117806.q: Which ratio of genotypes arises in the F2 from the cross Aa times Aa?
117806.e: Each parent passes on A or a with equal probability. This produces the combinations AA, Aa, aA and aa.
117806.m: The genotypes of the F2 are distributed one to two to one.

117807.q: Which ratio do the phenotypes show in the F2 of a dihybrid cross with dominant and recessive alleles?
117807.e: Two independently inherited traits combine freely: (3 to 1) times (3 to 1) gives 9 to 3 to 3 to 1.
117807.m: With two traits, the F2 splits nine to three to three to one.

117808.q: In the F2 of a cross AaBb times AaBb, what proportion of plants has the genotype aabb?
117808.e: The proportion of aa is 1/4 and the proportion of bb is also 1/4. With independent inheritance, 1/4 times 1/4 equals 1/16.
117808.m: Double recessive plants make up one sixteenth of the dihybrid F2.

117809.q: Which cross is called a backcross or test cross?
a: A cross with a pure-breeding recessive partner
A cross of two F1 plants
A cross of two wild plants
117809.e: If you cross an individual showing the dominant trait with aa, the offspring reveal whether it is AA or Aa.
117809.m: A test cross with aa reveals the genotype.

117810.q: Which ratio results from a test cross Aa times aa?
117810.e: Aa produces half A and half a gametes, aa produces only a gametes. So half the offspring are Aa and half are aa.
117810.m: The test cross of a heterozygote gives one to one.

117811.q: Which flower colour does the F1 of the four o'clock flower show when a pure-breeding red plant is crossed with a pure-breeding white one?
117811.e: In the four o'clock flower (Mirabilis jalapa) flower colour is inherited in an intermediate way. The heterozygotes show an in-between form.
117811.m: Intermediate inheritance gives pink flowers in the four o'clock flower.

117812.q: Which exception limits the law of independent assortment?
a: Gene linkage on the same chromosome
117812.e: Genes that lie close together on the same chromosome are usually inherited together. They then do not combine freely.
117812.m: Linked genes are not inherited independently.

a: More than two sets of chromosomes per cell
The absence of a single chromosome
The doubling of a single gene
The exchange of pieces of chromosome
117813.e: Polyploid cells contain three, four or more complete sets of chromosomes. This is very common in plants.
117813.m: Polyploid organisms have more than two sets of chromosomes.

117814.q: Which substance from the autumn crocus is used to cause polyploidy artificially?
117814.e: Colchicine blocks the formation of the spindle apparatus. The chromosomes are doubled but not shared out between two daughter cells.
117814.m: Colchicine doubles chromosome sets because it blocks the spindle.

117815.q: How many sets of chromosomes does modern bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) have?
117815.e: Bread wheat arose from crosses of three grass species and is hexaploid with 42 chromosomes.

117816.q: Why do most cultivated bananas not produce seeds that can germinate?
117816.e: With three sets of chromosomes, the chromosomes cannot pair up properly in meiosis. Hardly any working gametes are formed.
117816.m: Triploid plants such as the cultivated banana are largely sterile.

a: Multiplication of the plant's own chromosome sets
Doubling of only the sex chromosomes
117817.e: Allopolyploids combine chromosome sets from different species, for example after a cross between species followed by doubling. Autopolyploids multiply their own set.
117817.m: Allopolyploids carry chromosome sets from different species.

117818.q: Why is a cross between two species often infertile, but fertile after the chromosomes have been doubled?
a: After doubling, every chromosome finds a partner in meiosis
Doubling turns the plant into a single species
117818.e: The chromosomes of two species do not match and cannot pair up in meiosis. After doubling, every chromosome has an identical counterpart. This is how allopolyploids such as oilseed rape or wheat arose.
117818.m: Doubled chromosome sets make crosses between species fertile.

117819.q: What level of ploidy does the common cultivated potato have?
117819.e: The cultivated potato (Solanum tuberosum) has four sets of chromosomes with 48 chromosomes in total.

a: As a triploid cross between a tetraploid and a diploid plant
By removing the seeds by hand
117820.e: If you cross a tetraploid line with a diploid one, you get triploid plants. Their fruits contain only soft, undeveloped ovules.

117821.q: Which characteristic do polyploid plants often show compared with the original diploid form?
a: A shorter lifespan for each cell
117821.e: More genetic material in the nucleus often leads to larger cells. This is called gigantism and is used in plant breeding.
117821.m: Polyploidy often leads to larger plant organs.

117822.q: What is the most important genetic feature of offspring produced by vegetative reproduction?
a: They are clones of the parent plant
They mix the genes of two parents
117822.e: In vegetative reproduction, offspring arise from body cells without fertilisation. Their genes are the same as the parent plant's.
117822.m: Plants reproduced vegetatively are genetically the same as their parent.

117823.q: Which organs does the garden strawberry use to reproduce vegetatively?
117823.e: The strawberry forms runners above the ground, and new daughter plants take root at their nodes.

117824.q: Which storage organ is used for reproduction when potatoes are planted?
117824.e: The potato is a thickened underground stem. New plants sprout from its eyes, which are buds.
117824.m: The potato is a stem tuber.

117825.q: Which plant forms little plantlets along the edges of its leaves?
117825.e: In mother of thousands, complete little plants with roots form in the notches of the leaf edge. When they drop off, they keep growing on their own.
117825.m: Mother of thousands forms young plants on the edge of its leaves.

117826.q: What do you call an underground stem growing horizontally, like the one ginger forms?
117826.e: A rhizome is a stem, usually underground, with buds. If you divide it, new plants grow.

117827.q: Which historical disaster shows the danger of low genetic diversity caused by growing clones?
a: The Great Smog of London in 1952
117827.e: In Ireland, only a few potato varieties propagated vegetatively were grown. Potato blight destroyed the harvests everywhere.
117827.m: Growing clones makes crops vulnerable to disease.

117828.q: What is the method called in which a shoot is bent down into the soil and takes root there before it is cut off?
117828.e: In layering, the shoot stays connected to the parent plant until it has formed its own roots.
117828.m: A layer takes root before it is separated from the parent.

117829.q: Which method makes it possible to grow a great many virus-free clones in the laboratory from a small amount of tissue?
117829.e: In meristem culture, tiny pieces of the shoot tip are multiplied on a nutrient medium. The tip is often free of viruses.
117829.m: Meristem culture produces many virus-free clones.

117830.q: Which roots form on a cutting?
117830.e: Roots that grow from a stem or a leaf are called adventitious roots. They do not develop from the seedling's first root.
117830.m: Cuttings take root with adventitious roots.

117831.q: To which group of plant hormones do most rooting agents belong?
117831.e: Auxins such as indole-3-butyric acid encourage adventitious roots to form. The cut end is dipped in powder or gel.
117831.m: Auxins encourage cuttings to form roots.

117832.q: Where is a tip cutting usually cut?
117832.e: At the node, the cells are especially ready to form roots. That is why the cut is made just below it.
117832.m: Cuttings are cut just below a node.

117833.q: Why are cuttings often kept under a cover in damp air?
a: Otherwise they lose too much water
They must not get any light
117833.e: Without roots a cutting can hardly take up any water. High humidity reduces evaporation through the leaves.
117833.m: High humidity protects cuttings without roots from drying out.

117834.q: Which houseplant is classically propagated by leaf cuttings?
117834.e: With the African violet, you put a leaf with its stalk into soil. Roots and new rosettes form at the base.
117834.m: African violets grow again from leaf cuttings.

117835.q: Which woody plants take root especially easily from leafless hardwood cuttings?
117835.e: Willow twigs quickly form roots in water or damp soil. That is why they are also planted to protect riverbanks.
117835.m: Willows take root very easily from hardwood cuttings.

117836.q: What do you call a cutting taken from a piece of root?
