CO2 goes into the blood, oxygen into the air
Nitrogen goes into the blood, oxygen stays in the air
Water goes into the blood, CO2 stays in the blood
118091.e: By diffusion, each gas moves to where its concentration is lower. That is how oxygen gets into the blood and CO2 into the air you breathe out.
118091.m: In the air sacs, oxygen and CO2 swap places by diffusion.

118092.q: Which device takes over breathing in intensive care when someone can no longer breathe enough on their own?
118092.e: A ventilator blows air with oxygen into the lungs. A defibrillator gives electric shocks to the heart, a dialysis machine replaces the kidney.
118092.m: A ventilator helps when your own breathing is not enough.

118093.q: Which formula do you use to calculate hydrostatic pressure in a liquid at rest?
118093.e: The pressure increases with the density ρ of the liquid, the gravitational acceleration g and the depth h below the surface.
118093.m: Hydrostatic pressure is the product of density, gravitational acceleration and depth.

118094.q: What is the hydrostatic pressure at a water depth of 3 m (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)?
118094.e: p = 1000 kg/m³ · 9.81 m/s² · 3 m = 29,430 Pa, so about 29.4 kPa.
118094.m: Water pressure increases with every metre of depth.

118095.q: Roughly what is the hydrostatic pressure at the deepest point of Lake Zurich (136 m, g = 9.81 m/s²), not counting air pressure?
118095.e: p = 1000 kg/m³ · 9.81 m/s² · 136 m ≈ 1,334,000 Pa. That is about 13.3 bar.
118095.m: At the bottom of deep lakes the pressure is many bar.

118096.q: What is the hydrostatic pressure 20 m deep in the sea (ρ = 1025 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)?
118096.e: p = 1025 kg/m³ · 9.81 m/s² · 20 m = 201,105 Pa, so about 201 kPa.
118096.m: In denser seawater, pressure rises with depth a little faster than in fresh water.

118097.q: What is the hydrostatic pressure at the bottom of a mercury column 0.5 m high (ρ = 13,546 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)?
118097.e: p = 13,546 kg/m³ · 9.81 m/s² · 0.5 m ≈ 66,443 Pa, so about 66 kPa.
118097.m: A dense liquid produces high pressure even at a small height.

118098.q: What is the density of a liquid if the hydrostatic pressure 2 m deep is 15.7 kPa (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
118098.e: ρ = p / (g·h) = 15,700 Pa / (9.81 m/s² · 2 m) ≈ 800 kg/m³. That roughly matches ethanol.
118098.m: You can calculate the density of a liquid from pressure and depth.

118099.q: At what water depth is the hydrostatic pressure 50 kPa (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)?
118099.m: The depth is pressure divided by density times gravitational acceleration.

118100.q: What is the hydrostatic pressure right at the surface of a liquid at rest?
a: The same as at the bottom
Half as much as at the bottom
118100.e: There is no column of liquid above the surface, so h is 0. Only the outside air pressure acts there.
118100.m: Hydrostatic pressure starts at zero at the surface.

118101.q: What is the hydrostatic pressure in the Challenger Deep (about 10,935 m), calculated with ρ = 1025 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s²?
118101.e: p = 1025 kg/m³ · 9.81 m/s² · 10,935 m ≈ 1.1 · 10⁸ Pa, so about 1100 bar.
118101.m: In the deep sea the pressure is over a thousand bar.

118102.q: What causes the gravitational pressure in a liquid?
a: The weight of the liquid above
The movement of the molecules alone
118102.e: Each layer of liquid carries the weight of all the layers above it. The deeper you are, the greater this weight per area.
118102.m: Gravitational pressure comes from the weight of the liquid above.

118103.q: Which value is the standard air pressure at sea level?
118103.e: Standard atmospheric pressure is set at 101,325 Pa, which is 1013.25 hPa.

118104.q: How high is the mercury column of a barometer at standard pressure?
118104.e: Air pressure balances a mercury column about 760 mm high. That is where the unit mmHg comes from.
118104.m: Standard pressure holds up about 760 millimetres of mercury.

118105.q: Why can a suction pump lift water by at most about 10 m?
a: Air pressure can hold up a water column of at most about 10 m
The pump gets too hot at greater heights
The water turns to ice higher up
The pipes burst at greater heights
118105.e: A suction pump only creates low pressure. The water is pushed up by the outside air pressure, and this can balance a water column of at most about 10 m.
118105.m: A suction pump can only lift water about ten metres.

118106.q: What is one pascal equal to?
118106.e: Pressure is force per area. One pascal is a force of 1 N acting on 1 m².
118106.m: One pascal is one newton per square metre.

118107.q: Who showed the force of air pressure with the Magdeburg hemispheres?
118107.e: Otto von Guericke pumped the air out of two hemispheres placed together. Afterwards not even teams of horses could pull them apart.
118107.m: Otto von Guericke proved the force of air pressure with hemispheres.

118108.q: Which scientist invented the mercury barometer?
118108.e: Around 1643 the Italian Evangelista Torricelli filled a glass tube with mercury and stood it upside down in a dish. The height of the column showed the air pressure.

118109.q: What force acts on the 10 m² floor of a pool filled with water to a depth of 2 m (g = 9.81 m/s², ignoring air pressure)?
118109.m: The force on the floor is the pressure times the floor area.

118110.q: What is true for a liquid at rest in containers that are open at the top and connected at the bottom?
a: It stands at the same height everywhere
It stands highest in the narrowest container
It stands highest in the widest container
It keeps flowing back and forth
118110.e: In equilibrium the pressure at the same height must be the same everywhere. That is only the case if the liquid level is the same, whatever the shape.
118110.m: In connected containers a liquid stands at the same height everywhere.

118111.q: Which tradesperson's tool uses the principle of connected vessels?
118111.e: A water level hose is a hose filled with water with two transparent ends. Both water surfaces stand at the same height, so you can transfer heights over long distances.
118111.m: A water level hose lets you transfer equal heights.

118112.q: In a U-tube, a 10 cm column of oil (ρ = 800 kg/m³) stands on top of the water on one side. How high does the water stand on the other side above the boundary between the liquids?
118112.e: At the height of the boundary the pressures are equal: 800 · 10 cm = 1000 · h. It follows that h = 8 cm.
118112.m: In a U-tube a lighter liquid stands higher than a heavier one.

118113.q: Why does the trap under the washbasin keep bad smells from the sewer out?
a: Water in the U-bend blocks the air
A filter in the pipe absorbs the smells
The drain is under high pressure
118113.e: Some water always stays in the bent pipe because both arms are connected. This water seals off the way for the sewer gases.
118113.m: The water in the trap holds back smells.

118114.q: Which structure used in shipping is based on the principle of connected vessels?
118114.e: In a lock, the chamber is connected to the upper or lower water. The water level evens out by itself, and the ship is raised or lowered.
118114.m: A lock raises ships by evening out water levels.

118115.q: Why are water reservoirs usually higher up than the houses they supply?
a: The water in the pipes rises to the height of the water surface
The water stays cooler up there
118115.e: The reservoir and the taps are connected by the pipes. If the tap is lower than the water surface in the reservoir, the water flows out without a pump.
118115.m: A reservoir high up creates water pressure in the pipes.

118116.q: Why is the opening of a watering can's spout at least as high as the rim of the can?
a: Otherwise the can would spill out of the spout before it is full
Otherwise the can would be too heavy
Otherwise the water would flow too slowly
Otherwise foam would form in the water
118116.e: The can and the spout are connected vessels. The water in the spout rises as high as in the can and would run out too early if the opening were lower.
118116.m: The spout of a can limits how full it can be.

118117.q: A U-tube contains mercury (13.6 g/cm³). Water is poured into one side until the two mercury levels differ by 1 cm. How high is the water column?
118117.e: The pressures above the lower boundary must be equal: 1 g/cm³ · h = 13.6 g/cm³ · 1 cm. So h = 13.6 cm.
118117.m: Water must stand 13.6 times higher than mercury for the same pressure.

118118.q: What is a well called from which groundwater rises to the surface by itself without a pump?
118118.e: If a water-bearing layer lies between impermeable layers and its catchment area reaches higher up, the groundwater is under pressure. When you drill into it, it rises by itself.
118118.m: An artesian well gushes without a pump.

118119.q: What does the hydrostatic paradox state?
a: The pressure on the bottom depends only on the depth of liquid, not on the shape of the container
The pressure on the bottom depends only on the amount of liquid
Wide containers always have the greatest pressure on the bottom
Narrow containers always have the greatest pressure on the bottom
118119.e: Containers with the same depth of the same liquid have the same pressure on the bottom, even if they hold very different amounts of liquid.
118119.m: For the pressure on the bottom only the depth counts, not the shape.

118120.q: Why is the hydrostatic paradox called a paradox?
a: The pressure on the bottom does not depend on the amount of water, which is surprising
Water can be compressed in tall containers
118120.e: You would expect more water to mean more pressure on the bottom. In fact only the depth and density count, not the amount or the shape of the container.
118120.m: The paradox is that the amount of water does not matter for the pressure on the bottom.

118121.q: What is Blaise Pascal said to have burst using a little water in a long, thin tube?
118121.e: In the so-called barrel experiment, a tall, thin tube was fitted into a closed barrel. Because of the great height, even a little water in the tube created such high pressure that the barrel burst.
118121.m: Even a little water in a tall tube can burst a barrel.

118122.q: Three containers of different shapes each have a base area of 20 cm² and are filled with water to a depth of 30 cm. What is the force on the bottom (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
a: About 5.9 N for all of them
About 59 N for all of them
118122.e: p = 1000 · 9.81 · 0.3 = 2943 Pa. F = 2943 Pa · 0.002 m² ≈ 5.9 N, for all three containers.
118122.m: The same depth and the same base area give the same force on the bottom.

118123.q: A tube 10 m tall with a cross-section of 1 cm² is full of water and fitted into a barrel. What extra force does this put on the barrel lid of 0.5 m² (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
118123.e: The pressure is p = 1000 · 9.81 · 10 = 98,100 Pa. On 0.5 m², F = 98,100 Pa · 0.5 m² ≈ 49 kN, even though there is only 1 litre of water in the tube.
118123.m: A tall, thin column of water creates large forces on large areas.

118124.q: Why do scales show more weight for a container that is wide at the top than the force on the container's bottom?
a: The water also presses down on the sloping side walls
The water is denser in the wide part
The air presses harder on wide surfaces
The scales measure pressure instead of force
118124.e: The force on the bottom depends only on the depth and the base area. The rest of the water's weight is passed on to the scales through the walls sloping outwards.
118124.m: Sloping container walls carry part of the liquid's weight.

118125.q: In a container that is narrower at the top than at the bottom, how does the force on the bottom compare with the weight of the liquid?
118125.e: The force on the bottom is pressure times base area and equals the weight of an imagined column over the whole base. This column holds more water than the narrowing container.
118125.m: In a container narrow at the top, the force on the bottom exceeds the weight of the liquid.

118126.q: How does the water pressure on a dam of a narrow, long reservoir compare with that of a wide lake of the same depth?
a: Much greater for the long lake
Much greater for the wide lake
118126.e: The pressure on the dam depends only on the depth of the water, not on how much water lies behind it.
118126.m: For the pressure on a dam, depth counts, not the amount of water.

a: Pressure in an enclosed liquid spreads equally everywhere
A body loses weight in a liquid
Liquids always flow to the lowest point
118127.e: If you apply pressure to an enclosed liquid, it is passed on unchanged to every point of the liquid and the container wall.
118127.m: Pressure on an enclosed liquid acts equally everywhere.

118128.q: In a hydraulic press, a force of 50 N acts on the 2 cm² piston. What force does the 200 cm² piston produce?
118128.e: The pressure is the same on both sides: F₂ = F₁ · A₂ / A₁ = 50 N · 200 / 2 = 5000 N.
118128.m: The force increases in the ratio of the piston areas.

118129.q: In a frictionless hydraulic press, how does the work done on the small piston compare with the work done by the large piston?
a: It is smaller at the small piston
It is smaller at the large piston
It depends on the air pressure
118129.e: A hydraulic press increases force, not energy. Force times distance is the same on both sides if there is no friction.
118129.m: A hydraulic press does not save work.

118130.q: Which vehicle system is based on Pascal's principle?
118130.e: Pressing the brake pedal creates pressure in the brake fluid. It is passed on evenly to all the wheel brakes.
118130.m: The hydraulic brake passes on pressure through the brake fluid.

118131.q: The pressure in the master cylinder of a hydraulic braking system is 40 bar. What pressure acts in the wheel cylinders, ignoring differences in height?
a: 10 bar in each of the four wheel cylinders
20 bar at the front and 20 bar at the back
118131.e: In an enclosed liquid, pressure is passed on unchanged. So each wheel cylinder gets the same 40 bar.
118131.m: The pressure in the brake fluid is the same at all the wheels.

118132.q: Why do hydraulic systems use a liquid such as oil rather than air?
118132.e: Air would be squeezed together a lot under pressure, and the piston would spring. Oil is almost incompressible and transmits the pressure directly.
118132.m: Hydraulics need a liquid that can hardly be compressed.

118133.q: A force of 300 N acts on a piston with an area of 15 cm². What pressure is created in the liquid?
118133.e: p = F / A = 300 N / 0.0015 m² = 200,000 Pa. That is 2 bar.
118133.m: Pressure is force divided by area.

118134.q: A car lift is to raise a car weighing 12,000 N. The large piston has 0.03 m², the small one 0.0005 m². What force is needed on the small piston?
118134.m: With a small piston you can lift heavy loads.

118135.q: How does the draught of a cargo ship change when it sails from the sea into a freshwater river?
a: It rises a little out of the water
118135.e: Fresh water is less dense than seawater. To get the same buoyancy, the ship must displace more water and sinks deeper.
118135.m: A ship lies deeper in fresh water than in the sea.

118136.q: What buoyant force acts on a body with a volume of 2 dm³ that is completely under water (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
118136.e: The body displaces 2 dm³ of water, which is 2 kg. F = 2 kg · 9.81 m/s² ≈ 19.6 N.
118136.m: The buoyant force depends on the volume under water.

118137.q: When does a body float at the surface of water?
a: When its average density is less than that of water
When its volume is more than 1 litre
When it is made of a light material
When its mass is less than 1 kg
118137.e: If the average density is less than that of the liquid, the buoyancy becomes as large as the weight when the body is only partly under water.
118137.m: A body floats if its average density is less than the liquid's.

118138.q: What fraction of an iceberg (ρ = 917 kg/m³) lies below the surface in seawater (ρ = 1025 kg/m³)?
118138.e: The fraction under water equals the ratio of the densities: 917 / 1025 ≈ 0.89. So about 90 per cent is under water.
118138.m: Most of an iceberg lies under water.

118139.q: What percentage of its volume does a block of wood with a density of 600 kg/m³ have under water?
118139.e: When floating, the fraction under water equals the ratio of the densities: 600 / 1000 = 0.6, so 60 per cent.
118139.m: The fraction under water equals the ratio of the densities.

118140.q: What does a submarine do to dive?
a: It floods its ballast tanks with water
It pumps air into its ballast tanks
It heats the water around it
118140.e: Flooding the ballast tanks makes the submarine heavier while its volume stays the same. Its average density rises above that of water, and it sinks.
118140.m: A submarine dives by taking water into its ballast tanks.

118141.q: Why do you hardly sink in the Dead Sea?
a: The very salty water has a high density
The water there is especially warm
The air pressure there is very high
The water there is very shallow
118141.e: The Dead Sea contains an extremely large amount of dissolved salt. The high density creates a large buoyant force, so people float on top almost by themselves.
118141.m: Salty water holds you up better than fresh water.

118142.q: A stone weighs 30 N in air and 18 N on a spring balance under water. What is its density?
118142.e: The buoyant force is 30 N minus 18 N, so 12 N. The density is 30 / 12 times the density of water, so 2.5 · 1000 kg/m³ = 2500 kg/m³.
118142.m: You can find the density from the loss of weight in water.

118143.q: Why does a hot-air balloon rise?
a: The hot air in the balloon is less dense than the surrounding air
The hot air pushes off from the ground
The burner creates a recoil downwards
The balloon's envelope is lighter than air
118143.e: Heated air expands and becomes less dense. The buoyancy from the displaced cold air is then greater than the total weight of the balloon.
118143.m: Warm air rises because it is less dense.

118144.q: What other name is the areometer known by?
118144.e: The areometer is a glass float that is lowered into the liquid and floats freely. It is usually called a hydrometer.
118144.m: The areometer is also called a hydrometer.

118145.q: How deep does a hydrometer sink in a liquid with a higher density?
a: It sinks to the same depth
118145.e: In a denser liquid, a smaller displaced volume is enough to carry the weight of the hydrometer.
118145.m: In dense liquids the hydrometer floats higher.

118146.q: Where are the higher density values on a hydrometer's scale?
a: At the bottom of the stem
At the top of the stem
In the middle of the stem
118146.e: In a dense liquid the instrument floats high, and the surface cuts the scale further down. That is why the high values are at the bottom.
118146.m: On a hydrometer the high density values are at the bottom.

118147.q: Which unit for the must weight of grape juice is common in Switzerland?
118147.e: Winemakers measure the sugar content of the must with a must hydrometer. In Switzerland the result is given in degrees Oechsle.
118147.m: In Switzerland must weight is measured in degrees Oechsle.

118148.q: What is the density of a grape must with 80 degrees Oechsle?
118148.e: Degrees Oechsle tell you by how many thousandths the density is above 1 g/cm³. So 80 degrees Oechsle means 1.080 g/cm³.
118148.m: Oechsle degrees show how much denser than water the must is.

118149.q: What is a hydrometer that shows the alcohol content of a mixture of water and alcohol called?
118149.e: Ethanol is less dense than water. The more alcohol a mixture contains, the deeper the alcoholmeter sinks.
118149.m: An alcoholmeter finds the alcohol content through the density.

118150.q: What were hydrometers used for with car lead-acid batteries?
a: To check the state of charge through the acid's density
118150.e: When the battery discharges, sulphuric acid is used up and the density of the acid falls. So the measured density shows the state of charge.
118150.m: The acid's density reveals the state of charge of a lead-acid battery.

118151.q: Why does a hydrometer have a weighted bulb at the bottom, for example with lead shot?
a: So that it floats upright and steady
So that it measures the temperature
118151.e: The weight at the bottom lowers the centre of mass. This makes the stem stand upright in the liquid so you can read the scale accurately.
118151.m: A low centre of mass keeps the hydrometer upright.

118152.q: What does the barometric formula describe?
a: How air pressure decreases with height
The water pressure at great depth
118152.e: The formula tells you how air pressure decreases with increasing height above sea level.
118152.m: The barometric formula describes air pressure at altitude.

118153.q: In an atmosphere with the same temperature everywhere, how does air pressure decrease with height?
118153.e: Because air can be compressed, the air lower down is denser. So for each step in height the pressure always falls by the same factor.
118153.m: Air pressure falls exponentially with height.

118154.q: At sea level, roughly how much does the air pressure fall if you climb 8 m higher?
118154.e: Near the ground, air pressure falls by about 1 hPa for every 8 m of height. Higher up, it takes more metres of height for the same fall.
118154.m: Near the ground, air pressure falls by about one hectopascal every eight metres.

118155.q: Roughly what is the scale height of the Earth's atmosphere?
118155.e: The scale height is the height over which the pressure falls to the fraction 1/e. With H = R·T / (M·g), you get about 8.4 km at around 15 °C.
118155.m: The scale height of the atmosphere is about eight kilometres.

118156.q: What is the air pressure on the Dufourspitze (4634 m) according to p = p₀·e^(−h/H) with p₀ = 1013 hPa and H = 8000 m?
118156.m: On the highest Swiss peaks the air pressure is almost halved.

118157.q: What assumption does the simple form of the barometric formula make?
a: The air temperature is the same everywhere
The air density is the same everywhere
The air is completely dry and still
118157.e: The simple formula assumes an isothermal atmosphere. In reality the temperature in the troposphere falls with height, which more exact formulas take into account.
118157.m: The simple barometric formula assumes a constant temperature.

118158.q: According to p = p₀·e^(−h/H) with p₀ = 1013 hPa, what is the air pressure exactly one scale height above sea level?
118158.e: When h equals H, p = p₀ / e = 1013 hPa / 2.718 ≈ 373 hPa.
118158.m: After one scale height the pressure has fallen to about 37 per cent.

118159.q: Why does a barometric altimeter need to be reset regularly?
a: Air pressure also changes with the weather
The Earth turns away beneath it
118159.e: Such an altimeter converts air pressure into a height. If the pressure changes because of a high or a low, it shows the wrong height until you reset it at a known point.
118159.m: Changes in the weather make barometric altimeters inaccurate.

118160.q: In which unit is surface tension given?
118160.e: Surface tension is force per length or energy per area. Both give the unit N/m, which is the same as J/m².
118160.m: Surface tension is measured in newtons per metre.

118161.q: Roughly what is the surface tension of water at 20 °C?
118161.e: At 20 °C water has a surface tension of about 72.8 mN/m. That is a high value for an ordinary liquid.
118161.m: Water has a comparatively high surface tension.

118162.q: What causes the surface tension of a liquid?
a: Molecules at the surface are only pulled inwards
The air presses down on the liquid from above
The container wall attracts the molecules
118162.e: Inside the liquid, each molecule is pulled by neighbours on all sides. At the surface there are no neighbours on one side, so a force pulls inwards and the surface becomes as small as possible.
118162.m: Cohesion pulls the molecules at the surface inwards.

118163.q: How does washing-up liquid affect the surface tension of water?
118163.e: Washing-up liquid contains surfactants, which collect at the surface of the water. They reduce the surface tension, so water wets grease and dirt better.

118164.q: Why do small drops of water form spheres in weightlessness?
a: For a given volume, a sphere has the smallest surface
The air presses them round from all sides
118164.e: Surface tension tends towards the smallest possible surface. Without gravity, that is the shape of a sphere.
118164.m: Without gravity, surface tension forms spheres.

118165.q: How does the surface tension of water change as the temperature rises?
a: It suddenly drops to zero at 50 °C
118165.e: As the temperature rises, the molecules move more strongly and the attraction between them has less effect. So the surface tension falls.
118165.m: Warm water has a lower surface tension than cold water.

118166.q: Which liquid has a much higher surface tension than water?
118166.e: Mercury has a surface tension about six to seven times greater than water. Ethanol, acetone and petrol are well below the value for water.
118166.m: Mercury has a very high surface tension.

118167.q: What is the excess pressure inside a soap bubble with a radius of 2 cm and σ = 0.025 N/m (Δp = 4σ/r)?
118167.e: Δp = 4 · 0.025 N/m / 0.02 m = 5 Pa. The factor of 4 comes from the two surfaces of the soap film.
118167.m: Small soap bubbles have a higher pressure inside than large ones.

118168.q: How does mercury behave in a narrow glass tube standing in mercury?
a: It stands at exactly the same height
118168.e: Mercury does not wet glass because cohesion is stronger than adhesion. So it sinks in the capillary; this is called capillary depression.
118168.m: Mercury sinks in narrow glass tubes.

118169.q: According to Jurin's law, how does the capillary rise depend on the radius of the tube?
a: It is inversely proportional to the radius
It is proportional to the radius
It is proportional to the square of the radius
It does not depend on the radius
118169.e: According to Jurin, h = 2σ·cos θ / (ρ·g·r). If you halve the radius, the height of rise doubles.
118169.m: The narrower the tube, the higher the liquid rises.

118170.q: The height of rise in a capillary is inversely proportional to its radius. How does the height change if you take a tube with half the radius?
118170.e: According to Jurin's law, h ~ 1/r. So half the radius gives twice the height. That is why water rises especially high in very fine pores.
118170.m: The narrower the capillary, the higher the liquid rises.

118171.q: Which everyday example is based on capillary action?
a: The wick draws liquid wax up to the flame
A balloon rises into the air
An ice cube floats in a glass
118171.e: In the wick, the fibres form fine gaps. The melted wax rises in them as if in many little tubes.
118171.m: A candle wick uses capillary action.

118172.q: When does a liquid rise in a capillary?
a: When adhesion to the wall is stronger than cohesion
When cohesion is stronger than adhesion
When the liquid is denser than glass
When the air pressure is especially low
118172.e: If the molecules stick more strongly to the wall than to each other, the liquid wets the wall and pulls itself up it.
118172.m: Strong adhesion to the wall makes liquid rise in capillaries.

118173.q: What shape is the water surface in a narrow, clean glass tube?
a: Curved downwards, lower in the middle
Curved upwards, higher in the middle
118173.e: Water wets glass and pulls itself up at the edge. This creates a concave meniscus that is lower in the middle.
118173.m: Water forms a concave meniscus in glass tubes.

118174.q: Which process is mainly responsible for water reaching the crown of tall trees?
118174.e: Capillary action only lifts water a little in the vessels. What really matters is the pull created by evaporation from the leaves, which draws the continuous threads of water upwards.
118174.m: Evaporation from the leaves pulls water up in trees.

118175.q: Why is a damp-proof course built into walls?
a: To stop moisture rising by capillary action
To keep out noise from outside
To prevent heat loss in winter
118175.e: Masonry contains fine pores in which water from the ground rises. A watertight layer interrupts these capillaries and keeps the wall dry.
118175.m: A damp-proof course stops rising damp in masonry.

118176.q: Against which two kinds of failure must a gravity dam mainly be secured?
118176.e: The water pressure pushes the dam horizontally and creates a torque about its downstream foot. Friction and the dam's own weight must prevent sliding and tipping.
118176.m: A gravity dam must neither slide nor tip over.

118177.q: Why is fresh concrete cooled, for example with cooling pipes, when building large gravity dams?
a: So that the heat from setting does not cause cracks
So that the concrete freezes faster
So that the water stays cooler later
So that the dam becomes lighter
118177.e: Heat is produced when cement sets. In thick masses of concrete it builds up, and cracks could form when the concrete later cools and shrinks.
118177.m: Large masses of concrete must be cooled during construction.

118178.q: At what height does the resultant water pressure force act on a vertical dam wall?
a: At one third of the water depth, measured from the bottom
At two thirds of the water depth, measured from the bottom
Exactly at the base of the dam
118178.e: Pressure increases linearly from the surface to the bottom, so the pressure distribution is a triangle. The centroid of a triangle lies at one third of its height above the base.
118178.m: The water force on a dam acts in the lower third.

118179.q: What cross-section does a gravity dam typically have?
118179.e: Water pressure increases with depth. That is why the dam must be widest and heaviest at the bottom.
118179.m: Gravity dams are wider at the bottom than at the top.

118180.q: What is the water pressure at the foot of a dam with a water depth of 100 m (g = 9.81 m/s², ignoring air pressure)?
118180.m: At the foot of high dams the water pressure is many bar.

118181.q: What water force acts on a 1 m wide strip of a vertical dam with a water depth of 100 m (F = ½·ρ·g·h² per metre, g = 9.81 m/s²)?
118181.e: F = 0.5 · 1000 · 9.81 · 100² ≈ 49,050,000 N, so about 49 MN per metre of dam width. Because the pressure increases linearly from top to bottom, you use half the pressure at the bottom.
118181.m: The force on a dam grows with the square of the water depth.

118182.q: Which type of dam is especially suitable for wide valleys whose sides cannot take a large arch thrust?
118182.e: An arch dam passes the load through the arch into the valley sides and needs solid rock there. A gravity dam, by contrast, carries the load into the ground through its weight.
118182.m: Gravity dams are often built in wide valleys.

118183.q: Why are seals and drains built under large gravity dams?
a: So that seeping water does not lift the dam from below
So that the reservoir fills faster
So that the dam does not freeze in winter
So that fish can swim under the dam
118183.e: Water seeps into joints under the dam and presses against it from below. This uplift reduces the stabilising effect of the dam's own weight; seals and drains keep it small.
118183.m: Water under the dam pushes it upwards.

a: The pressure of gases or liquids
118184.e: A manometer is a pressure gauge. It usually shows the pressure above the air pressure.
118184.m: A manometer is a pressure gauge.

118185.q: In a U-tube manometer filled with water, the difference in height is 15 cm. What is the measured pressure difference (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
118185.m: The difference in height in the U-tube shows the pressure difference.

118186.q: Which curved tube is the measuring element of many dial pressure gauges?
118186.e: The Bourdon tube is a flattened, curved, closed tube. When the pressure inside rises, it uncurls and moves the needle through a gear.
118186.m: A Bourdon tube uncurls under pressure and moves the needle.

118187.q: A tyre gauge shows 2.2 bar. Roughly what is the absolute pressure in the tyre at sea level?
118187.e: Tyre gauges show the pressure above that of the surroundings. Add the air pressure of about 1 bar, and you get an absolute pressure of about 3.2 bar.
118187.m: Absolute pressure is gauge pressure plus air pressure.

118188.q: In which unit is blood pressure traditionally given?
118188.e: Blood pressure used to be measured with mercury manometers. That is why it is still given in millimetres of mercury today.
118188.m: Blood pressure is given in millimetres of mercury.

118189.q: Why is the tube of a liquid manometer for very small pressures set at a slant?
a: The distance you read becomes longer and more accurate
The tube is less likely to break
118189.e: In an inclined manometer, the small difference in height is spread over a longer distance along the tube. This lets you read it more finely.
118189.m: A slanted tube makes small pressure differences easier to see.

118190.q: Roughly how many millimetres of mercury is a pressure of 1 kPa?
118190.e: 760 mmHg equals 101.325 kPa. So 1 kPa is about 760 / 101.3 ≈ 7.5 mmHg.
118190.m: One kilopascal is about seven and a half millimetres of mercury.

118191.q: Why are liquid manometers for higher pressures filled with mercury instead of water?
a: Its high density keeps the column short
118191.e: Mercury is more than ten times denser than water. So the same pressure needs a much shorter column, and the device stays easy to handle.
118191.m: A dense measuring liquid makes a manometer shorter.

118192.q: Which feature did the new high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice typically have in the Green Revolution?
a: High protein content in the straw
118192.e: Semi-dwarf varieties with short stalks do not bend over even with heavy fertilising and heavy ears. This meant fertiliser could be turned into grain yield.
118192.m: Short stalks stopped heavily fertilised cereals from falling over.

118193.q: What is the bending over of cereal stalks called, which the semi-dwarf varieties were meant to prevent?
118193.e: When cereals fall over because of wind, rain or heavy ears, this is called lodging. Short-stalked varieties are more resistant to it.
118193.m: Lodged cereals lie flat on the ground and give a smaller yield.

118194.q: Which rice variety became known as “miracle rice” in 1966 through the International Rice Research Institute IRRI?
118194.e: IR8 was a semi-dwarf high-yielding variety from the IRRI. With fertiliser it gave much higher yields than traditional varieties.
118194.m: The rice variety IR8 became famous as the “miracle rice” of the Green Revolution.

118195.q: In which country is the International Rice Research Institute IRRI?
118195.e: The IRRI was founded in 1960 in Los Baños in the Philippines. Important rice varieties of the Green Revolution were developed there.
118195.m: The rice research institute IRRI is based in the Philippines.

118196.q: What did the high-yielding varieties of the Green Revolution need in order to reach their potential?
a: Mineral fertiliser, irrigation and crop protection
A cool climate and little water
118196.e: The new varieties responded strongly to fertiliser and water. Without irrigation, mineral fertiliser and pesticides, yields often stayed low.
118196.m: High-yielding varieties need a lot of fertiliser, water and crop protection.

118197.q: Which ecological consequence of the Green Revolution is especially often criticised in the Indian Punjab?
118197.e: Intensive growing of rice and wheat with well irrigation has made the groundwater in the Punjab drop sharply. Added to this are soil pollution and the loss of old varieties.
118197.m: Intensive irrigation in the Punjab has made the groundwater level drop sharply.

118198.q: Which loss is the Green Revolution blamed for from the point of view of biodiversity?
a: The end of rice growing in Asia
118198.e: A few high-yielding varieties replaced many traditional landraces over large areas. This meant genetic diversity in the fields was lost.
118198.m: The Green Revolution pushed many old landraces out of the fields.

118199.q: Which plant breeder received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970 for his wheat varieties of the Green Revolution?
118199.e: Norman Borlaug bred short-stalked, high-yielding wheat varieties in Mexico. They helped to prevent famines in India and Pakistan.
118199.m: Norman Borlaug is considered the father of the Green Revolution.

118200.q: Which Nobel Prize did the agricultural scientist Norman Borlaug receive in 1970?
118200.e: Borlaug received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970 because his wheat breeding helped to prevent famines. There is no Nobel Prize for agricultural science.
118200.m: Norman Borlaug was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970 for his fight against hunger.

118201.q: In which country did Norman Borlaug begin his wheat breeding in the 1940s?
118201.e: From 1944 Borlaug worked in a programme in Mexico funded by the Rockefeller Foundation. The research centre CIMMYT later grew out of it.
118201.m: Borlaug's wheat breeding began in Mexico.

118202.q: Which feature did Borlaug's high-yielding wheat varieties have?
a: Ears with no grains at all
118202.e: Borlaug bred semi-dwarf wheat varieties. Their short stalks do not bend over under heavy ears and lots of fertiliser.
118202.m: Borlaug's wheat had short, sturdy stalks.

118203.q: What is meant by the “shuttle breeding” used by Borlaug?
a: Two breeding generations a year at two locations
118203.e: Borlaug grew wheat alternately in two places with different climates, in the highlands and in the north-west of the country. This gave him two generations a year and varieties adapted to different day lengths.
118203.m: Shuttle breeding doubles the number of breeding generations per year.

118204.q: Which fungal disease were Borlaug's wheat varieties meant to be especially resistant to?
118204.e: Stem rust (Puccinia graminis) destroyed wheat harvests again and again. Borlaug bred resistance to it into his varieties.
118204.m: Borlaug's wheat was meant to resist dangerous stem rust.

118205.q: Which prize for achievements against hunger did Norman Borlaug create in 1986?
118205.e: Borlaug proposed the World Food Prize, which has been awarded every year since 1987. It is seen as a kind of Nobel Prize for food and agriculture.
118205.m: The World Food Prize goes back to Norman Borlaug.

118206.q: Which country did Norman Borlaug come from?
118206.e: Borlaug was born in 1914 in the US state of Iowa, and his family had Norwegian roots. He died in Dallas in 2009.
118206.m: Norman Borlaug was an American agricultural scientist.

118207.q: What is Norman Borlaug often called because of his role in increasing yields?
118207.e: His wheat varieties were at the heart of the Green Revolution in Mexico, India and Pakistan. That is why he is seen as its most important pioneer.
118207.m: Norman Borlaug is considered the father of the Green Revolution.

118208.q: Which crops does the CIMMYT centre in Mexico, which grew out of Borlaug's programme, research?
118208.e: CIMMYT is the international research centre for maize and wheat. It continues Borlaug's breeding work.

118209.q: Which extra substance does Golden Rice produce in its grains?
118209.e: Golden Rice produces beta-carotene, a precursor of vitamin A, in the endosperm. This is also where its yellow colour comes from.
118209.m: Golden Rice contains beta-carotene, a precursor of vitamin A.

118210.q: Which deficiency is Golden Rice meant to help against?
118210.e: In countries where rice is the staple food, many children suffer from vitamin A deficiency. This can lead to blindness and a seriously weakened immune system.
118210.m: Golden Rice is meant to fight vitamin A deficiency in rice-eating countries.

118211.q: Which illness is a typical result of vitamin A deficiency?
118211.e: Vitamin A is needed for the visual pigment rhodopsin. Without it, people see badly at dusk and may later go blind.
118211.m: Vitamin A deficiency first leads to night blindness.

118212.q: In which part of the rice grain is beta-carotene produced in Golden Rice?
118212.e: Normal rice produces carotenoids only in green parts of the plant, not in the endosperm. Thanks to the added genes, the metabolic pathway runs in the endosperm, which is the part that is eaten.
118212.m: In Golden Rice, beta-carotene forms in the edible endosperm.

118213.q: With which method was Golden Rice produced?
118213.e: Genes from other organisms were inserted into the rice, first from the daffodil and a bacterium. This allows the rice to produce beta-carotene in the grain.
118213.m: Golden Rice was created through genetic engineering.

118214.q: Which improvement did Golden Rice 2, presented in 2005, bring?
118214.e: With a phytoene synthase gene from maize, the beta-carotene content rose many times over. So a normal portion can cover a large part of the vitamin A requirement.
118214.m: Golden Rice 2 contains much more beta-carotene than the first version.

118215.q: Which country was the first to allow the commercial growing of Golden Rice in 2021?
118215.e: In 2021 the Philippines became the first country to approve its cultivation. In 2024 a Philippine court temporarily stopped the growing again.
118215.m: In 2021 the Philippines became the first country to approve Golden Rice.

118216.q: Which countries classed Golden Rice as safe to eat in 2018 without growing it themselves?
118216.e: The food authorities of Australia and New Zealand, Canada and the USA assessed Golden Rice as safe in 2018. This would mean imported Golden Rice, for example, would be allowed as food there.
118216.m: Several countries declared Golden Rice safe as food in 2018.

118217.q: At which university did Ingo Potrykus develop Golden Rice?
118217.e: Potrykus was a professor at the Institute of Plant Sciences at ETH Zurich. Golden Rice was developed there at the end of the 1990s.
118217.m: Ingo Potrykus developed Golden Rice at ETH Zurich.

118218.q: Which substance does Golden Rice produce in its grains that gives it its yellow colour?
118218.e: Potrykus and Peter Beyer inserted genes so that the rice produces beta-carotene in the grain. The body turns it into vitamin A.
118218.m: Golden Rice contains beta-carotene, a precursor of vitamin A.

118219.q: In which year did Potrykus and his team publish Golden Rice in the journal “Science”?
118219.e: The paper appeared in “Science” in January 2000. In the same year, “Time” magazine put Golden Rice on its cover.
118219.m: Golden Rice was presented to the public in 2000.

118220.q: Which country does the plant biologist Ingo Potrykus, who did research in Switzerland for a long time, come from?
118220.e: Potrykus was born in 1933 in Hirschberg in the Giant Mountains, which belonged to Germany at the time and is now in Poland. He is regarded as a German plant biologist.
118220.m: Ingo Potrykus is a German plant biologist.

118221.q: According to Potrykus, under which conditions should poor farmers be allowed to use Golden Rice?
a: Free of charge through humanitarian licences
Only with hybrid seed bought new every year
118221.e: Potrykus and Beyer agreed with companies that smallholder farmers on low incomes may grow the rice without fees and save seed to sow again.
118221.m: Golden Rice is meant to be available free of charge to smallholder farmers.

118222.q: Which nutrient deficiency is Golden Rice meant to help against in poor countries?
118222.e: In children, vitamin A deficiency can lead to blindness and serious illnesses. Golden Rice provides a precursor of vitamin A.
118222.m: Golden Rice is meant to prevent vitamin A deficiency.

118223.q: With which argument did Ingo Potrykus defend Golden Rice against critics?
a: Strict regulation was delaying help against vitamin A deficiency
Rice was unnecessary as a food
Genetic engineering was cheaper than any breeding
118223.e: Potrykus criticised the fact that approval procedures lasting decades had delayed its use while children suffered from vitamin A deficiency.
118223.m: Potrykus criticised the long delay to Golden Rice caused by regulation.

118224.q: With which method was Golden Rice created?
118224.e: Genes from other organisms, such as the daffodil and a bacterium, were inserted into Golden Rice. That is why it is a genetically modified plant.
118224.m: Golden Rice is a genetically modified plant.

118225.q: Which two researchers received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020 for the CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors?
118225.e: In 2012 Charpentier and Doudna described how CRISPR/Cas9 can be programmed to target specific places. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020.
118225.m: Charpentier and Doudna won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the gene scissors.

118226.q: What is the original function of the CRISPR/Cas system in bacteria?
118226.e: Bacteria store pieces of foreign virus DNA in the CRISPR region. When a new infection happens, Cas recognises the virus genes and cuts them up.
118226.m: CRISPR/Cas is originally an immune system that bacteria use against viruses.

118227.q: What guides the enzyme Cas9 to the right place in the genome?
118227.e: The guide RNA is built to match a target sequence of the DNA. It binds there and brings Cas9 to exactly that spot.
118227.m: The guide RNA shows Cas9 where to cut the DNA.

118228.q: What does Cas9 do at the target site in the DNA?
a: It cuts through both DNA strands
It translates the DNA into protein
118228.e: Cas9 is a nuclease and makes a double-strand break. The cell then repairs it, and changes can arise or be inserted in the process.
118228.m: Cas9 cuts the DNA at a precisely chosen spot.

118229.q: For which hereditary disease was a therapy using CRISPR/Cas approved for the first time in 2023?
118229.e: At the end of 2023 a CRISPR therapy for sickle cell disease was approved in Great Britain and the USA. In it, the patients' blood stem cells are changed outside the body.
118229.m: The first approved CRISPR therapy treats sickle cell disease.

118230.q: What does the abbreviation CRISPR stand for?
a: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats
Chromosomal Repair by Integrated Special Proteins
Cell nucleus Recombination In Specific Plant Regions
Chemical Regulation of Intracellular Signalling Proteins
118230.e: CRISPR stands for Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats. This means short repeats in the bacterial genome with pieces of virus between them.
118230.m: CRISPR refers to regularly interrupted short repeats in the bacterial genome.

118231.q: How did the European Court of Justice rule in 2018 on genome-edited plants, for example those made with CRISPR?
a: They count as genetically modified organisms
118231.e: In July 2018 the European Court of Justice ruled that organisms made with new mutagenesis methods fall under genetic engineering law. Since then the EU has been working on new rules.
118231.m: According to the 2018 European Court ruling, CRISPR plants count as GMOs.

118232.q: What advantage does CRISPR/Cas have over classic mutation breeding?
a: Changes can be made precisely at a particular spot
It always changes the whole genome
118232.e: In mutation breeding, mutations arise randomly throughout the genome. CRISPR, by contrast, changes a spot chosen in advance.
118232.m: CRISPR changes the genome in a targeted way instead of randomly.

118233.q: After the Cas9 cut, what can a cell do if it is given a matching piece of DNA as a template?
118233.e: The cell repairs the double-strand break. If a matching template is available, it can copy it and so insert a new sequence at the cut site.
118233.m: With a template, new DNA can be inserted after the cut.

118234.q: In which year did Swiss voters accept the initiative for a moratorium on genetic engineering in agriculture?
118234.e: On 27 November 2005 the popular initiative “for food from GM-free agriculture” was accepted. For the time being it banned the commercial growing of GM plants.
118234.m: The GM moratorium was decided by the people in 2005.

118235.q: What does the Swiss GM moratorium ban?
a: The commercial growing of genetically modified plants
The production of medicines with genetic engineering
118235.e: The moratorium concerns putting genetically modified plants and animals for agriculture on the market. Research and medicine are not affected.
118235.m: The moratorium bans the commercial growing of GM plants in Switzerland.

118236.q: According to the 2005 initiative, how many years was the GM moratorium originally meant to last?
118236.e: The initiative called for a moratorium of five years. After that, parliament extended it several times.
118236.m: The moratorium was at first limited to five years.

118237.q: Until when did parliament extend the GM moratorium in 2025?
118237.e: The moratorium would have expired at the end of 2025. In 2025 the National Council and the Council of States extended it by five years until the end of 2030.
118237.m: After the 2025 extension, the GM moratorium applies until the end of 2030.

118238.q: Are field trials with genetically modified plants allowed in Switzerland despite the moratorium?
a: Yes, for research purposes with a permit
118238.e: The moratorium makes an exception for research. Agroscope runs a protected trial site in Zurich-Reckenholz for approved field trials.
118238.m: GM field research is allowed in Switzerland with a permit.

118239.q: What is the federal law called that regulates the handling of genetically modified organisms outside the human field in Switzerland?
118239.e: The Gene Technology Act of 2003 regulates the handling of GMOs in animals, plants and the environment. The moratorium is written into it as a transitional provision.
118239.m: The Gene Technology Act regulates the handling of GMOs in Switzerland.

118240.q: Apart from the moratorium, which new rule does the Federal Council want to create for new breeding methods such as genome editing?
a: A duty to use mutation breeding
118240.e: Parliament called for risk-based rules for new breeding technologies. The Federal Council proposed a separate law for this.
118240.m: The federal government is planning a separate law for new breeding methods.

118241.q: How many cantons voted for the GM-free initiative in 2005?
118241.e: The initiative won around 56 per cent of the votes and was accepted in every canton. At the time this was a surprise.
118241.m: The GM-free initiative was accepted in all cantons in 2005.

118242.q: Under Swiss and EU law, what is a genetically modified organism (GMO)?
a: An organism whose genes have been changed in a way that does not happen naturally
Any cultivated crop that has been bred
118242.e: What matters is that the genes were not changed by crossing or natural recombination. Classic breeding does not produce GMOs in the legal sense.
118242.m: A GMO has genes that were changed in an unnatural way.

118243.q: Which genetically modified food was the first to go on sale in the USA in 1994?
118243.e: The Flavr Savr tomato was meant to soften more slowly. It was not a commercial success and soon disappeared again.
118243.m: The Flavr Savr tomato was the first GM food on sale in 1994.

118244.q: What applies in Switzerland to foods that contain genetically modified ingredients?
a: They may be sold without any notice
They are only available in chemists
They are only allowed as animal feed
118244.e: GM ingredients must be declared. Only accidental, technically unavoidable traces below 0.9 per cent per ingredient are exempt from labelling.
118244.m: Genetically modified ingredients must be declared.

a: The genome contains genes from another species
The plant has only been crossed
The gene comes from the same plant
118245.e: In transgenic organisms, genes from another species have been inserted, for example bacterial genes into maize. In cisgenic plants the genes come from the same species or one it can be crossed with.
118245.m: Transgenic organisms carry genes from a foreign species.

118246.q: Which method shoots gold or tungsten particles coated with DNA into plant cells?
118246.e: With the gene gun, tiny metal particles are loaded with DNA and shot into cells at high speed. This gets genes into plants that are difficult to modify with bacteria.
118246.m: The gene gun shoots DNA-coated metal particles into cells.

118247.q: Which international agreement regulates the movement of genetically modified organisms across borders?
118247.e: The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety adds to the Convention on Biological Diversity. It came into force in 2003, and Switzerland is also a party to it.
118247.m: The Cartagena Protocol regulates the international trade in GMOs.

118248.q: Which characteristic did the Roundup Ready soya introduced in 1996 have?
118248.e: The soya survives being sprayed with glyphosate, while weeds do not. Herbicide tolerance is still one of the most common GM traits today.
118248.m: Roundup Ready soya tolerates the herbicide glyphosate.

118249.q: What were antibiotic resistance genes often used for in early genetically modified plants?
a: As markers to pick out modified cells
To protect the plant from insects
As a nutrient for the plant
118249.e: Only cells that had taken up the new gene together with the marker survived on a nutrient medium containing an antibiotic. Today people try to avoid such markers.
118249.m: Marker genes help to find cells that have been successfully modified.

118250.q: In which group of plants was gene transfer with Agrobacterium tumefaciens much easier at first?
118250.e: In nature, Agrobacterium mainly infects dicot plants. In cereals the method only worked later with improved procedures, which is why the gene gun was often used there.
118250.m: Agrobacterium is especially well suited to dicot plants.

118251.q: What is the plasmid called that Agrobacterium tumefaciens uses to change plant cells?
118251.e: Ti stands for “tumour-inducing”. A section of this plasmid is inserted into the genome of the plant cell.
118251.m: The Ti plasmid is the tool of Agrobacterium.

118252.q: What is the section of DNA called that Agrobacterium transfers into the plant's genome?
118252.e: The transfer DNA (T-DNA) lies on the Ti plasmid between two border sequences. Genetic engineers replace its contents with the genes they want.
118252.m: The T-DNA is inserted into the plant genome by the bacterium.

118253.q: How does the bacterium benefit from infected plant cells producing opines?
a: It can use the opines as food
The opines make the plant invisible
The opines serve as a spore coat
118253.e: The transferred genes make the plant cells produce opines, which almost only Agrobacterium can use. In this way the bacterium creates its own food source.
118253.m: Agrobacterium makes the plant produce opines as food for itself.

118254.q: Why is Agrobacterium tumefaciens often called a “natural genetic engineer”?
a: Because it naturally inserts genes into plants
118254.e: Long before humans used genetic engineering, the bacterium was transferring its own genes into plant cells. Researchers use exactly this mechanism.
118254.m: Agrobacterium naturally transfers genes into plants.

118255.q: Which disease does Agrobacterium tumefaciens cause in plants?
118255.e: The bacterium inserts genes into plant cells that make them grow out of control. This produces tumour-like swellings at the root collar, called galls.

118256.q: With which plant was one of the first genetic modifications using Agrobacterium achieved in 1983?
118256.e: Tobacco is easy to grow in the laboratory and to regenerate from single cells. That is why it was one of the first transgenic plants.
118256.m: Tobacco was one of the first plants modified with Agrobacterium.

118257.q: In nature, how does Agrobacterium tumefaciens get into a plant?
a: Through injuries at the root collar or trunk
118257.e: Injured plant tissue releases phenols such as acetosyringone. These attract the bacterium and switch on the genes for gene transfer.

118258.q: Where does the gene come from that makes Bt maize produce an insect-killing protein?
118258.e: Bt stands for Bacillus thuringiensis. This soil bacterium produces Cry proteins, which are poisonous to certain insect larvae.
118258.m: Bt maize carries a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis.

118259.q: Against which pest was Bt maize mainly developed in Europe?
118259.e: The caterpillars of the European corn borer bore into maize stalks and weaken the plant. The Cry protein in Bt maize kills these caterpillars.
118259.m: Bt maize protects against the European corn borer.

118260.q: Why is the Bt protein harmless to humans but deadly to certain insect larvae?
a: It is only activated in the alkaline gut of the larvae and needs matching receptors
It only works in the cold
118260.e: The protein is split in the alkaline insect gut and binds to special receptors in the gut wall. Mammals have neither these conditions nor these receptors.
118260.m: Bt protein only works in the alkaline gut of certain insects.

118261.q: How is the growing of genetically modified plants such as Bt maize regulated in Switzerland?
a: It is only allowed in Ticino
It is only allowed for organic farms
118261.e: After a popular vote in 2005, Switzerland has had a GM moratorium for agriculture. Parliament has extended it several times since then.
118261.m: Switzerland has a GM moratorium on growing such crops.

118262.q: In what form is the Bt protein also used in organic farming?
a: As a spray containing the bacteria or their proteins
As a seed treatment against fungi
118262.e: Products made from Bacillus thuringiensis are allowed as insecticides in organic farming. They are sprayed onto the outside of the plants.
118262.m: Bt products are also sprayed in organic farming.

118263.q: What are the so-called refuges next to Bt maize fields meant to prevent?
a: Pests developing resistance to the Bt protein
118263.e: Maize without the Bt gene grows in the refuges. Sensitive insects survive there and mate with resistant ones, which slows the spread of resistance.
118263.m: Refuges slow down the development of resistance to Bt plants.

118264.q: Which group of insects does the European corn borer, which Bt maize works against, belong to?
118264.e: The European corn borer is a small moth. Its caterpillars eat their way into maize stalks and are killed by the Bt protein.
118264.m: The European corn borer is a moth.

118265.q: What advantage is Bt maize meant to bring for crop protection?
a: Fewer insecticide sprayings against boring caterpillars
118265.e: Caterpillars inside the stalk are hard to reach with sprays. Because the plant produces the toxin itself, insecticides can often be avoided.
118265.m: Bt maize can save insecticide sprayings.

118266.q: Where is the International Union for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants (UPOV) based?
118266.e: UPOV was founded in 1961 by a convention signed in Paris. It is based in Geneva and is closely linked with WIPO.
118266.m: The plant variety union UPOV is based in Geneva.

118267.q: Which three technical criteria must a variety meet to receive plant variety protection?
118267.e: The DUS test (distinctness, uniformity, stability) checks whether the variety clearly stands out, is uniform and stays the same over generations. Novelty and a variety name are also required.
118267.m: A protected variety must be distinct, uniform and stable.

118268.q: What does the so-called breeders' exemption in plant variety protection allow?
a: Using protected varieties freely to breed new varieties
Selling other people's varieties under your own name
118268.e: Other breeders may use a protected variety for crosses without permission. This clearly distinguishes plant variety protection from a patent.
118268.m: Thanks to the breeders' exemption, protected varieties may be used for further breeding.

118269.q: What applies to a plant variety once its protection has expired?
a: Anyone may freely propagate and sell it
It may no longer be grown
It becomes the property of the state
118269.e: Plant variety protection is limited in time, in Switzerland usually to 25 years, and to 30 years for vines and trees. After that the variety can be used freely.
118269.m: Once protection expires, a variety can be used freely.

118270.q: What does the farmers' privilege allow?
a: Sowing harvested seed of a protected variety again on your own farm
Registering any variety as your own
118270.e: With the farmers' privilege, farmers may sow seed they have harvested themselves on their own farm for certain species. Selling it remains forbidden.
118270.m: The farmers' privilege allows saved seed to be sown again on your own farm.

118271.q: Which federal office is responsible for granting plant variety protection in Switzerland?
a: The Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH)
The Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN)
118271.e: The Plant Variety Protection Office is part of the Federal Office for Agriculture. It checks applications and grants the protection titles.
118271.m: In Switzerland the FOAG grants plant variety protection.

118272.q: Can plant varieties as such be patented in Europe?
a: No, they are excluded from patent protection
Yes, every variety is automatically patented
118272.e: The European Patent Convention excludes plant varieties from being patented. Plant variety protection exists for them instead.
118272.m: In Europe plant varieties are protected by plant variety protection instead of patents.

118273.q: What is the international organisation UPOV, based in Geneva, responsible for?
a: The protection of newly bred plant varieties
The protection of endangered wild plants
118273.e: UPOV is based on a convention from 1961. It makes sure that breeders can have their new varieties protected in many countries under the same rules. Switzerland is a member.
118273.m: UPOV regulates international plant variety protection.

118274.q: What is the aim of the Swiss foundation ProSpecieRara?
a: Preserving rare livestock breeds and crop varieties
118274.e: ProSpecieRara saves breeds and varieties of cultural, historical and genetic value from dying out. To do this it works with farmers, gardeners and variety keepers.
118274.m: ProSpecieRara saves old livestock breeds and crop plants.

118275.q: What did ProSpecieRara focus on first when it was founded?
118275.e: The foundation was set up in 1982 and first looked after endangered livestock breeds. Crop varieties were added later.
118275.m: ProSpecieRara began by saving old livestock breeds.

118276.q: Which breed of goat is looked after by ProSpecieRara?
118276.e: The booted goat from the St Gallen Oberland had almost died out in the 1980s. ProSpecieRara helped to build up its numbers again.
118276.m: The booted goat is a goat breed saved by ProSpecieRara.

118277.q: Which breed of cattle from the Grisons was rebuilt thanks to ProSpecieRara?
118277.e: The Rhaetian Grey was thought to be extinct in Switzerland. From the 1980s it was reintroduced using animals from Tyrol.
118277.m: The Rhaetian Grey returned to Switzerland thanks to ProSpecieRara.

118278.q: Which old Swiss chicken breed with a forward-pointing crest of feathers is preserved by ProSpecieRara?
118278.e: The Appenzeller Spitzhauben had almost died out by around 1950. ProSpecieRara started a conservation project for the breed in 1983.
118278.m: The Appenzeller Spitzhauben is an old Swiss chicken breed.

118279.q: How does ProSpecieRara keep old vegetable varieties alive?
a: By having many gardeners grow them and save their seed
Only by freezing them in the laboratory
118279.e: The varieties are grown in gardens and on farms, and their seed is collected anew every year. This way they stay adapted to their environment and alive.
118279.m: ProSpecieRara preserves varieties by having them grown regularly in many gardens.

118280.q: Why are most ProSpecieRara varieties suitable for saving your own seed, but modern F1 hybrids hardly at all?
a: Because they are open-pollinated and breed true
118280.e: Open-pollinated varieties pass their characteristics on to their offspring. In F1 hybrids the traits split up in the next generation.
118280.m: Open-pollinated varieties can be grown again from your own seed.

118281.q: In which city does the ProSpecieRara foundation have its head office?
118281.e: The head office is in Basel on the Brüglingen site. There are also offices in French-speaking Switzerland and in Ticino.
118281.m: ProSpecieRara has its head office in Basel.

118282.q: In mutation breeding, how are changes in the genes triggered?
118282.e: Seeds or plant parts are treated with gamma rays, X-rays or chemicals, for example. The random mutations that result are then selected.
118282.m: Mutation breeding uses radiation or chemicals to create random mutations.

a: A substance or radiation that causes mutations
118283.e: Mutagens such as UV radiation, X-rays or certain chemicals change the genes. In mutation breeding they are used deliberately.
118283.m: Mutagens cause changes in the genes.

118284.q: Do plants from classic mutation breeding legally count as GMOs that must be labelled in the EU and Switzerland?
a: No, they are exempt from genetic engineering regulation
Only if they come from Japan
118284.e: Conventional mutagenesis is exempt because it has been used safely for a long time. Such varieties are also widespread in organic farming.
118284.m: Classic mutation breeding is exempt from GMO regulation.

118285.q: Which international organisations jointly run a database of over 3,000 mutant varieties?
118285.e: The joint division of the Food and Agriculture Organization FAO and the International Atomic Energy Agency IAEA promotes mutation breeding. Its database lists over 3,000 varieties worldwide.
118285.m: FAO and IAEA jointly promote mutation breeding.

118286.q: Why do a great many plants have to be checked after seeds have been irradiated?
a: Most mutations are useless or harmful
Every plant has the same mutation
118286.e: The mutations arise randomly. Only very rarely does one of them improve a desired characteristic, which is why a large selection is needed.

118287.q: Are foods from plants produced by mutation breeding radioactive themselves?
a: No, only the genes were changed
Yes, they give off radiation for life
118287.e: The radiation changes the DNA of the treated seeds but does not make them radioactive. The offspring are normal plants with changed characteristics.
118287.m: Mutation breeding does not make plants radioactive.

118288.q: Which kind of radiation can damage the genes of skin cells in humans, just as in mutation breeding?
118288.e: UV radiation can change the DNA in skin cells. Such mutations can cause skin cancer, which is why sun protection is important.
118288.m: UV radiation can damage the genes.

118289.q: What is the biggest disadvantage of mutation breeding compared with genome editing?
a: The mutations are undirected, so many plants have to be searched
It is banned in every country
It does not change the genes at all
118289.e: Radiation or chemicals hit the genome randomly in many places. That is why thousands of plants have to be checked to find a useful mutant.
118289.m: Mutation breeding is undirected and needs a large selection.

118290.q: What is a “gamma garden” in plant breeding?
a: A trial field around a radiation source to cause mutations
A garden with only plants of the genus Gamma
A school garden with three beds
118290.e: In gamma gardens, plants grow in circles around a radioactive source, usually cobalt-60. The closer they are, the stronger the radiation and the more mutations there are.
118290.m: In gamma gardens, plants are irradiated for mutation breeding.

118291.q: For which discovery did Wolfgang Pauli receive the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1945?
118291.e: The Pauli principle states that two electrons in an atom never agree in all their quantum numbers. It explains the structure of the periodic table.
118291.m: The Pauli principle explains why electrons occupy shells.

118292.q: In which city was the later Swiss physicist Wolfgang Pauli born?
118292.e: Pauli was born in Vienna in 1900. From 1928 he taught at ETH Zurich and in 1949 became a Swiss citizen.
118292.m: Wolfgang Pauli came from Vienna and worked in Zurich.

118293.q: At which university was Wolfgang Pauli professor of theoretical physics from 1928?
118293.e: Pauli was appointed to ETH Zurich in 1928 and stayed there until his death in 1958, with a break in the USA during the Second World War.
118293.m: Pauli taught at ETH Zurich for about three decades.

118294.q: Which particle did Wolfgang Pauli postulate in 1930 to explain the loss of energy in beta decay?
118294.e: In beta decay energy seemed to disappear. Pauli proposed a neutral, very light particle, which was detected only in 1956.
118294.m: Pauli predicted the neutrino long before it could be detected.

118295.q: With which famous form of address does Pauli’s letter of 1930, in which he proposed the neutrino, begin?
118295.e: Pauli wrote the letter to a conference of physicists in Tübingen, which he did not attend. The humorous greeting is still well known today.
118295.m: Pauli’s neutrino letter begins with “Dear Radioactive Ladies and Gentlemen”.

118296.q: What is meant by the humorous “Pauli effect”?
a: Experiments supposedly broke down when Pauli was nearby
118296.e: An anecdote went round among colleagues that equipment failed as soon as the theorist Pauli entered a laboratory. Physically, of course, it is no effect.
118296.m: The Pauli effect is an anecdote about broken experiments near Pauli.

118297.q: Which property of electrons did Pauli describe mathematically with the matrices named after him?
118297.e: The Pauli matrices describe the spin of the electron in quantum mechanics. Spin is a kind of intrinsic angular momentum with two possible settings.
118297.m: Pauli matrices describe the spin of electrons.

118298.q: Which famous physicist nominated Wolfgang Pauli for the Nobel Prize?
118298.e: Einstein nominated Pauli for the prize of 1945. Pauli was then in Princeton, where Einstein worked too.
118298.m: Albert Einstein nominated Pauli for the Nobel Prize.

118299.q: In which city was the physicist Felix Bloch born in 1905?
118299.e: Bloch was born in Zurich and studied at ETH. Later he emigrated to the USA and taught at Stanford University.
118299.m: Felix Bloch was a native of Zurich.

118300.q: For what did Felix Bloch receive the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1952?
a: For new methods of nuclear magnetic resonance
For the discovery of the electron
For the invention of the laser
118300.e: Bloch developed methods to measure the magnetic properties of atomic nuclei precisely. NMR spectroscopy in chemistry and biology is built on this.
118300.m: Felix Bloch laid foundations for nuclear magnetic resonance.

118301.q: Which medical imaging method is based on the nuclear magnetic resonance that Felix Bloch helped to discover?
118301.e: Felix Bloch and Edward Purcell discovered nuclear magnetic resonance independently of each other. MRI uses it to produce pictures of the inside of the body without X-rays.
118301.m: MRI is based on nuclear magnetic resonance.

118302.q: In which branch of physics is the Bloch theorem, named after Felix Bloch, fundamental?
118302.e: The Bloch theorem describes how electrons behave in a regular crystal lattice. It is the basis for understanding metals and semiconductors.
118302.m: The Bloch theorem describes electrons in crystals.

118303.q: What position did Felix Bloch take on in Geneva in 1954?
a: Rector of the University of Geneva
118303.e: From 1954 to 1955 Bloch was the first Director-General of the newly founded European Organization for Nuclear Research. After that he returned to Stanford.
118303.m: Felix Bloch was the first Director-General of CERN.

118304.q: For which discovery did the Swiss physicist Felix Bloch receive the Nobel Prize in 1952?
a: For the discovery of the neutron
For the invention of the laser
For the fission of the uranium nucleus
118304.e: Bloch and Edward Purcell developed, independently of each other, methods to measure the magnetic properties of atomic nuclei. Magnetic resonance imaging is based on this today.
118304.m: Felix Bloch received the Nobel Prize for nuclear magnetic resonance.

118305.q: At which US university did Felix Bloch do research after his emigration?
118305.e: Because of the Nazis’ seizure of power, Bloch left Germany in 1933. From 1934 he taught at Stanford in California.

118306.q: Which medical imaging method is based on the nuclear magnetic resonance that Felix Bloch helped to discover?
118306.e: MRI uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to measure the signals of hydrogen nuclei in the body. X-rays and CT, by contrast, work with X-radiation, and ultrasound with sound waves.
118306.m: MRI is based on the nuclear magnetic resonance of Felix Bloch.

118307.q: In which Swiss company did Heinrich Rohrer and Gerd Binnig develop the scanning tunnelling microscope?
a: In the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon
118307.e: Rohrer and Binnig worked in the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon near Zurich. The first measurements succeeded in 1981, and in 1986 they received the Nobel Prize.
118307.m: The scanning tunnelling microscope arose at IBM in Rüschlikon.

118308.q: With which components is the tip of the scanning tunnelling microscope moved extremely finely?
118308.e: Piezo crystals deform minimally when a voltage is applied. In this way the tip can be controlled to fractions of a nanometre.
118308.m: Piezo elements move the microscope tip with atomic accuracy.

118309.q: In which environment can a scanning tunnelling microscope be operated?
a: In a vacuum, in air and even in liquids
118309.e: Unlike an electron microscope, the scanning tunnelling microscope needs no vacuum, because the electrons only cross a tiny gap. For the cleanest measurements, however, people often work in ultra-high vacuum.
118309.m: A scanning tunnelling microscope also works in air and in liquids.

118310.q: Which researcher received in 1986 the other half of the Nobel Prize in Physics that Rohrer and Binnig shared?
118310.e: Ernst Ruska was honoured for developing the electron microscope in the 1930s. The prize thus honoured two generations of microscopy.
118310.m: In 1986 the Nobel Prize in Physics also honoured Ernst Ruska for the electron microscope.

118311.q: What was made directly visible for the first time with the scanning tunnelling microscope?
118311.e: The scanning tunnelling microscope scans surfaces so finely that single atoms appear as bumps. This convinced the scientific world and brought the Nobel Prize in 1986.
118311.m: The scanning tunnelling microscope makes single atoms visible.

118312.q: Which country did Heinrich Rohrer’s partner Gerd Binnig come from?
118312.e: Gerd Binnig is a German physicist who worked with Rohrer at IBM in Rüschlikon. Later he also co-invented the atomic force microscope.
118312.m: Gerd Binnig is a German physicist.

118313.q: What can you do with a scanning tunnelling microscope, as well as imaging?
118313.e: With the tip, atoms can be moved on a surface. In 1989 IBM researchers used it to write the company logo from 35 xenon atoms.
118313.m: With a scanning tunnelling microscope, single atoms can be moved.

118314.q: What condition must a sample meet for a classic scanning tunnelling microscope?
118314.e: Because a tunnelling current has to flow between the tip and the sample, conducting or semiconducting samples are needed. For insulators the atomic force microscope was developed later.
118314.m: The scanning tunnelling microscope needs conductive samples.

118315.q: What did Karl Alexander Müller and Georg Bednorz discover in 1986?
118315.e: In a copper oxide material they found superconductivity at much higher temperatures than previously known. This set off intensive research worldwide.
118315.m: Müller and Bednorz discovered high-temperature superconductivity.

a: A material conducts no current at all
A material glows in the dark
118316.e: Below a transition temperature, a superconductor loses its electrical resistance completely. It also expels magnetic fields from its interior.
118316.m: A superconductor conducts current with no resistance at all.

118317.q: How soon after the discovery did Müller and Bednorz receive the Nobel Prize in Physics?
118317.e: The discovery of 1986 was quickly confirmed and honoured with the Nobel Prize as early as 1987. This is one of the fastest awards ever.
118317.m: Müller and Bednorz received the Nobel Prize only a year after their discovery.

118318.q: To which class of materials did the superconducting material studied by Müller and Bednorz belong?
118318.e: The material consisted of lanthanum, barium, copper and oxygen. Ceramics had until then been regarded as rather poor conductors.
118318.m: The first high-temperature superconductors were copper oxide ceramics.

118319.q: Where did Müller and Bednorz work when they made their Nobel Prize discovery?
a: The IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon
118319.e: Both did research at the IBM laboratory in Rüschlikon on Lake Zurich. A different Nobel Prize project in physics had arisen there shortly before.
118319.m: High-temperature superconductivity was discovered at IBM in Rüschlikon.

118320.q: In which city was Karl Alexander Müller born in 1927?
118320.e: Müller was born in Basel and studied physics at ETH Zurich. He died in January 2023.
118320.m: Karl Alexander Müller was born in Basel.

118321.q: At roughly what temperature did the first material of Müller and Bednorz become superconducting?
118321.e: Earlier superconductors needed temperatures of around 20 kelvin or less. The new material reached about 35 kelvin, that is about -238 degrees Celsius.
118321.m: The first cuprate superconductor became superconducting at about 35 kelvin.

118322.q: What advantage did later cuprate superconductors with transition temperatures above 77 kelvin bring?
a: They can be cooled with liquid nitrogen
118322.e: Liquid nitrogen boils at 77 kelvin and is much cheaper than liquid helium. This made technical applications easier.
118322.m: High-temperature superconductors can be cooled with cheap liquid nitrogen.

118323.q: Which country does Johannes Georg Bednorz, the partner of Karl Alexander Müller, come from?
118323.e: Bednorz is a German mineralogist and physicist who worked at the IBM laboratory in Rüschlikon. He and Müller received the Nobel Prize together.
118323.m: Georg Bednorz is a German researcher.

118325.q: At which university did Kurt Wüthrich mainly do research?
118325.e: Wüthrich worked at ETH Zurich from 1969 and became professor of biophysics there.
118325.m: Kurt Wüthrich did research at ETH Zurich.

118326.q: What advantage does Kurt Wüthrich’s NMR method have over X-ray crystallography?
a: Proteins can be studied in solution without crystallising them
It works only at very high temperatures
It breaks the proteins down into single atoms
118326.e: For X-ray crystallography proteins first have to be crystallised, which is often difficult. With NMR they are measured in solution, similar to in the cell.

118327.q: What does the abbreviation NMR stand for in Kurt Wüthrich’s method?
118327.e: Atomic nuclei in a strong magnetic field absorb radio waves of particular frequencies. These frequencies reveal how the atoms in a molecule are arranged.

118328.q: Which atomic nuclei are especially important for determining protein structures with NMR?
118328.e: Proteins contain very many hydrogen atoms. From the distances between hydrogen nuclei, measured through the nuclear Overhauser effect, the spatial structure is calculated.
118328.m: In NMR, hydrogen nuclei reveal the shape of a protein.
