118830.m: The liver gets blood from the portal vein and the hepatic artery.

118831.q: What are the widened capillaries between the rows of liver cells called?
118831.e: In the sinusoids, blood from the portal vein and hepatic artery mixes. Their leaky walls make the exchange of substances easier.
118831.m: Liver sinusoids are the capillaries of the liver.

118832.q: What are the resident macrophages in the liver sinusoids called?
118832.e: Kupffer cells eat bacteria, cell debris and old red blood cells from the portal vein blood. They are considered the largest group of resident macrophages in the body.
118832.m: Kupffer cells are the scavenger cells of the liver.

118833.q: Why does the wall of the liver capillaries have gaps?
a: So that substances pass easily between blood and liver cells
So that blood cells get into the bile
So that the liver grows faster
118833.e: Through the gaps, blood plasma reaches a narrow gap called the space of Disse. There the liver cells take up some substances and release others.
118833.m: Capillaries with gaps make exchange of substances in the liver easier.

118834.q: Roughly what shape does a classic liver lobule have in cross-section?
118834.e: The classic liver lobule is a roughly six-sided prism. The portal areas lie at its corners.
118834.m: A liver lobule is roughly hexagonal.

118835.q: Which vitamin does the liver store in especially large amounts?
118835.e: Most of the body's vitamin A is stored in the liver, mainly in the Ito cells. With chronic damage, these cells can also form scar tissue.
118835.m: The liver is the body's big vitamin A store.

118836.q: In which direction does bile flow in the liver lobule compared with the blood?
a: The opposite way, from the middle outwards
At right angles to it, into the central vein
Not at all, it stays in the cells
118836.e: Blood flows from the portal areas to the central vein. Bile flows the other way in the bile canaliculi, to the bile ducts at the edge.
118836.m: Bile and blood flow in opposite directions in the liver lobule.

118837.q: Why does a fatty liver often go unnoticed for a long time?
a: It usually causes no complaints for a long time
118837.e: The liver has no pain fibres inside it. A fatty liver is therefore often discovered by chance in an ultrasound or because of raised liver values.
118837.m: A fatty liver causes no complaints for a long time.

118838.q: Apart from being overweight, which habit is a common cause of fatty liver?
118838.e: The liver breaks down alcohol. This produces substances that promote fat storage in the liver cells. Even regular moderate amounts can make the liver fatty.
118838.m: Alcohol is an important trigger of fatty liver.

118839.q: Which drink, in large amounts, especially promotes non-alcoholic fatty liver?
118839.e: Soft drinks contain a lot of sugar, especially fructose. The liver easily turns extra fructose into fat and stores it.
118839.m: A lot of sugar in drinks can make the liver fatty.

118840.q: In what form is the fat in a fatty liver mainly stored?
118840.e: In fatty liver, mainly triglycerides collect in fat droplets of the liver cells. They form when more fatty acids arrive than are broken down or exported.
118840.m: A fatty liver mainly stores triglycerides.

118841.q: What is a fatty liver called when inflammation with cell damage is added?
118841.e: In steatohepatitis, liver cells die and inflammatory cells move in. It can progress to scarring of the liver.
118841.m: An inflamed fatty liver is called steatohepatitis.

118842.q: Which serious long-term consequence can a progressing fatty liver disease have?
118842.e: Over years, inflammation can turn into fibrosis and finally cirrhosis. This also increases the risk of liver cancer.
118842.m: An untreated fatty liver can turn into cirrhosis.

118843.q: What are the most important risk factors for non-alcoholic fatty liver?
a: Lack of vitamin C and sunburn
118843.e: Metabolic fatty liver is closely linked to being overweight, insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. High blood pressure and raised blood fats also play a part.
118843.m: Being overweight and diabetes favour fatty liver.

118844.q: What is the most important treatment for metabolic fatty liver?
a: Losing weight through diet and exercise
118844.e: Even losing a few per cent of body weight can clearly lower liver fat. Exercise also improves sensitivity to insulin.
118844.m: Losing weight and exercise are the best therapy for fatty liver.

118845.q: Which organ does the hepatitis B virus mainly attack?
118845.e: Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver. The hepatitis B virus multiplies in the liver cells and can damage the liver permanently.
118845.m: The hepatitis B virus attacks the liver.

118846.q: What is the most effective protection against hepatitis B in Switzerland?
a: A vaccination, ideally as a baby or teenager
None, because there is no vaccine
118846.e: The FOPH recommends the hepatitis B vaccination for all babies and for teenagers who have not yet been vaccinated. It protects very reliably.
118846.m: A vaccination protects against hepatitis B.

118847.q: How do you check whether a hepatitis B vaccination has worked?
a: You measure the antibodies in the blood
You take an X-ray of the liver
118847.e: After the vaccination, the body makes antibodies against the virus. If their level in the blood is high enough, you are considered protected.
118847.m: Antibodies in the blood show vaccine protection.

118848.q: Why can you not get hepatitis B from the hepatitis B vaccination?
a: It contains only one part of the virus coat, not a whole virus
It only works after ten years
118848.e: The vaccine contains only one protein from the virus coat. The immune system learns from it to recognise the virus, but an infection is impossible.
118848.m: The hepatitis B vaccine contains no virus that can multiply.

118849.q: In whom does a hepatitis B infection especially often become chronic?
118849.e: The immune system of babies usually cannot get rid of the virus. In adults, on the other hand, the infection usually heals.
118849.m: In babies, hepatitis B especially often becomes chronic.

118850.q: Which serious long-term consequences can chronic hepatitis B have?
a: Cirrhosis of the liver and liver cell cancer
118850.e: The constant inflammation leads to scarring of the liver. In addition, the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma rises sharply.
118850.m: Chronic hepatitis B can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

118851.q: Through which route, among others, is the hepatitis B virus passed on?
a: Through blood, for example via shared syringes
118851.e: The virus is present in the blood in high concentration and is very contagious. Even tiny amounts of blood on needles can cause an infection.
118851.m: Hepatitis B is passed on mainly through blood and body fluids.

118852.q: Why do antibiotics not help against hepatitis B?
a: Because hepatitis B is caused by a virus
Because the liver breaks down antibiotics immediately
Because hepatitis B is an allergy
Because antibiotics only work in children
118852.e: Antibiotics only work against bacteria. Against viruses such as the hepatitis B virus, antiviral medicines are needed.
118852.m: Antibiotics do not work against viruses.

118853.q: Which organ can become scarred over years in chronic hepatitis C?
118853.e: The hepatitis C virus often inflames the liver unnoticed for years. This can lead to cirrhosis of the liver.
118853.m: Hepatitis C can scar the liver.

118854.q: Which statement about vaccination against hepatitis C is true (as of 2025)?
a: It is part of the measles vaccination
A single dose protects for life
118854.e: Because the virus changes so much, no vaccine has been approved so far. Protection comes mainly from avoiding contact with blood and treating infected people.
118854.m: There is no vaccine against hepatitis C yet.

118855.q: Which medicines are mostly used to cure hepatitis C today?
118855.e: Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) specifically block virus proteins. Treatment usually lasts 8 to 12 weeks.

118856.q: What is the cure rate for hepatitis C with modern direct-acting antivirals?
118856.e: With today's combination therapies, the virus is permanently removed in well over 90 per cent of patients. Earlier interferon therapies were much less effective.
118856.m: Hepatitis C can almost always be cured today.

118857.q: What did the discovery of the hepatitis C virus, honoured with the Nobel Prize in 2020, make possible?
a: Blood tests for blood donations and targeted medicines
118857.e: Since the virus has been known, blood donations can be tested for it. Medicines have also been developed that now almost always cure hepatitis C.
118857.m: The discovery of the hepatitis C virus made blood tests and cures possible.

118858.q: How does a hepatitis C infection often progress without treatment?
a: It becomes chronic in a large share of infected people
It always heals within a week
It always causes a high fever
118858.e: In most infected people, the virus stays in the body permanently. The infection often goes on for years with almost no complaints.
118858.m: Hepatitis C often becomes chronic without being noticed.

118859.q: What is the most important way the hepatitis C virus is passed on in Switzerland?
a: Blood contact, for example when sharing syringes
118859.e: Hepatitis C is passed on almost only through blood. Today this mainly concerns sharing injecting equipment when using drugs.
118859.m: Hepatitis C is passed on mainly through blood.

118860.q: How long does a modern treatment for hepatitis C usually last?
118860.e: Modern antiviral tablets are usually taken for 8 to 12 weeks. Afterwards the virus is gone in the vast majority of patients.
118860.m: Hepatitis C can be cured in a few weeks today.

118861.q: Which enzyme in the blood is most specific for damage to liver cells?
118861.e: Alanine aminotransferase is found mainly in the cytoplasm of liver cells. When the cells are damaged, it passes into the blood.
118861.m: ALT is the most typical liver cell value.

118862.q: For which causes is gamma-GT in the blood typically raised?
a: Drinking alcohol and blocked bile flow
118862.e: Gamma-glutamyl transferase reacts sensitively to alcohol and cholestasis. It is therefore a common screening value.
118862.m: A raised gamma-GT often points to alcohol or blocked bile flow.

118863.q: Which lab value typically rises together with gamma-GT when bile flow is blocked?
118863.e: In cholestasis, more alkaline phosphatase is made in the bile ducts. However, it can also come from bone.
118863.m: Alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT show blocked bile flow.

118864.q: Why should you not do hard sport before a blood test for liver values?
118864.e: Intense exercise releases enzymes from the muscles, including AST. A raised value could then wrongly be read as liver damage; the De Ritis ratio of AST to ALT helps to interpret it.
118864.m: Hard sport can distort liver values such as AST.

118865.q: Which clotting value quickly shows that the liver is producing less?
118865.e: Many clotting factors are made in the liver and have a short half-life. If the liver produces less, the Quick value falls and the INR rises.
118865.m: The prothrombin time shows how well the liver is producing.

118866.q: Which blood protein is made in the liver and falls in chronic liver failure?
118866.e: Albumin is the most common plasma protein and is made by the hepatocytes. Because of its long half-life, it only falls when the liver has been weak for a longer time.
118866.m: Low albumin can show chronic liver weakness.

118867.q: Why is AST less specific to the liver than ALT?
a: Because it is also plentiful in heart and skeletal muscle
Because it is made only in the brain
Because it never gets into the blood
118867.e: Aspartate aminotransferase is found in many tissues, especially in muscle cells. A raised AST can therefore also come from muscle damage.
118867.m: AST can also come from muscles.

118868.q: Why do low levels of albumin and clotting factors show a weakened liver?
a: The liver breaks these proteins down
These proteins are made in the kidney
118868.e: The liver makes many blood proteins, such as albumin, clotting factors and cholinesterase. If their levels fall, the liver's production is limited.
118868.m: Low liver-made blood proteins show weak liver production.

118869.q: What made liver transplantation a successful treatment from the 1980s onwards?
118869.e: Thomas Starzl attempted the first liver transplant in 1963, but many recipients rejected the organ. Only with ciclosporin from the early 1980s did many survive long-term.
118869.m: Medicines against rejection made transplants successful.

118870.q: Why can a living person also donate for a liver transplant?
a: Because part of the liver can be removed and grows back
Because the liver is not needed for life
Because only the gall bladder is transplanted
118870.e: The liver has a great ability to regenerate. After part of it is removed, the liver parts grow back considerably in both donor and recipient.
118870.m: The liver can grow back after part of it is removed.

118871.q: Which foundation runs the national allocation of donor organs in Switzerland?
118871.e: Swisstransplant runs the national allocation office on behalf of the Confederation. For the liver, urgency counts most, measured with the MELD score.
118871.m: Swisstransplant allocates donor organs in Switzerland.

118872.q: Which visible sign of liver disease goes with a high bilirubin level?
118872.e: Bilirubin is a yellow breakdown product of the red blood pigment, which the liver excretes. It is also one of the values in the MELD score, together with INR and creatinine.
118872.m: A high bilirubin level turns skin and eyes yellow.

118873.q: Where is a donor liver usually placed during a transplant?
a: In the place of the removed diseased liver
In the pelvis next to the bladder
Under the skin of the thigh
In the chest, next to the old liver
118873.e: The diseased liver is removed and the donor liver is put in its place. Experts call this orthotopic, meaning “in the right place”. Kidneys, on the other hand, are usually placed in the pelvis.
118873.m: The donor liver usually goes in the place of the old liver.

118874.q: Why is a liver transplant for liver cancer only an option in early stages?
a: Because otherwise the cancer keeps growing despite the new liver
Because otherwise the donor liver is too small
Because large tumours do not allow anaesthesia
118874.e: If the cancer has already spread, it keeps growing despite the new liver, especially as the medicines against rejection weaken the immune defences. The Milan criteria set how large and how many the tumours may be.
118874.m: For liver cancer, a transplant only helps early on.

118875.q: Which medicines do recipients of a donor liver usually have to take for life?
a: Blood pressure lowerers such as ramipril
118875.e: The immune system recognises the foreign organ and would reject it. Immunosuppressants damp down this reaction.
118875.m: After a transplant, immunosuppressants prevent rejection.

118876.q: What happens in newborn babies with blocked bile ducts (biliary atresia)?
a: Bile builds up and the liver scars
The stomach no longer makes acid
118876.e: In biliary atresia, bile cannot drain away. The children turn yellow and the liver scars quickly; this is the most common reason for liver transplants in children.
118876.m: Blocked bile ducts damage the liver of newborns.

118877.q: What is a transplant called in which a donor liver is divided and supplies two recipients?
118877.e: In a split liver, the organ is usually divided into a smaller left part for a child and a larger right part for an adult. That way one donor organ helps two people.
118877.m: A split liver supplies two recipients.

118878.q: What does ammonia in the human body mainly come from?
a: From the breakdown of amino acids
From the breakdown of fatty acids
118878.e: When amino acids are broken down, the amino group is released as ammonia. Gut bacteria also make ammonia from protein.
118878.m: Ammonia is produced when amino acids are broken down.

118879.q: Which condition arises when a lot of ammonia reaches the brain in liver failure?
118879.e: Ammonia is toxic to nerve cells and astrocytes. It causes confusion, drowsiness and, in the worst case, coma.
118879.m: Too much ammonia damages the brain.

118880.q: In which organ is poisonous ammonia turned into urea?
118880.e: The liver converts ammonia into harmless urea in the urea cycle. This is then excreted through the kidneys.
118880.m: The liver turns ammonia into urea.

118881.q: How does the urea made from ammonia mainly leave the body?
118881.e: Urea dissolves well in water and is filtered from the blood by the kidneys. It is the most important nitrogen-containing component of urine.

118882.q: Which amino acid is the most important harmless way to transport ammonia in the blood?
118882.e: Many tissues attach ammonia to glutamate and release glutamine into the blood. In the liver and kidney, the nitrogen is released again.
118882.m: Glutamine carries ammonia safely through the blood.

118883.q: Which enzyme attaches ammonia to glutamate?
118883.e: Glutamine synthetase uses ATP and makes glutamine from glutamate and ammonia.
118883.m: Glutamine synthetase detoxifies ammonia into glutamine.

118884.q: In what form is ammonia mainly found in the blood at normal pH?
118884.e: The pKa of ammonium is about 9.2. At a blood pH of 7.4, by far the largest part is therefore protonated.
118884.m: In the blood, ammonia is mostly present as ammonium.

118885.q: Which organ excretes ammonium and so helps remove acid from the body?
118885.e: The kidney tubules make ammonia from glutamine, which binds protons in the urine. In this way acids are excreted as ammonium.
118885.m: The kidney also excretes acid as ammonium.

118886.q: What does the zeroth law of thermodynamics state?
a: Two systems in thermal equilibrium with a third are also in equilibrium with each other
Energy can be neither created nor destroyed
The entropy of an isolated system never decreases
118886.e: The zeroth law makes temperature a measurable quantity. A thermometer is exactly such a third system.
118886.m: The zeroth law is the basis of temperature measurement.

118887.q: What do you call the state in which the macroscopic quantities of a system no longer change over time?
118887.e: In equilibrium, temperature, pressure and composition are constant everywhere and no longer change. State variables are only clearly defined for such states.
118887.m: In thermodynamic equilibrium nothing changes macroscopically any more.

118888.q: What is typical of an isolated system?
a: It exchanges neither energy nor matter with its surroundings
It exchanges only matter, but no energy
It exchanges energy and matter freely
It exchanges only heat, but no work
118888.e: An isolated system is completely separated from its surroundings. So its total energy stays constant.
118888.m: An isolated system exchanges nothing with its surroundings.

118889.q: What is typical of a closed system in thermodynamics?
a: Energy can be exchanged, but matter cannot
Matter can be exchanged, but energy cannot
Neither energy nor matter is exchanged
It always has a constant volume
118889.e: A closed saucepan on the hob is an example. Heat gets in, but no water escapes.
118889.m: A closed system exchanges energy, but not matter.

118890.q: Which of the following is not a state variable but a process quantity?
118890.e: State variables depend only on the current state. How much heat is transferred, by contrast, depends on the path between two states.
118890.m: Heat is a process quantity, not a state variable.

118891.q: What is a change of state in which the volume stays constant called?
118891.e: The prefix “iso” means equal, and “choric” comes from the Greek for space. In isobaric processes, by contrast, the pressure stays the same.
118891.m: In an isochoric change of state the volume stays the same.

118892.q: What do you call a change of state without heat exchange with the surroundings?
118892.e: In an adiabatic process the gas is thermally insulated or the process happens very quickly. Changes in temperature then come only from work.
118892.m: An adiabatic process happens without heat exchange.

118893.q: Roughly what volume does 1 mol of an ideal gas take up at 0 °C and 1013.25 hPa?
118893.e: From p·V = n·R·T it follows that V = 1 mol · 8.314 J/(mol·K) · 273.15 K / 101,325 Pa, so about 0.0224 m³. That is about 22.4 litres.
118893.m: One mole of ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres under standard conditions.

118894.q: What is the first law if W is the work done on the system?
a: ΔU equals W divided by Q
118894.e: The internal energy changes by the heat supplied and the work done on the system. This is the law of conservation of energy for thermodynamic systems.
118894.m: Internal energy changes by the heat and work supplied.

118895.q: Which machine does the first law of thermodynamics rule out?
a: A perpetual motion machine of the first kind
A perpetual motion machine of the second kind
118895.e: A perpetual motion machine of the first kind would deliver work without any energy being supplied. That contradicts the conservation of energy.
118895.m: No machine can keep doing work without an energy supply.

118896.q: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. By how much does its internal energy change?
118896.e: ΔU is 500 J minus 200 J. The work given off is subtracted from the heat absorbed, so U increases by 300 J.
118896.m: Work given off reduces the gain in internal energy.

118897.q: An ideal gas absorbs 800 J of heat during an isothermal expansion. How much work does it give off to its surroundings?
118897.e: In an isothermal change of state, the temperature, and so the internal energy of an ideal gas, stays the same. So all the heat is given off as work.
118897.m: In isothermal expansion, all the heat supplied becomes work.

118898.q: 150 J of work is done on a thermally insulated gas during compression. What happens?
a: The internal energy rises by 150 J and the gas gets warmer
The internal energy falls by 150 J and the gas cools down
The internal energy stays the same
The gas gives off 150 J of heat
118898.e: Without heat exchange, Q is zero. All the work increases the internal energy, which makes the temperature rise.

118899.q: 1200 J of heat is supplied to a gas in a rigid container. What is the change in internal energy?
118899.e: At constant volume, the gas does no expansion work. All the heat supplied increases the internal energy.
118899.m: At constant volume, all the heat goes into internal energy.

118900.q: A gas expands by 3 litres at a constant pressure of 2·10⁵ Pa. How much expansion work does it do?
118900.e: The expansion work is p times ΔV, so 2·10⁵ Pa times 3·10⁻³ m³. That gives 600 J.
118900.m: Expansion work is pressure times change in volume.

118901.q: Why is the molar heat capacity of an ideal gas greater at constant pressure than at constant volume?
a: Because at constant pressure part of the heat is given off as expansion work
Because the gas does not warm up at constant pressure
Because heat is lost at constant volume
Because the particles get heavier at constant pressure
118901.e: If the gas expands, it does work on its surroundings. So it needs more heat for the same rise in temperature; the difference is exactly R per mole.
118901.m: At constant pressure a gas needs more heat to warm up.

118902.q: 1 mol of a monatomic ideal gas is heated by 20 K at constant pressure. Roughly how much heat must be supplied?
118902.e: At constant pressure Q = 5/2 · n·R·ΔT, because the expansion work n·R·ΔT is added to the internal energy (3/2 n·R·ΔT). So 2.5 · 1 · 8.314 · 20, which gives about 416 J.
118902.m: At constant pressure a gas needs extra heat for the expansion work.

118903.q: What is Clausius's statement of the second law?
a: Heat never flows by itself from a colder to a warmer body
Energy is conserved in an isolated system
The entropy of a crystal is zero at 0 K
Pressure and volume are inversely proportional at constant temperature
118903.e: Transferring heat from cold to warm is only possible with extra effort. By themselves, temperatures always even out.
118903.m: Heat flows by itself only from warm to cold.

118904.q: What is a perpetual motion machine of the second kind?
a: A machine that turns heat from a single reservoir completely into work
A machine that creates energy out of nothing
A machine that runs without friction
A machine that conducts heat from warm to cold
118904.e: Such a machine could, for example, drive a ship just by cooling the seawater. The second law rules this out.
118904.m: Heat from only one reservoir cannot be turned completely into work.

118905.q: What does Carnot's theorem say about engines working between the same two heat reservoirs?
a: None has a higher efficiency than a reversible engine
All have exactly the same efficiency
The efficiency depends only on the working gas
118905.e: If there were a better engine, you could couple it with a reversible engine running backwards. The result would break the second law.
118905.m: A reversible engine is unbeatable between two reservoirs.

118906.q: Which physicist stated in 1851 that no cyclically working machine can turn heat from just one reservoir into work?
118906.e: William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, set out this statement in 1851. Max Planck later gave it a similar form.
118906.m: Lord Kelvin formulated a version of the second law in 1851.

118907.q: Which quantity decreases in a spontaneous process at constant pressure and constant temperature?
118907.e: At constant pressure and constant temperature, the second law can be expressed through the Gibbs energy G. A process happens spontaneously if ΔG is negative.
118907.m: Spontaneous processes lower the Gibbs energy at constant pressure and temperature.

118908.q: Why does a fridge not break the second law, even though it moves heat from the cold inside to the outside?
a: Because work is supplied to it for this
Because the inside contains no heat at all
Because it only runs at night
118908.e: The second law only forbids heat flowing from cold to warm without any further effort. The compressor supplies the work needed.
118908.m: With work, heat can be pumped from cold to warm.

118909.q: What follows from the second law for every cyclically working heat engine?
a: Its efficiency is always less than 100 per cent
Its efficiency is always exactly 50 per cent
It gives off no waste heat
118909.e: Part of the heat taken in must always be given off to a colder reservoir. So never can all the heat be turned into work.
118909.m: Every heat engine must give off waste heat.

118910.q: What is the direction of time set by the second law called?
118910.e: Irreversible processes such as milk mixing into coffee only run in one direction. This tells you what came earlier and what came later.
118910.m: The increase in entropy gives time a direction.

118911.q: What is the hypothetical final state of the universe called, in which there are no longer any differences in temperature?
118911.e: If the temperature is the same everywhere, no more work can be obtained. The idea goes back to thoughts of Lord Kelvin around 1852.
118911.m: In heat death there would be no usable temperature differences left.

118912.q: Which quantity always increases in an isolated system during irreversible processes?
118912.e: According to the second law, the entropy of an isolated system can never decrease. In irreversible processes such as mixing or friction it increases, while the energy is conserved.
118912.m: In isolated systems entropy never decreases.

118913.q: Which physical chemist formulated the third law of thermodynamics around 1906?
118913.e: The third law is also called the Nernst theorem or Nernst heat theorem. Nernst received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1920.
118913.m: Walther Nernst formulated the third law.

118914.q: What does the unattainability statement of the third law say?
a: Absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of steps
Heat never flows from cold to warm
118914.e: Each cooling step brings the system only a fraction closer to 0 K. You can approach absolute zero, but never quite reach it.
118914.m: You can never quite reach absolute zero.

118915.q: According to the third law, what is the entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero?
118915.e: At 0 K a perfect crystal has only one possible microstate. So its entropy becomes zero.
118915.m: A perfect crystal has no entropy at zero kelvin.

118916.q: Which Celsius temperature is absolute zero?
118916.e: 0 K is minus 273.15 °C. Minus 459.67 is the same point in degrees Fahrenheit.

118917.q: How does the heat capacity of a solid behave as the temperature approaches absolute zero?
118917.e: Close to 0 K hardly any vibrations can be excited. According to the Debye model, the heat capacity of insulators falls in proportion to T³.
118917.m: At the lowest temperatures the heat capacity disappears.

118918.q: Why does water ice still have some entropy even at absolute zero?
a: The hydrogen atoms can be arranged in many equivalent ways
The atoms vibrate especially strongly at 0 K
118918.e: In the ice lattice there are many equivalent ways of arranging the hydrogen atoms. This disorder stays frozen in as it cools. It is called residual entropy.
118918.m: Even at 0 K, ice is not a perfect crystal.

118919.q: Which element stays liquid at normal pressure even very close to absolute zero?
118919.e: Helium only becomes solid under high pressure. Its atoms are very light and attract each other only weakly, so their zero-point motion prevents freezing.
118919.m: At normal pressure helium stays liquid almost down to 0 K.

118920.q: In which SI unit is entropy given?
118920.e: Entropy links an energy with an absolute temperature. This gives the unit J/K.
118920.m: Entropy is measured in joules per kelvin.

118921.e: Clausius formed the word from the Greek “tropē” for transformation. It was deliberately meant to sound similar to “energy”.
118921.m: Rudolf Clausius coined the term entropy in 1865.

118922.q: Which formula is on Ludwig Boltzmann's gravestone in Vienna?
a: S equals k times log W
p times V equals n times R times T
118922.e: The formula links the entropy S with the number W of possible microstates. The constant k is called the Boltzmann constant.
118922.m: Boltzmann linked entropy with the number of microstates.

118923.q: 600 J of heat is supplied reversibly to a system at 300 K. What is its change in entropy?
118923.e: At constant temperature, ΔS = Q / T. So 600 J divided by 300 K gives 2 J/K.
118923.m: Change in entropy is heat divided by temperature.

118924.q: 1 kg of ice melts at 0 °C; the specific latent heat of fusion is 334 kJ/kg. Roughly how large is the increase in entropy?
118924.e: ΔS = Q / T, so 334,000 J divided by 273.15 K. That gives about 1223 J/K, or 1.22 kJ/K.

118925.q: From the point of view of statistical physics, what does entropy describe?
a: The number of microstates that match a macrostate
The average speed of the particles
The total mass of a system
118925.e: The more microscopic arrangements give the same macroscopic state, the greater the entropy. In simple terms it is often called disorder.
118925.m: Many possible microstates mean high entropy.

118926.q: 1000 J of heat flows from a body at 400 K to a body at 200 K. How does the total entropy change?
118926.e: The hot body loses 1000/400 = 2.5 J/K, the cold body gains 1000/200 = 5 J/K. Overall the entropy rises by 2.5 J/K.
118926.m: Heat conduction from warm to cold increases the total entropy.

118927.q: What happens to the entropy when two different ideal gases mix?
118927.e: Each gas spreads out over a larger volume, which allows more microstates. This increase is called the entropy of mixing.
118927.m: Entropy rises when different gases mix.

118928.q: A gas flows from one container into a second, empty container and spreads out over both. What happens to its entropy?
118928.e: In the larger volume there are many more possible arrangements of the particles. So the entropy rises, and the gas never returns into one container by itself.
118928.m: More volume means more entropy for a gas.

118929.q: What is meant by the internal energy of a system?
a: The sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its particles
The kinetic energy of the whole body
The potential energy of the body in the gravitational field
The energy it radiates as light
118929.e: Internal energy includes the random motion of the particles and the interactions between them. The motion of the body as a whole is not part of it.
118929.m: Internal energy is stored in the particles of a body.

118930.q: For a fixed amount of substance, what does the internal energy of an ideal gas depend on?
a: On the shape of the container
118930.e: In an ideal gas there are no interactions between the particles. So the internal energy consists only of kinetic energy and depends on T alone.
118930.m: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on the temperature.

118931.q: Roughly what is the internal energy of 1 mol of a monatomic ideal gas at 300 K?
118931.e: For a monatomic ideal gas, U = 3/2 · n·R·T. With 1.5 · 8.314 · 300 you get about 3741 J.
118931.m: A monatomic gas has one and a half times R of internal energy per mole and kelvin.

118932.q: Why does nitrogen (N₂) need more heat per mole than helium for the same rise in temperature?
118932.e: Helium atoms store energy only in their movement from place to place. Diatomic molecules can also rotate and so take in more energy for the same rise in temperature.
118932.m: Diatomic gases also store heat in the rotation of their molecules.

118933.q: How does the average kinetic energy of the particles of an ideal gas depend on the temperature?
a: It is proportional to the absolute temperature
It is proportional to the Celsius temperature
It does not depend on the temperature
It is proportional to the square of the temperature
118933.e: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. If the temperature in kelvin doubles, this energy doubles too.
118933.m: Twice the kelvin temperature means twice the average kinetic energy.

118934.q: By how much does the internal energy of 2 mol of a monatomic ideal gas rise when it is heated by 10 K?
118934.e: ΔU = 3/2 · n·R·ΔT, so 1.5 · 2 · 8.314 · 10. That gives about 249 J.
118934.m: The change in internal energy is proportional to the change in temperature.

118935.q: What is the change in the internal energy of a working gas after a complete cycle?
a: Equal to the work given off
Equal to the heat taken in
118935.e: Internal energy is a state variable. After a complete cycle the gas is back in its starting state.
118935.m: After a cycle the gas has the same internal energy again.

118936.q: Which quantity is defined as the sum of the internal energy and the product of pressure and volume?
118936.e: Enthalpy H is especially useful for processes at constant pressure. Its change then equals the heat exchanged.
118936.m: Enthalpy is internal energy plus pressure times volume.

118937.q: Who described the Carnot cycle in 1824 in his work on the motive power of fire?
118937.e: The French engineer Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot published the “Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu” in 1824. Lazare Carnot was his father.
118937.m: Sadi Carnot described the ideal cycle in 1824.

118938.q: Which four changes of state make up the Carnot cycle?
118938.e: Heat is only exchanged at a constant high and a constant low temperature. In between, the gas changes its temperature without exchanging heat.
118938.m: The Carnot cycle consists of two isotherms and two adiabats.

118939.q: Why is the Carnot cycle important for engineers, even though no machine achieves it?
a: It shows the highest possible efficiency between two temperatures
It describes exactly what happens in a car engine
It delivers more work than the heat supplied
118939.e: No heat engine working between the same two temperatures can have a higher efficiency than the ideal Carnot cycle. So it serves as a benchmark.
118939.m: The Carnot cycle sets the upper limit for efficiency.

118940.q: In which step of the Carnot cycle does the working gas take in heat?
a: During the isothermal expansion at high temperature
During the isothermal compression at low temperature
118940.e: During the isothermal expansion the gas is in contact with the hot reservoir. During the isothermal compression, by contrast, it gives off heat to the cold reservoir.
118940.m: Heat is taken in during the hot isothermal expansion.

118941.q: In the p-V diagram of the Carnot cycle, what corresponds to the work gained per cycle?
a: The area enclosed by the cycle
The length of the upper isotherm
The highest pressure in the process
The largest volume in the process
118941.e: Work is the integral of p with respect to V. Over a closed cycle this gives exactly the enclosed area.
118941.m: The enclosed area in the p-V diagram is the work.

118942.q: What do you get if the Carnot cycle is run in the opposite direction?
a: An ideal refrigerator or heat pump
118942.e: Run anticlockwise, work is supplied and heat is carried from the cold to the warm reservoir. That is the principle of the fridge and the heat pump.
118942.m: A reversed Carnot cycle pumps heat from cold to warm.

118943.q: Why can the Carnot cycle not be put into practice exactly?
a: Because it would have to run infinitely slowly and without losses
Because it only works with hydrogen
Because it delivers more energy than is supplied
Because it only works in a vacuum
118943.e: The isothermal steps need heat exchange without a temperature difference, which takes infinitely long. Real machines also have friction.
118943.m: The Carnot cycle is an unreachable ideal.

118944.q: A Carnot cycle takes in 1000 J of heat at 600 K and gives off heat at 300 K. How much heat does it give off?
118944.e: For the Carnot cycle, Q_out / Q_in = T_cold / T_hot, so 300/600. So 500 J is given off and 500 J is gained as work.
118944.m: In the Carnot cycle the heats are in the same ratio as the temperatures.

118945.q: How does the entropy of the working gas change over one complete Carnot cycle?
118945.e: The gas takes in exactly as much entropy at the high temperature as it gives off at the low temperature. After the cycle it is back in its starting state.
118945.m: After a Carnot cycle the working gas has the same entropy.

118946.q: How do you calculate the Carnot efficiency with the temperatures T_h (hot) and T_c (cold)?
118946.e: The Carnot efficiency depends only on the absolute temperatures of the two reservoirs. It is the upper limit for every heat engine.
118946.m: The Carnot efficiency depends only on the two temperatures.

118947.q: What is the Carnot efficiency between 500 K and 300 K?
118947.e: It is 1 minus 300/500, so 1 minus 0.6. That gives 0.4, or 40 per cent.
118947.m: The smaller the temperature ratio, the greater the efficiency.

118948.q: What is the Carnot efficiency between 800 K and 300 K?
118948.e: It is 1 minus 300/800, so 1 minus 0.375. That gives 0.625, or 62.5 per cent.
118948.m: Higher upper temperatures improve the Carnot efficiency.

118949.q: An engine works between 427 °C and 27 °C. Roughly what is its Carnot efficiency?
118949.e: In kelvin these are about 700 K and 300 K. It is 1 minus 300/700, so about 57 per cent; using Celsius values you would wrongly get 94 per cent.
118949.m: For the Carnot efficiency, temperatures must be in kelvin.

118950.q: Why must the temperatures in the Carnot efficiency be given in kelvin?
a: Because only absolute temperature is proportional to the heats transferred
Because Celsius only applies to water
Because the kelvin is a unit of energy
118950.e: The derivation is based on the ratio of the heats, which equals the ratio of the absolute temperatures. A shifted scale like Celsius distorts this ratio.
118950.m: Only absolute temperatures give correct efficiencies.

118951.q: How can the Carnot efficiency of a heat engine be increased?
a: With a higher upper or a lower lower temperature
With more working gas at the same temperatures
With a different working gas at the same temperatures
By turning more slowly at the same temperatures
118951.e: The Carnot efficiency depends only on the ratio of T_c to T_h. This gets smaller when T_h rises or T_c falls.
118951.m: Large temperature differences make high efficiencies possible.

118952.q: What upper temperature is needed to reach a Carnot efficiency of 60 per cent with T_c = 280 K?
118952.e: From 0.6 = 1 − 280/T_h it follows that 280/T_h = 0.4. So T_h = 280/0.4, which is 700 K.
118952.m: You can calculate the temperature needed from the efficiency you want.

118953.q: Why do real power stations not reach the Carnot efficiency?
a: Because of friction, heat losses and finite temperature differences
Because they burn too little fuel
Because they work with water instead of air
Because the Carnot efficiency only applies at night
118953.e: Real processes run quickly and therefore irreversibly. Every irreversibility creates entropy and lowers the efficiency.
118953.m: Irreversible losses push the efficiency below the Carnot value.

118954.q: What does a heat engine do?
a: It turns heat partly into mechanical work
It turns work completely into heat
It carries heat from cold to warm
118954.e: A heat engine takes in heat from a hot reservoir, gives off part of it as work and the rest as waste heat. Examples are the steam engine, the internal combustion engine and the turbine.
118954.m: A heat engine turns heat into work.

118955.q: What ignites the compressed petrol-air mixture in a petrol engine?
a: The spark from a spark plug
The hot, highly compressed air alone
An open flame in the cylinder
118955.e: In a petrol engine an electric spark from the spark plug starts the combustion. In a diesel engine, by contrast, the fuel ignites by itself in the hot air.
118955.m: In a petrol engine a spark plug ignites the mixture.

118956.q: How does the fuel ignite in a diesel engine?
a: It ignites by itself in the highly compressed, hot air
Through the spark of a spark plug
Through a glowing wire in the exhaust
Through a flame in the tank
118956.e: In a diesel engine, pure air is compressed so much that it becomes several hundred degrees hot. The diesel injected into it ignites by itself.
118956.m: The diesel engine works with self-ignition.

118957.q: What is special about the Stirling engine compared with a petrol engine?
a: The heat is supplied from outside
It burns fuel in the cylinder
118957.e: The Stirling engine works with an enclosed amount of gas that is heated and cooled from outside. So it can run on any heat source, for example heat from the Sun.
118957.m: A Stirling engine is heated from outside.

118958.q: Which invention by James Watt decisively improved the efficiency of the steam engine?
a: The condenser separate from the cylinder
118958.e: In older engines the cylinder was cooled down with every stroke. Watt let the steam condense in a separate condenser so that the cylinder stayed hot.
118958.m: Watt's separate condenser made the steam engine much more economical.

118959.q: An engine takes in 2000 J of heat per cycle and gives off 1400 J of waste heat. What is its thermal efficiency?
118959.e: The work is 2000 J minus 1400 J, so 600 J. The efficiency is 600 J divided by 2000 J, so 30 per cent.
118959.m: Efficiency is useful work divided by heat supplied.

118960.q: An engine delivers 30 kW of mechanical power and has an efficiency of 25 per cent. What is the heat power supplied?
118960.e: The power supplied is the useful power divided by the efficiency. 30 kW divided by 0.25 gives 120 kW.
118960.m: With a low efficiency, a lot of heat must be supplied.

118961.q: Which Swiss company put the first gas turbine for generating electricity into service in Neuchâtel in 1939?
118961.e: The gas turbine from BBC in Baden served as an emergency power plant in Neuchâtel. It is seen as the first commercially operated gas turbine for generating electricity and worked on the Joule cycle.
118961.m: The first gas turbine for generating electricity came from BBC in Switzerland.

118962.q: What does a refrigerating machine do?
a: It uses work to carry heat from a colder to a warmer place
It creates cold out of nothing
It turns heat completely into work
118962.e: Cold is not a form of energy of its own but a lack of heat. The machine pumps heat out of the cold space.
118962.m: A refrigerating machine pumps heat out of a cold space.

118963.q: What mainly drives an absorption refrigerator?
a: Heat, for example waste heat or solar heat
118963.e: Instead of a mechanical compressor, it uses a solvent that absorbs the refrigerant and releases it again when heated. Such devices work almost silently, for example in minibars.
118963.m: An absorption refrigerator runs on heat instead of work.

118964.q: Which component in a compression refrigerator lowers the pressure of the refrigerant before the evaporator?
118964.e: In the expansion or throttle valve, the liquid refrigerant expands. As it does so, it cools down strongly.
118964.m: The expansion valve lets the refrigerant expand and cool.

118965.q: What do you call a refrigerating machine whose warm side is used to heat a building?
118965.e: A heat pump takes heat from the surroundings, for example the air, the ground or groundwater. It gives this off at a higher temperature to the heating system.
118965.m: A heat pump is a refrigerating machine used for heating.

118966.q: Where does a household fridge give off the heat it removes from the inside?
a: At the condenser, usually on the back
118966.e: In the condenser, the compressed, hot refrigerant gives off heat to the room air and becomes liquid. That is why the back of a fridge is warm.
118966.m: A fridge gives off its heat to the room at the back.

118967.q: What happens to the temperature of a closed, thermally insulated room if a fridge runs there with its door open?
a: It falls at first and then stays low
118967.e: The heat is only carried round in a circle, but electrical energy is also supplied. In the end this ends up as heat in the room.
118967.m: An open fridge heats a closed room.

118968.q: Which effect is used in the Linde process to liquefy air?
118968.e: When air expands through a throttle below its inversion temperature, it cools down. Carl von Linde combined this with a counter-current heat exchanger.
118968.m: The Linde process cools air by letting it expand.

118969.q: Why were CFCs as refrigerants gradually banned by the Montreal Protocol of 1987?
a: Because they damage the ozone layer
118969.e: Chlorofluorocarbons release chlorine atoms in the stratosphere. These destroy ozone molecules as catalysts.
118969.m: CFCs were banned because they destroy the ozone layer.

118970.q: How is the coefficient of performance of a heat pump defined?
a: Heat delivered divided by work supplied
Work supplied divided by heat delivered
Work divided by heat from the environment
118970.e: The coefficient of performance tells you how much useful heat you get for each unit of work put in. It is often shortened to COP.
118970.m: The coefficient of performance measures useful heat per unit of work.

118971.q: A heat pump delivers 4 kW of heating power and needs 1 kW of electrical power to do so. What is its coefficient of performance?
118971.e: The coefficient of performance is 4 kW divided by 1 kW. The other 3 kW come from the surroundings.
118971.m: A coefficient of performance of four means four times as much heat as electricity.

118972.q: Roughly what is the ideal coefficient of performance of a heat pump between an outside temperature of 5 °C and a flow temperature of 35 °C?
118972.e: The Carnot coefficient of performance is T_h divided by T_h minus T_c. With 308.15 K and a difference of 30 K, you get about 10.3.
118972.m: Small temperature differences give high coefficients of performance.

118973.q: What is the ideal coefficient of performance of a refrigerator that cools at 255 K and gives off heat at 300 K?
118973.e: The Carnot coefficient of performance of a refrigerator is T_c divided by T_h minus T_c. With 255/45 you get about 5.7.
118973.m: A refrigerator's coefficient of performance depends on the temperature difference.

118974.q: How are the coefficients of performance of the same machine as a heat pump and as a refrigerator related?
a: The heat pump value is greater by 1
The refrigerator value is greater by 1
One is the reciprocal of the other
118974.e: The heat given off is the heat taken in plus the work. Dividing by the work gives the refrigerator value plus 1.
118974.m: As a heat pump, a machine has a coefficient of performance one higher.

118975.q: What does the seasonal performance factor of a heat pump tell you?
a: The ratio of heat delivered to electricity used over a whole year
The number of operating hours per year
The maximum coefficient of performance on one day
118975.e: The coefficient of performance varies with the outside temperature. The seasonal performance factor averages over all operating conditions in a year and shows the real efficiency.
118975.m: The seasonal performance factor shows a heat pump's average efficiency over the year.

118976.q: Why does a coefficient of performance greater than 1 not break the law of conservation of energy?
a: Because heat is also taken in from the surroundings
Because the heat pump creates energy
Because electricity contains more energy than stated
118976.e: The heat given off is made up of the driving work and the heat from the environment. So the energy balance adds up.
118976.m: Heat pumps use free heat from the environment.

118977.q: A fridge with a coefficient of performance of 3 removes 600 J of heat from its inside. How much heat does it give off to the kitchen?
118977.e: The work needed is 600 J divided by 3, so 200 J. It gives off 600 J plus 200 J = 800 J.
118977.m: A fridge gives off more heat than it removes from its inside.

118978.q: What is typical of a reversible process?
a: It can be reversed without leaving any changes in the surroundings
It changes the mass of the system
118978.e: In a reversible process, the system and the surroundings can be brought back completely to their starting state. In nature this is only a limiting case.
118978.m: A reversible process leaves no trace after being reversed.

118979.q: What do you call a process that runs so slowly that the system is always in equilibrium?
118979.e: A quasi-static process passes through a series of equilibrium states. Without friction it is reversible.
118979.m: Quasi-static processes pass through equilibrium states.

118980.q: Which of the following processes is irreversible?
a: Heat conduction between bodies at different temperatures
An infinitely slow isothermal process without friction
An ideal frictionless pendulum swinging in a vacuum
118980.e: With a finite temperature difference, heat only flows in one direction. Entropy is created in the process.
118980.m: Heat conduction across a temperature difference is irreversible.

118981.q: A drop of ink spreads out in a glass of water. Why does it never gather together again by itself?
a: The ink dissolves chemically and disappears
The water is too cold for that
The ink becomes heavier than water
118981.e: The colour particles spread through the whole of the water through their random thermal motion. That they would all gather in one place again is so unlikely that it is never observed. The entropy rises as they spread.

118982.q: How does the total entropy of system and surroundings change in a reversible process?
118982.e: In reversible processes entropy is only moved around, not created. Only irreversible processes increase the total entropy.

118983.q: What do you call a change of state of a gas without heat exchange with the surroundings?
118983.e: In an adiabatic change of state, no heat flows across the boundary of the system. That is why the air warms up noticeably when you pump up a bike tyre quickly.

118984.q: Which statement about real processes in nature and technology is true?
a: They are all more or less irreversible
118984.e: Real processes run at a finite speed and involve friction or heat conduction. Reversible processes are therefore idealised limiting cases.
118984.m: In reality every process is partly irreversible.

118985.q: What do you call the conversion of work into heat, for example through friction?
118985.e: In dissipation, ordered energy is turned into the random motion of heat. This process is irreversible.

118986.q: Which growth tissue in a tree produces new wood towards the inside and bast towards the outside?
118986.e: The cambium is a ring-shaped dividing tissue between wood and bark. It forms xylem (wood) towards the inside and phloem (bast) towards the outside.
118986.m: The cambium makes the trunk grow thicker.

118987.q: Which type of cell makes up by far the greatest part of softwood?
118987.e: Softwood has a simple structure and consists of around 90 per cent tracheids. They conduct water and also provide strength.
118987.m: In softwood, tracheids conduct water and support the trunk.

118988.q: Which cells are found in hardwood but practically not in softwood?
118988.e: Hardwoods have wide vessels that are visible as “pores” in cross-section. Softwoods do not have such vessels.
118988.m: Vessels are the hallmark of hardwood.

118989.q: Which native type of wood is ring-porous, meaning it has large vessels mainly in the earlywood?
118989.e: In ring-porous woods such as oak and ash, the large vessels form a ring in the earlywood. Beech, maple and birch are diffuse-porous.
118989.m: Oak and ash are ring-porous hardwoods.

118990.q: What are the bands of tissue called that run radially from the inside to the outside in the trunk?
118990.e: Wood rays (medullary rays) consist mainly of parenchyma cells. They conduct and store substances across the axis of the trunk.
118990.m: Wood rays run like spokes from the pith to the bark.

118991.q: Which cut runs at right angles to the axis of the trunk and shows the annual rings as circles?
118991.e: The cross-section, called end grain in wood, runs across the grain. Radial and tangential sections run along the axis.
118991.m: On the end grain you can see the annual rings as circles.

118992.q: Which native softwood, unlike spruce, normally has no resin canals?
118992.e: Spruce, larch, pine and Douglas fir have resin canals. The silver fir normally has none, which is why its wood is free of resin.

118993.q: Why is oak especially well suited for wine and whisky barrels?
a: Its vessels are blocked and watertight in the heartwood
It contains especially large amounts of resin
It is the lightest native wood
It does not absorb any water at all
118993.e: In oak heartwood the vessels are sealed by outgrowths of cells. This makes the wood watertight and suitable for barrels.
118993.m: Oak is watertight in the heart and therefore good for barrels.

118994.q: Which three main components form the cell wall of wood?
118994.e: Wood consists of roughly 40 to 50 per cent cellulose, plus hemicelluloses and lignin. Together they form a natural fibre composite.
118994.m: Wood is a composite of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin.

118995.q: What is the main job of lignin in the cell wall of wood?
a: It makes the cell wall resistant to pressure and stiff
It stores sugar for the winter
It carries water to the leaves
118995.e: Lignin is deposited between the cellulose fibres and makes the cell wall woody. Cellulose mainly resists pulling forces, lignin mainly pressure.
118995.m: Lignin makes wood resistant to pressure.

118996.q: Where does the name “lignin” come from?
a: From the Latin word lignum for wood
From the Greek word for light
From the name of its discoverer Lignier
From the English word for light in weight
118996.e: Lignum is the Latin word for wood. The deposit of lignin in cell walls is called lignification.
118996.m: Lignin gets its name from the Latin word for wood.

118997.q: Which two substances together make up most of the mass of wood?
118997.e: Wood consists mainly of cellulose fibres that are cemented together and stiffened by lignin. Hemicelluloses and small amounts of other substances are added to these.
118997.m: Wood consists mainly of cellulose and lignin.

118998.q: Which living things can effectively break down lignin in the forest?
118998.e: Lignin is very hard to break down. Wood-decaying fungi in particular have enzymes that can break it down, and so they turn dead wood back into soil.
118998.m: It is mainly fungi that break down the lignin in wood.

118999.q: Why does cheap newsprint turn yellow in sunlight?
a: Because it still contains a lot of lignin, which oxidises in light
Because the cellulose breaks down into sugar
Because it gives off chlorine from bleaching
118999.e: Paper made from ground wood still contains almost all the lignin. Under light and oxygen, yellow compounds form from it.
118999.m: Lignin makes paper turn yellow in light.

119000.q: What happens to the lignin when pulp is made using the sulphate process?
a: It is ground mechanically into fibres
119000.e: In the sulphate or kraft process, a hot alkaline solution dissolves the lignin out of the wood. What remains are the cellulose fibres for bright, long-lasting paper.
119000.m: To make pulp, the lignin is dissolved out of the wood.

119001.q: Which group of woods usually contains more lignin?
119001.e: Softwoods usually contain about 26 to 32 per cent lignin, native hardwoods often about 18 to 25 per cent. Hardwoods, on the other hand, have more hemicelluloses.
119001.m: Softwood usually has more lignin than hardwood.

119002.q: What does it mean when a plant cell wall becomes lignified?
a: Lignin is deposited in the cell wall
119002.e: During lignification the cell deposits lignin between the cellulose fibres. This makes the wall hard and resistant to pressure, and the cell often dies afterwards.

119003.q: How does earlywood differ from latewood?
119003.e: In spring the tree needs a lot of water transport and forms wide, thin-walled cells. In summer narrow, thick-walled latewood cells form for strength.
119003.m: Earlywood conducts water, latewood provides strength.

119004.q: Why does latewood usually look darker than earlywood?
a: Because it is denser and has thicker cell walls
Because it is discoloured by fungi
Because it is older than the earlywood of the same year
119004.e: Thick-walled latewood cells contain more cell wall material per volume. This makes latewood look darker and denser.

119005.q: What makes up a single annual ring?
a: The earlywood and latewood of one year
The bark and bast of one year
119005.e: An annual ring forms in one growing season and consists of the light earlywood and the darker latewood. The sharp boundary lies between the latewood and the earlywood of the following year.
119005.m: An annual ring consists of earlywood and latewood.

119006.q: What effect does a higher proportion of latewood have on the wood?
119006.e: Latewood is denser than earlywood. If its proportion rises, the density and strength of the wood increase.
119006.m: Plenty of latewood makes wood stronger.

119007.q: Why is a wide annual ring in oak usually denser than a narrow one?
a: Because the earlywood zone stays almost the same width and only the dense latewood increases
Because wide rings have more vessels
Because wide rings form in winter
Because narrow rings cannot contain latewood
119007.e: In ring-porous woods the earlywood zone full of pores stays about the same width. A wide ring therefore consists mainly of extra dense latewood.
119007.m: In oak, wide annual rings usually mean denser wood.

119008.q: Why are narrow annual rings in spruce considered a sign of quality, for example for tonewood?
a: Because the wood is more even and denser
Because narrow rings contain more resin
Because the wood then has no knots
119008.e: Slow-growing spruces from mountain areas have narrow, even rings. Such wood is relatively strong and is used, for example, for the soundboards of violins and pianos.
119008.m: Narrow annual rings make spruce wood even and valuable.

119009.q: Why do many trees in the tropical rainforest show hardly any clear annual rings?
a: Because the climate has no distinct seasons
Because they only live for one year
Because they only store water in their roots
119009.e: Annual rings form through the change between periods of growth and rest. Where the climate stays the same all year round, this rhythm is often missing.
119009.m: Without seasons, hardly any clear annual rings form.

119010.q: When does a native tree mainly form latewood?
a: Right when the leaves come out in spring
119010.e: Latewood is formed in the second half of the growing season. In winter the cambium rests.

119011.q: Why can tree rings be used to date wood?
a: The width of the rings varies with each year's weather
Every ring is exactly the same width
Trees grow by the same amount every year
The bark stores the date of felling
119011.e: In good years trees form wide rings, in bad years narrow ones. The pattern of wide and narrow rings is typical of a region and can be matched to a time.
119011.m: The pattern of ring widths reveals the age of wood.

119012.q: In dendrochronology, what is meant by the “waney edge”?
a: The last annual ring directly under the bark
The boundary between heartwood and sapwood
The edge of a piece of forest
The oldest ring near the pith
119012.e: If the waney edge is preserved, the year the tree was felled can be determined exactly. If it is missing, only the earliest possible felling year can be given.
119012.m: The waney edge is used to find the felling year.

119013.q: What is the method called in which the ring patterns of different pieces of wood are lined up so that they overlap?
119013.e: Overlapping patterns from living trees, old beams and bog wood are synchronised. This produces chronologies covering many thousands of years.
119013.m: Cross-dating is used to extend tree-ring calendars.

119014.q: What is dendrochronology especially important for in Swiss archaeology?
a: For dating prehistoric pile-dwelling settlements to the exact year
For finding the age of glacier ice
119014.e: The piles of the lakeside settlements on Swiss lakes are preserved in the damp ground. Their rings often show exactly in which year a house was built.
119014.m: Thanks to tree rings, pile dwellings can be dated to the exact year.

119015.q: How do you get tree-ring samples from living trees without felling them?
a: With an increment borer, which removes a thin core
With an X-ray of the crown
119015.e: The increment borer (Pressler borer) pulls a core of wood as thin as a pencil out of the trunk. The tree usually survives this small procedure.
119015.m: An increment borer provides tree rings without felling.

119016.q: What are long tree-ring chronologies used for in radiocarbon dating?
a: To replace the measurement of C14
119016.e: The C14 content of the atmosphere varied in the past. Wood samples dated to the exact year show these variations and allow C14 ages to be converted into calendar years.

119017.q: Roughly how far back does the Central European tree-ring chronology from oaks and pines go?
119017.e: The Hohenheim tree-ring chronology joins oak and pine wood into an unbroken series of over 12,000 years. It reaches back to the end of the last ice age.
119017.m: The Central European tree-ring calendar goes back over 12,000 years.

a: The outer part of the wood that still conducts water
The innermost part around the pith
119018.e: In sapwood, parenchyma cells are still alive, and it conducts water from the roots to the crown. Towards the inside it gradually turns into heartwood or ripewood over time.
119018.m: Sapwood is the living, water-conducting part of the trunk.

119019.q: Why is sapwood usually more vulnerable to fungi and insects than heartwood?
a: Because it contains nutrients such as starch and sugar but hardly any protective substances
119019.e: Sapwood stores reserve substances that attract pests. It largely lacks protective heartwood substances such as tannins.
119019.m: Sapwood is rich in nutrients and therefore not very durable.

119020.q: Which tree species is a typical sapwood tree without a clearly marked heartwood?
119020.e: In sapwood trees such as birch, maple, alder or hornbeam, the cross-section of the trunk is uniformly light. Oak, larch and black locust form a coloured heartwood.
119020.m: The birch is a sapwood tree.

119021.q: What colour is the sapwood usually in heartwood species such as larch or pine?
119021.e: In heartwood species, dark substances are deposited in the heartwood. The sapwood therefore stays lighter and is clearly marked off.
119021.m: In heartwood species the sapwood is lighter than the heartwood.

119022.q: Which zone of a freshly felled spruce trunk usually contains the most water?
a: The inner part of the trunk
119022.e: In spruce and fir, the sapwood conducts water and is very damp. The inner part of the trunk is much drier.
119022.m: In spruce, the sapwood is much damper than the inside.

119023.q: Why is sapwood often removed or protected in outdoor building parts?
a: Because it has low natural durability
119023.e: The durability of wood is given for the heartwood. In almost all species, sapwood is considered not very durable.
119023.m: Outdoors, sapwood rots faster than heartwood.

119024.q: Which living cells are still found in sapwood?
119024.e: Almost all wood cells are dead after a short time. Only the parenchyma cells in the sapwood live on for a few years and store substances.
119024.m: Parenchyma cells are still alive in the sapwood.

119025.q: What happens inside a trunk when heartwood forms?
a: The cells die and heartwood substances are deposited
The wood turns back into bast
119025.e: In the change from sapwood to heartwood, the last parenchyma cells die. Before that they produce substances such as tannins, resins and phenols.
119025.m: When heartwood forms, protective substances are deposited.

119026.q: Why is the heartwood of many species more durable than the sapwood?
a: Because heartwood substances hold back fungi and insects
119026.e: Tannins, resins and other heartwood substances act against organisms that destroy wood. There are also no nutrients, and the vessels are often blocked.

119027.q: Which native wood is considered especially durable and is therefore valued for posts and playgrounds outdoors?
119027.e: The heartwood of the black locust is one of the most durable woods in Europe. Beech, spruce and poplar are not very durable in contact with the ground.
119027.m: Black locust wood lasts a very long time outdoors.

119028.q: Why do spruce and beech usually not show a dark heartwood in cross-section like the walnut?
a: They hardly deposit any dark colouring substances inside
All their wood conducts water right to the pith
119028.e: In spruce and beech the inner wood is drier, but without deposited dark heartwood substances. Experts call them ripewood trees.
119028.m: Spruce and beech usually form no dark coloured heartwood.

119029.q: What is the red heart of the beech?
a: A reddish discolouration inside older beeches
A fungus that only attacks young beeches
The normal colour of all beech wood
119029.e: Beeches do not regularly form heartwood. In older trees a reddish-brown false heartwood can form inside, which often lowers the price of the wood.
119029.m: Red heart is a discolouration inside older beeches.

119030.q: Why is larch heartwood often used untreated for façades and shingles in Switzerland?
a: Because it is rich in resin and weather-resistant
Because it does not turn grey
Because it is lighter than balsa
119030.e: The resin-rich heartwood of the larch is relatively durable for a native softwood. Untreated, it turns silvery grey over time.
119030.m: Larch heartwood stands up to the weather even without paint.

119031.q: Which type of wood has a clearly dark heartwood and is one of the heartwood trees?
119031.e: The walnut has a light sapwood and a dark brown heartwood. Maple, birch and lime are light woods without a coloured heartwood.
119031.m: Walnut is a heartwood tree with a dark heartwood.

119032.q: Does the heartwood of a living tree still conduct water?
a: Yes, it conducts the most water
119032.e: The heartwood is dead and no longer conducts water. But it still supports the trunk mechanically.
119032.m: Heartwood supports the tree but no longer conducts water.

119033.q: How is glued laminated timber (glulam) made?
a: From at least three layers of boards glued with the grain parallel
From layers of boards glued crosswise
119033.e: In glulam, dried boards (laminations) are glued on top of each other with the grain running the same way. Crosswise layers, by contrast, are typical of cross-laminated timber.
119033.m: Glulam consists of laminations glued with the grain parallel.

119034.q: Why is building with glulam considered climate-friendly?
a: Wood stores carbon that the tree took in as CO2
Glulam constantly gives off oxygen in the building
Wood is processed without any energy at all
119034.e: As they grow, trees take CO2 from the air and store the carbon in the wood. As long as the wood is used in a building, this carbon stays stored.
119034.m: Wood used in buildings stores carbon.

119035.q: Why is glulam more even in strength than a beam of solid wood?
a: Because flaws such as knots are spread over many laminations
Because it is made of tropical wood
119035.e: Knots and other flaws in single boards are bridged by the other laminations. Weak spots can also be cut out before gluing.
119035.m: Glulam spreads flaws in the wood over many layers.

119036.q: Why are the boards kiln-dried before being glued into glulam?
a: So that the component hardly warps or cracks later
So that the wood burns better
So that no glue is needed
So that the wood becomes darker
119036.e: Wood shrinks and swells when its moisture changes. Dried laminations keep their shape, and the glue sticks better.
119036.m: Dry laminations make glulam keep its shape.

119037.q: What does the number 24 in the strength class GL24h indicate?
a: The characteristic bending strength in N/mm²
The moisture content of the wood in per cent
119037.e: The number gives the characteristic bending strength of 24 newtons per square millimetre. Higher numbers such as GL28 or GL32 mean timber that can bear more load.
119037.m: In glulam the number stands for the bending strength.

119038.q: Which advantage of glulam makes large hall roofs without columns possible?
a: It can be made in great lengths and cross-sections, and curved
119038.e: Finger joints and gluing produce beams that are much longer and deeper than any tree trunk. This lets timber trusses span sports halls and bridges.

119039.q: How does cross-laminated timber (CLT) differ from glulam?
a: Its layers of boards are glued crosswise
It is nailed rather than glued
119039.e: Cross-laminated timber consists of layers glued crosswise and is suitable for flat walls and ceilings. Glulam with parallel layers is mainly used for beams and columns.
119039.m: CLT has crosswise layers, glulam parallel ones.

119040.q: In glulam, how are the individual boards joined lengthwise into endless laminations?
119040.e: In finger jointing, the ends of the boards are milled into a comb shape, glued and pressed together. This produces long laminations without much loss of strength.
119040.m: Finger joints join the boards lengthwise.

119041.q: From what total height does a building count as a high-rise under Swiss fire protection law?
119041.e: The fire protection regulations of the Association of Cantonal Fire Insurers (VKF) define high-rises as buildings with a total height of more than 30 metres. Stricter requirements apply to them.
119041.m: In Switzerland a high-rise is over 30 metres tall.

119042.q: What did the Swiss fire protection regulations of 2015 make possible in timber construction?
a: Wood as a load-bearing structure even in high-rises
A ban on wood in residential buildings
Timber buildings only up to two storeys
119042.e: Since the 2015 fire protection regulations, wood has been allowed in all building categories as long as the requirements are met. This triggered a boom in timber high-rises in Switzerland.
119042.m: Since 2015, timber high-rises have been possible in Switzerland.

119043.q: Why can a thick wooden beam stay able to bear loads for a long time in a fire?
a: Because the outer layer of charcoal insulates the core
Because wood gets harder in heat
Because lignin releases water and puts the fire out
119043.e: Wood burns from the outside inwards at a fairly predictable rate. The layer of char that forms insulates the remaining cross-section, which continues to bear the load.
119043.m: The layer of char protects the wooden core in a fire.

119044.q: In a fire, a beam loses about 0.7 mm per minute on each side exposed to the flames. Roughly how much wood burns away per side in 60 minutes?
119044.e: 0.7 mm/min times 60 min gives 42 mm. This charring depth is included when designing a timber component for 60 minutes of fire resistance.
119044.m: The charring depth is the charring rate times the duration of the fire.

119045.q: In which country is the Mjøstårnet timber tower, completed in 2019 and around 85 metres tall?
119045.e: Mjøstårnet in Brumunddal on Lake Mjøsa is 85.4 metres tall. When it opened in 2019, it was the tallest timber building in the world.

119046.q: What is the name of the timber high-rise project, around 80 metres tall with 27 storeys, in the town of Zug?
119046.e: The “Pi” project in Zug has 27 storeys and is around 80 metres tall, and it is being built by Implenia. Rocket is a timber high-rise project in Winterthur, Roche Tower and Prime Tower are high-rises made of steel and concrete.
119046.m: The timber high-rise Pi is in Zug.

119047.q: Why do many timber high-rises have a core of reinforced concrete?
a: For bracing and as a protected escape and access route
Because concrete is lighter than wood
119047.e: A concrete stairwell and lift shaft brace the building against wind and earthquakes. At the same time they form safe escape routes; this is called hybrid construction.
119047.m: Many timber high-rises are hybrid buildings with a concrete core.

119048.q: Which climate advantage is credited to timber high-rises compared with concrete buildings?
a: Wood stores carbon, and producing it causes less CO2
119048.e: As they grow, trees take up CO2, and the carbon stays stored in the wood used in the building. Producing cement, on the other hand, causes large CO2 emissions.
119048.m: Wood used in buildings stores carbon.

119049.q: Roughly how large is the stock of wood in living trees in the Swiss forest (NFI, survey 2018 to 2022)?
119049.e: The National Forest Inventory found around 420 million cubic metres of wood in living trees. This makes the Swiss forest one of the richest in timber in Europe.
119049.m: There are around 420 million cubic metres of wood standing in the Swiss forest.

119050.q: Which tree species has the largest share of the stock of wood in Switzerland?
119050.e: According to the 2025 Forest Report, around 42 per cent of the stock is spruce. In the Plateau, however, its share is falling because of drought and bark beetles.
119050.m: Spruce is the tree species with the largest stock of wood in Switzerland.

119051.q: Why has the share of spruce in the Swiss Plateau been falling clearly in recent decades?
a: Because of drought, storms and bark beetle infestation
Because spruces were banned in Switzerland
Because spruces now only grow in Ticino
Because of winters that are too cold
119051.e: The shallow-rooted spruce suffers from heat and drought in the warm, low-lying Plateau. Weakened trees are easily attacked by bark beetles or blown down by storms.
119051.m: Spruce in the Plateau suffers from climate change.

119052.q: According to the NFI, the gross growth of wood in the Swiss forest is around 10.6 million m³ a year, and the net growth after deducting trees that have died naturally is around 8.0 million m³. So how much wood dies naturally each year?
119052.e: 10.6 minus 8.0 gives 2.6 million m³. This wood often stays in the forest as dead wood and is important for many living things.
119052.m: Net growth is gross growth minus natural mortality.

119053.q: According to the NFI, around 10.6 million m³ of wood grow each year (gross), and around 7.1 million m³ are used. Roughly what percentage of the gross growth is used?
119053.e: 7.1 divided by 10.6 gives about 0.67, so around 67 per cent. Part of the growth is also lost through natural mortality.
119053.m: The usage rate compares timber use with growth.

119054.q: Who, in the “Sylvicultura oeconomica” of 1713, set out the principle of not cutting more wood than grows back?
119054.e: The Saxon mining official Hans Carl von Carlowitz called for a “sustained use” of the forest. He is considered the originator of the idea of sustainability.
119054.m: The idea of sustainability comes from forestry.

119055.q: A piece of forest of 12 hectares has a stock of 350 m³ per hectare. How large is the total stock of wood?
119055.e: 12 times 350 m³ gives 4,200 m³. The stock of wood is given in cubic metres of stem wood.
119055.m: Total stock is area times stock per hectare.

119056.q: Which federal law of 1876 laid the foundation for protecting the Swiss forest?
a: The Nature and Cultural Heritage Protection Act
119056.e: After major floods, the federal government passed the Forest Police Act for the high mountains in 1876. It restricted clear-cutting and clearing and was later extended to the whole of Switzerland.
119056.m: The Forest Police Act of 1876 protected the Swiss forest.

119057.q: What is meant by the cascading use of wood?
a: Using wood as material for as long as possible and only burning it at the end
Storing wood in steps on a slope
119057.e: In cascading use, wood is first used as building timber or furniture, then reused or recycled into materials. Only at the end is the energy in the wood used.
119057.m: In cascading use, wood is only burned at the very end.

a: Roof beam, chipboard, combined heat and power plant
Combined heat and power plant, chipboard, roof beam
Chipboard, roof beam, combined heat and power plant
Combined heat and power plant, roof beam, chipboard
119058.e: First comes the high-value use as a material in the form of a beam. Then the waste wood is turned into chips, and only at the end is it used for energy.

119059.q: Why does cascading use make sense for climate policy?
a: Because the carbon stays locked in the wood for longer
Because wood then grows back faster
119059.e: As long as wood is used as a product, the carbon stays stored. Using it several times extends this storage time and often replaces energy-intensive materials.
119059.m: Using wood for a long time keeps carbon locked in it.

119060.q: Roughly how much CO2 is locked up in one cubic metre of wood used in building?
119060.e: A cubic metre of softwood contains about a quarter of a tonne of carbon. This corresponds to around one tonne of CO2 that the tree took out of the air.
119060.m: A cubic metre of wood stores around one tonne of CO2.

119061.q: Which stage comes right at the end of a cascade?
119061.e: Once wood is burned, it is lost as a material. That is why burning should only come when no sensible use as a material is possible any more.
119061.m: Burning is the last stage of the cascade.

119062.q: Which wood-based material is often made from waste wood and sawmill by-products?
