119062.e: Small pieces of wood are enough for chipboard, so waste wood and sawdust are suitable. Glulam and solid wood, on the other hand, need fresh sawn timber.
119062.m: Chipboard uses waste wood and offcuts.

119063.q: What does the substitution effect mean in the use of wood?
a: Wood replaces materials or fuels with higher CO2 emissions
119063.e: If wood replaces concrete, steel or heating oil, for example, emissions are avoided. This effect comes on top of the storage effect in the wood.
119063.m: Wood can replace materials that harm the climate more.

119064.q: Why must contaminated waste wood, such as wood treated with preservatives, not be burned in ordinary wood stoves?
a: Because it provides too little energy
119064.e: Paints and preservatives can contain poisonous substances. Such waste wood belongs in special plants that clean the flue gases.
119064.m: Contaminated waste wood belongs in plants with flue gas cleaning.

a: The umbrella organisation of the Swiss forestry and timber industry
A timber construction firm from Bern
119065.e: Lignum brings together many associations and organisations of the industry under one roof. It represents their shared interests towards politicians and the public.
119065.m: Lignum is the umbrella organisation of the Swiss timber industry.

119066.q: Which label does Lignum award to products made from wood that was grown and processed in Switzerland?
119066.e: The Swiss Wood origin label shows that at least a large part of the wood comes from Swiss forests and was processed here. FSC, by contrast, certifies forest management worldwide.
119066.m: The Swiss Wood origin label comes from Lignum.

119067.q: Which award for outstanding timber buildings has Lignum presented every three years since 2009?
119067.e: The Prix Lignum honours innovative, high-quality use of wood in building, interior fittings and design. It is awarded regionally and nationally.
119067.m: The Prix Lignum honours good timber buildings.

119068.q: Why is building with Swiss wood considered climate-friendly?
a: Wood stores carbon and has short transport routes
Wood gives off oxygen during building
119068.e: As they grow, trees take up CO2, and the carbon stays stored in the wood used in the building. Native wood also does not have to be transported far.
119068.m: Wood used in buildings stores carbon.

119069.q: Roughly what share of Switzerland's area is covered by forest?
119069.e: Forest covers about 32 per cent of the country's area. It provides the raw material for the Swiss timber industry.
119069.m: Around a third of Switzerland is forest.

119070.q: Why can a thick wooden beam stay able to bear loads for longer in a fire than an unprotected steel girder?
a: A layer of char protects the inside of the wood
Wood cools down as it burns
119070.e: In a fire, an insulating layer of char forms on the outside of the wood. The inside stays cool and able to bear loads for a long time, while steel goes soft in great heat.
119070.m: A layer of char protects thick wooden beams in a fire.

119071.q: What is one main aim of Lignum's work?
a: To promote the use of wood, especially Swiss wood
To ban the export of wood
To turn forests into building land
119071.e: Lignum informs, advises and does public relations work for wood as a material. Native wood in particular should be used more.
119071.m: Lignum promotes the use of Swiss wood.

119072.q: In wood technology, what is moisture content in wood calculated in relation to?
a: The mass of the oven-dry wood
The mass of the wet wood
119072.e: Moisture content is the mass of water divided by the oven-dry mass, times 100 per cent. This is why it can be over 100 per cent in very wet wood.
119072.m: Moisture content refers to the oven-dry wood.

119073.q: A wood sample weighs 150 g wet and 120 g oven-dry. What is its moisture content?
119073.e: The mass of water is 150 g minus 120 g, which gives 30 g. 30 g divided by 120 g gives 0.25, so 25 per cent.
119073.m: Moisture content is mass of water divided by oven-dry mass.

119074.q: What does it mean when wood is “oven-dry”?
a: It has been dried in an oven until it loses no more water
It has been stored in the open air for a year
It has been preserved with salt
It has exactly 10 per cent moisture content
119074.e: For the oven-drying method, a wood sample is dried in an oven at just over 100 degrees until its mass stays the same. This oven-dry mass is used as the reference value for moisture content.
119074.m: Oven-dry wood contains practically no water any more.

119075.q: What does the fibre saturation point at about 28 to 30 per cent moisture content describe?
a: The cell walls are full of water, the cell cavities empty
The cell cavities are full to the brim with water
119075.e: Below this point, wood gives off water from the cell walls and begins to shrink. Above it, only free water evaporates from the cavities without any change in shape.
119075.m: Below the fibre saturation point, wood shrinks.

119076.q: In which direction does wood shrink most when it dries?
a: Tangentially, in the direction of the annual rings
Radially, from the pith to the bark
119076.e: Tangential shrinkage is about twice as large as radial shrinkage. Along the grain, wood shrinks only very slightly, usually less than 0.3 per cent.

119077.q: Roughly what moisture content do furniture pieces reach in heated living rooms?
119077.e: Wood adjusts its moisture to the room climate; this is called equilibrium moisture content. In heated rooms it is usually about 8 to 10 per cent.
119077.m: Wood adjusts its moisture to the room climate.

119078.q: From what moisture content does the risk of fungal attack rise sharply?
119078.e: Wood-destroying fungi need constant moisture above about 20 per cent. Dry, well-ventilated wood is therefore protected.
119078.m: Below 20 per cent moisture content, wood is largely protected from fungi.

119079.q: How is the moisture content of wood usually measured quickly on a building site?
119079.e: Two electrodes are hammered into the wood, and the device measures the electrical resistance. Damp wood conducts better, and the value is converted into moisture content.
119079.m: Damp wood conducts electricity better than dry wood.

119080.q: A board of fresh wood has a moisture content of 80 per cent and an oven-dry mass of 10 kg. How much water does it contain?
119080.e: 80 per cent of 10 kg oven-dry mass gives 8 kg of water. So the wet board weighs 18 kg in total.
119080.m: Mass of water is moisture content times oven-dry mass.

119081.q: Which discolouration caused by fungi mainly occurs in the sapwood of pine?
119081.e: Blue stain fungi grow in the nutrient-rich sapwood and colour it bluish grey. They hardly reduce the strength of the wood.
119081.m: Blue stain colours the sapwood of pine bluish grey.

119082.q: Which industries are united under the umbrella of Lignum?
a: Forestry, sawmills, timber construction and wood processing
119082.e: Lignum covers the whole value chain from the forest to the finished wood product. It also includes planners, architects and research institutions.
119082.m: Lignum links the whole wood value chain.

119083.q: What connects neighbouring wood cells so that water can flow from cell to cell?
119083.e: Pits are thin places in the cell wall. In softwood they are usually bordered pits with a movable sealing plate.
119083.m: Pits connect wood cells with each other.

119084.q: Which tree species in North America, at over 4,800 years old, is one of the oldest known individual trees and provided long tree-ring records?
119084.e: The Great Basin bristlecone pine (Pinus longaeva) grows in the White Mountains of California. One tree called “Methuselah” is over 4,800 years old.
119084.m: Bristlecone pines are among the oldest trees in the world.

119085.q: What does the Swiss National Science Foundation support with its “Agora” instrument?
a: Projects that bring research closer to the public
119085.e: Agora supports projects that start a conversation between research and society, for example exhibitions or dialogue formats. The name recalls the marketplace in ancient Greece.
119085.m: Agora promotes dialogue between research and the public.

119086.q: Who is the SNSF instrument “Ambizione” intended for?
a: Young researchers who want to lead a project of their own independently
Grammar school pupils with a Matura project
119086.e: With Ambizione, young researchers can carry out a project of their own design at a Swiss university after their doctorate and thus also fund their own salary. The last submission deadline is in November 2026, after which a new postdoc programme replaces the instrument.
119086.m: Ambizione promotes the independence of young researchers.

119087.q: Which SNSF programme, until 2023, specifically funded projects in which several groups worked across disciplines on a shared question?
119087.e: Sinergia supported the collaboration of usually two to four research groups. Since 2023 this kind of collaborative project has been integrated into regular project funding.
119087.m: Sinergia funded the collaboration of several research groups.

119088.q: Which instrument did the SNSF create as an interim solution when Swiss researchers could no longer receive ERC grants during the period of non-association?
119088.e: Because Switzerland was temporarily not associated with Horizon Europe, the SNSF, on behalf of the Confederation, launched its own Starting Grants. They were modelled on the European Research Council.
119088.m: The SNSF Starting Grants temporarily replaced the ERC grants.

119089.q: Who decides the research topic in the SNSF instrument “Project funding”?
119089.e: Project funding follows the bottom-up principle: researchers submit their own ideas. Topics are set in advance, however, in National Research Programmes, for example.
119089.m: In project funding, the researchers decide the topic.

119090.q: What is a large part of SNSF project money often used for?
a: Salaries of doctoral students and postdocs
The salary of the professor herself
119090.e: A large part of the funds pays for project staff, often doctoral students. The salaries of the applicants themselves are usually paid by the university.
119090.m: SNSF projects often fund young researchers.

119091.q: What are the topic-based programmes called whose topics are set by the Federal Council and which are run by the SNSF?
119091.e: For NRPs the Federal Council sets a topic of social importance, for example on nutrition or energy. The SNSF announces them and oversees them.
119091.m: National Research Programmes deal with topics chosen by the Federal Council.

119092.q: Which document has the SNSF required with applications since 2017 in order to plan the handling of research data?
119092.e: In the data management plan, researchers describe how they collect and store data and make it as openly accessible as possible. This helps make research reproducible.
119092.m: A data management plan governs the handling of research data.

a: The rectors' conference of the universities
119093.e: Innosuisse promotes science-based innovation in the interest of business and society. It is a public-law institution of the Confederation.
119093.m: Innosuisse is the Confederation's innovation agency.

119094.q: Which organisation was replaced by Innosuisse on 1 January 2018?
a: The Commission for Technology and Innovation (CTI)
The Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property
119094.e: Until the end of 2017 the CTI was a commission of the Confederation. With the switch to Innosuisse, innovation funding received its own legal personality.
119094.m: Since 2018 Innosuisse has been the successor to the CTI.

119095.q: Who works together in a typical Innosuisse innovation project?
a: A research institution and an implementation partner, such as a company
Only a canton and the Confederation
119095.e: In innovation projects, universities develop new products or processes with companies or other partners. The company is supposed to bring the results to market.

119096.q: Where does the funding go in classic Innosuisse innovation projects?
a: To the research partner, not to the company
Directly to the company as a subsidy
119096.e: Innosuisse mainly funds the work of the research partners. The company makes a contribution of its own, for example through working time or money.
119096.m: In Innosuisse projects the research side receives the money.

119097.q: What is a spin-off in a university setting?
a: A company founded to put the research results of a university to use
A degree programme with a semester abroad
A department of the university administration
119097.e: Spin-offs bring knowledge from research to market as a product or service. ETH Zurich and EPFL have already produced hundreds of such companies.
119097.m: Spin-offs carry university knowledge into the market.

119098.q: Which target group does Innosuisse especially support with coaching, in addition to research projects?
119098.e: Innosuisse offers start-ups coaching, training and support with internationalisation. The aim is for young, science-based companies to grow.

119099.q: What legal form does Innosuisse have?
119099.e: Innosuisse is a public-law institution with its own legal personality. The SNSF, by contrast, is a private-law foundation.
119099.m: Innosuisse is an institution of the Confederation.

119100.q: In which city is Innosuisse based?
119100.e: The Innosuisse office is in Bern. The SNSF and the SERI are also based in Bern.

119101.q: Which two universities belong to the ETH Domain?
a: ETH Zurich and the University of Zurich
EPFL and the University of Lausanne
ETH Zurich and the University of Basel
119101.e: The two Federal Institutes of Technology are ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne. The cantonal universities do not belong to the ETH Domain.
119101.m: ETH Zurich and EPFL form the core of the ETH Domain.

119102.q: Which research institute does NOT belong to the ETH Domain?
119102.e: CERN is an international organisation based near Geneva and does not belong to the ETH Domain. PSI, Empa and Eawag, by contrast, are research institutes of the Confederation.
119102.m: CERN is international and not part of the ETH Domain.

119103.q: Which large research facility at the Paul Scherrer Institute produces very intense X-ray light in a storage ring?
119103.e: In the SLS, electrons circulate at almost the speed of light and emit synchrotron radiation. It is used to study materials and protein structures, for example.
119103.m: The Swiss Light Source is at the PSI.

119104.q: Which research institute of the ETH Domain operates the spallation neutron source SINQ?
119104.e: In SINQ, neutrons are produced by protons hitting a heavy-metal target. Neutron beams are used to study materials.
119104.m: The neutron source SINQ is at the Paul Scherrer Institute.

119105.q: How many universities and research institutes make up the ETH Domain altogether?
119105.e: The ETH Domain consists of two universities and four research institutes: PSI, WSL, Empa and Eawag. Its strategic governing body is the ETH Board.
119105.m: The ETH Domain comprises two universities and four research institutes.

119106.q: Which federal act forms the legal basis of the ETH Domain?
a: The Higher Education Funding and Coordination Act alone
119106.e: The Federal Act on the Federal Institutes of Technology, ETH Act for short, regulates the tasks and organisation of the ETH Domain. The HEdA concerns the coordination of all universities.
119106.m: The ETH Domain is based on the ETH Act.

119107.q: How does the Federal Council steer the ETH Domain politically?
a: It sets strategic objectives for four years at a time
119107.e: The Federal Council gives the ETH Domain strategic objectives for a four-year period. Implementation is up to the ETH Board and the institutions.
119107.m: The Federal Council steers the ETH Domain through strategic objectives.

119108.q: Who is the responsible body for the universities and institutes of the ETH Domain?
119108.e: The ETH Domain is run and funded by the Confederation. The cantonal universities, by contrast, are mainly run by the cantons.
119108.m: The ETH Domain is a matter for the Confederation.

119109.q: What is a National Centre of Competence in Research (NCCR)?
a: A long-term research network on a topic of strategic importance
119109.e: NCCRs bring together groups from several universities around one topic. They are meant to build research of the highest quality and lasting structures at the home institution.
119109.m: An NCCR is a long-term research network.

119110.q: For how long at most can a National Centre of Competence in Research be funded by the Confederation?
119110.e: An NCCR generally runs for up to twelve years in several phases. After that the home institution is supposed to continue the structures.
119110.m: An NCCR lasts up to twelve years.

119111.q: Which organisation runs the National Centres of Competence in Research on behalf of the Confederation?
119111.e: The SNSF announces the NCCRs and oversees them. The decision to launch new NCCRs is taken by the Federal Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research.
119111.m: The SNSF looks after the National Centres of Competence in Research.

119112.q: Roughly since when have National Centres of Competence in Research existed in Switzerland?
119112.e: The first 14 NCCRs began in 2001. Since then several further series have been launched.

119113.q: What is the university called that leads and hosts an NCCR?
119113.e: The home institution leads the NCCR and coordinates the groups involved. It also commits to contributions of its own.
119113.m: The home institution leads an NCCR.

119114.q: What distinguishes an NCCR from a National Research Programme (NRP)?
a: NCCRs are proposed by researchers, while NRP topics are set by the Federal Council
NRPs belong to the ETH Domain
119114.e: Topics for NCCRs arise bottom-up from proposals by researchers. For NRPs the Federal Council sets the topic with social problems in mind.
119114.m: NCCR topics come from researchers, NRP topics from the Federal Council.

119115.q: Besides top-level research, which aim do NCCRs expressly pursue?
a: Promoting young researchers and knowledge transfer
Abolishing the universities of applied sciences
119115.e: NCCRs are meant to support young researchers, promote equal opportunities and carry knowledge into society and business. Building structures at the universities is also an aim.
119115.m: NCCRs also promote young researchers and knowledge transfer.

119116.q: Which field of research does the NCCR “PlanetS” deal with?
a: The formation and study of planets
The planetary boundaries of the economy
119116.e: PlanetS is led by the Universities of Bern and Geneva, with other universities such as ETH Zurich taking part. It studies the formation, development and properties of planets, including those outside the Solar System.

119117.q: Which body of Horizon Europe especially supports start-ups and SMEs with groundbreaking innovations?
119117.e: The European Innovation Council belongs to the “Innovative Europe” pillar. It supports high-risk technologies from the idea to market readiness.
119117.m: The EIC supports groundbreaking innovations by start-ups.

119118.q: What are the “missions” in Horizon Europe?
a: Targeted programmes on major challenges such as cancer or climate adaptation
119118.e: The EU missions set measurable goals up to around 2030, for example on cancer, healthy soils, oceans, climate-neutral cities and climate adaptation. They link research with politics and society.
119118.m: EU missions bring together research on major challenges.

119119.q: Roughly how large is the budget of Horizon Europe?
119119.e: Around 95.5 billion euros are available for Horizon Europe (2021 to 2027). It is regarded as the largest transnational research funding programme in the world.
119119.m: Horizon Europe has about 95 billion euros.

119120.q: Which network advises researchers in Switzerland on applications for EU research programmes?
119120.e: Euresearch is the information and advisory network for European research cooperation, co-funded by the Confederation. It has regional offices at universities.
119120.m: Euresearch advises Swiss researchers on EU programmes.

119121.q: From when does Switzerland's association with Horizon Europe apply, according to the agreement signed in 2025?
119121.e: The agreement was signed in Bern in November 2025 and applies retroactively from 1 January 2025. It also covers Digital Europe and the Euratom programme.
119121.m: Since 2025 Switzerland has been associated with Horizon Europe again.

119122.q: Which Horizon Europe body awards prestigious grants for basic research to individual researchers?
119122.e: The ERC awards Starting, Consolidator and Advanced Grants purely on the basis of scientific excellence. The grants are considered especially prestigious.
119122.m: The ERC funds top-level research by individual researchers.

119123.q: Which federal body is responsible in Switzerland for participation in Horizon Europe?
a: The State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation (SERI)
119123.e: The SERI negotiates and oversees participation in the EU research programmes. It also organised the transitional measures during the period of non-association.
119123.m: The SERI looks after Swiss participation in Horizon Europe.

119124.q: How many pillars does the structure of Horizon Europe have (not counting the cross-cutting part)?
119124.e: Pillar 1 is scientific excellence, pillar 2 global challenges and industrial competitiveness, pillar 3 innovative Europe. There is also a cross-cutting part.
119124.m: Horizon Europe rests on three pillars.

a: The rectors' conference of Swiss universities
119125.e: In Swissuniversities, the heads of the universities, universities of applied sciences and universities of teacher education work together. It represents the universities jointly.
119125.m: Swissuniversities is the rectors' conference of the universities.

119126.q: Since which year has Swissuniversities existed in its present form?
119126.e: When the Higher Education Funding and Coordination Act (HEdA) came into force in 2015, the three earlier rectors' conferences were merged into Swissuniversities.

119127.q: Who is mainly responsible for the universities in Switzerland?
a: The cantons, with the Confederation for the ETH
119127.e: The cantonal universities are run by their cantons. The Confederation is responsible for ETH Zurich and EPFL; both work together in the higher education sector.
119127.m: Universities are a matter for the cantons, the ETH belongs to the Confederation.

119128.q: Which three types of university are represented in the chambers of Swissuniversities?
a: Universities, universities of applied sciences and universities of teacher education
Grammar schools, vocational schools and universities
Universities, art schools and sports schools
Universities of applied sciences, colleges of higher education and grammar schools
119128.e: Swissuniversities has a chamber for each type of university. This way concerns can be dealt with both by type and jointly.
119128.m: Swissuniversities has three chambers for three types of university.

119129.q: What do you generally need in Switzerland in order to study at a university of applied sciences?
a: Only a secondary school leaving certificate
A completed degree at a university
119129.e: The typical route to a university of applied sciences is via an apprenticeship and the vocational Matura. With a grammar school Matura you usually also need a year of work experience.
119129.m: The vocational Matura opens the way to a university of applied sciences.

119130.q: Among other things, what task does Swissuniversities take on for prospective students from abroad?
a: It provides information on admission with foreign qualifications
119130.e: Swissuniversities publishes recommendations and country lists on admission with foreign school-leaving certificates. However, each university itself decides on admission.
119130.m: Swissuniversities provides information on admission with foreign qualifications.

119131.q: In which city is the seat of Swissuniversities?
119131.e: The General Secretariat of Swissuniversities is in Bern. Many other education and research organisations are also based there.
119131.m: Swissuniversities has its seat in Bern.

119132.q: Which university is the only Italian-speaking university in Switzerland?
119132.e: The USI was founded in Ticino in 1996 and has sites in Lugano and Mendrisio. Fribourg is bilingual in German and French.
119132.m: The USI is the university of Italian-speaking Switzerland.

119133.q: What is the focus of universities of applied sciences in Switzerland?
119133.e: Universities of applied sciences provide practical training and carry out applied research, often with companies. Universities place more emphasis on basic research.
119133.m: Universities of applied sciences are practice-oriented and application-oriented.

119134.q: Which route typically leads to a university of applied sciences after a vocational apprenticeship?
119134.e: The vocational Matura adds general education to the Federal Certificate of Proficiency. It entitles you to enter a university of applied sciences in a related field without an entrance examination.
119134.m: The vocational Matura opens the way to a university of applied sciences.

119135.q: Which degrees do Swiss universities of applied sciences award?
119135.e: Universities of applied sciences offer Bachelor’s and Master’s programmes under the Bologna system. They do not have the right to award doctorates themselves in Switzerland.
119135.m: Universities of applied sciences award Bachelor’s and Master’s degrees.

119136.q: Can Swiss universities of applied sciences award doctorates independently (as of 2025)?
a: No, only in cooperation with universities
No, doctorates are awarded only by the Confederation
119136.e: The right to award doctorates lies with the universities. Universities of applied sciences offer doctoral programmes only in cooperation with universities.
119136.m: In Switzerland only universities award doctorates.

119137.q: When did the first Swiss universities of applied sciences start operating?
119137.e: The Universities of Applied Sciences Act of 1995 formed the basis. From 1997 the universities of applied sciences emerged, mainly from earlier colleges of higher education such as engineering schools.
119137.m: Swiss universities of applied sciences have existed since the late 1990s.

119138.q: What is usually also required for admission to a university of applied sciences with a grammar school Matura?
a: At least one year of work experience
119138.e: Anyone who wants to enter a university of applied sciences with a grammar school Matura needs a year-long work placement in many fields. This is how you gain the required practical experience.
119138.m: Grammar school graduates usually need a year of practical experience for a university of applied sciences.

119139.q: With which partners do universities of applied sciences most often carry out research projects?
119139.e: Applied research is often carried out on commission from, or in collaboration with, companies, hospitals or administrations. Innosuisse often funds such projects.
119139.m: Universities of applied sciences do research in close contact with practice.

119140.q: Which university of applied sciences in French-speaking Switzerland has schools in seven cantons?
119140.e: HES-SO (Haute école spécialisée de Suisse occidentale) is the university of applied sciences of French-speaking Switzerland. ZHAW, FHNW and HSLU are in German-speaking Switzerland.
119140.m: HES-SO is the university of applied sciences of French-speaking Switzerland.

119141.q: What is the written piece of research called that you submit for a doctorate?
119141.e: The dissertation must make an independent contribution to research. This is usually followed by an oral examination or defence.
119141.m: For a doctorate you write a dissertation.

119142.q: What does the abbreviation “Dr. h.c.” mean?
119142.e: An honorary doctorate is awarded without a dissertation for special services. Honoris causa means “for the sake of honour”.
119142.m: Dr. h.c. is an honorary doctorate.

119143.q: Which Latin grade is the highest for a doctorate?
119143.e: Summa cum laude means “with highest praise”. It is followed by magna cum laude, cum laude and rite.
119143.m: Summa cum laude is the best doctoral grade.

119144.q: What is the public oral defence of the dissertation called at many universities?
119144.e: In the disputation the doctoral candidate defends her results before a committee. At some universities the oral examination is also called a rigorosum.
119144.m: In the disputation you defend the dissertation.

119145.q: Which qualification is normally a requirement for admission to a doctorate in Switzerland?
119145.e: For a doctorate, a university Master’s or an equivalent qualification is generally required. A Bachelor’s alone is usually not enough.
119145.m: Before a doctorate you usually need a Master’s.

119146.q: What does the internationally widespread abbreviation “PhD” stand for?
119146.e: PhD stands for Philosophiae Doctor and is used internationally for doctorates in many subjects. The name goes back to the medieval Faculty of Philosophy.

119147.q: How long does a doctorate typically take in Switzerland?
119147.e: Many doctoral students work on their dissertation for three to five years. They are often employed as assistants or on a project.
119147.m: A doctorate usually takes three to five years.

119148.q: What is the person called who supervises a doctoral thesis academically?
119148.e: The supervisor accompanies the research project and usually assesses the dissertation. There is often also a supervisory committee.
119148.m: A supervisor accompanies the doctoral thesis.

119149.q: What do you traditionally acquire with the habilitation?
a: The right to teach at a university (venia legendi)
119149.e: The habilitation proves the ability to represent a subject independently in research and teaching. It confers the right to teach, in Latin venia legendi.
119149.m: The habilitation confers the right to teach.

119150.q: What title do people who have habilitated but do not yet hold a professorship often bear?
119150.e: After the habilitation you may teach at the university as a Privatdozent. A professorship is not yet attached to it.
119150.m: Habilitated people without a professorship are called Privatdozenten.

a: A substantial piece of research after the doctorate
The application for a degree course
A seminar paper in the Bachelor’s
119151.e: The habilitation thesis is a larger piece of independent research after the doctorate. Today it can often also consist of several journal articles (cumulative habilitation).
119151.m: The habilitation thesis follows the dissertation.

119152.q: Which career path is increasingly replacing the habilitation as the route to a professorship at many universities?
119152.e: With tenure track, an assistant professorship is converted into a permanent professorship after a successful evaluation. This career path comes from the English-speaking world.
119152.m: The tenure track is an alternative to the habilitation.

119153.q: In which countries is the habilitation traditionally especially widespread?
a: In the German-speaking world and parts of Central and Eastern Europe
119153.e: The habilitation is typical of Germany, Austria, Switzerland and some countries of Central and Eastern Europe. In the English-speaking world it practically does not exist.
119153.m: The habilitation is widespread in the German-speaking world.

119154.q: What does a newly habilitated person often give as a ceremonial conclusion to the procedure?
119154.e: With the public inaugural lecture the person introduces themselves to the university. New professors, too, often give such a lecture.
119154.m: After the habilitation an inaugural lecture often follows.

a: A habilitation based on several published journal articles
A habilitation at several universities at once
119155.e: Instead of a single monograph, several peer-reviewed publications are submitted. This form is especially common in the natural and life sciences.
119155.m: A cumulative habilitation consists of several publications.

119156.q: Which addition to the doctoral title shows a successful habilitation in Germany?
119156.e: In Germany, habilitated people may use the addition “habil.”. By contrast, “h.c.” stands for an honorary doctorate, and “rer. nat.” and “med.” for subject areas.
119156.m: Dr. habil. denotes a habilitated person.

119157.q: What are third-party funds at a university?
a: Research money from sources outside the core funding
119157.e: Third-party funds come, for example, from the SNSF, Innosuisse, the EU, foundations or companies. They are usually won in competition for specific projects.
119157.m: Third-party funds are additional research money won through applications.

119158.q: An institute has a budget of 8 million francs, of which 3 million francs are third-party funds. What is the third-party funding rate?
119158.e: 3 million divided by 8 million gives 0.375, that is 37.5 per cent. The rate shows how heavily an institute depends on funds it has won.
119158.m: The third-party funding rate is third-party funds divided by the total budget.

119159.q: What does the so-called overhead cover in research grants?
a: Indirect costs such as infrastructure and administration
119159.e: Besides the direct project costs there are costs for rooms, energy and administration. The SNSF pays the universities an overhead contribution for these.
119159.m: The overhead covers indirect research costs.

119160.q: Which risk is especially discussed in connection with third-party funds from the private sector?
a: Possible conflicts of interest and influence on academic freedom
119160.e: If funders have interests of their own, the independence of research could suffer. Universities therefore lay down rules and transparency for sponsorship contracts.

119161.q: A project receives 450,000 francs for 3 years. How much is available per year on average?
119161.e: 450,000 francs divided by 3 years gives 150,000 francs per year. The actual split may vary depending on the project plan.
119161.m: The annual average is the total amount divided by the years.

119162.q: How are competitive third-party funds typically awarded?
a: In a competition with review of the applications
Automatically according to the number of students
According to the age of the researchers
119162.e: Researchers submit applications, which are judged on quality. Only some of them are approved.
119162.m: Competitive third-party funds have to be won in competition.

119163.q: What is research called that a company orders and pays for from a university?
119163.e: In contract research the client sets the question and receives the results. The rights to the results are regulated by contract.
119163.m: Contract research is ordered by third parties.

119164.q: A funding programme approves 300 of 1,200 submitted applications. What is the success rate?
119164.e: 300 divided by 1,200 gives 0.25, that is 25 per cent. The success rate shows how fierce the competition for funding is.
119164.m: The success rate is approvals divided by applications.

119165.q: What does an embargo mean in green open access?
a: A period during which an article may not yet appear freely in the repository
A trade ban on academic journals
119165.e: Publishers often allow self-archiving only after a waiting period of, for example, 6 to 12 months. Plan S and many funders reject such embargoes.
119165.m: An embargo delays free access to an article.

119166.q: What is meant by the “green route” of open access?
a: Self-archiving a version in a repository
Publishing in a journal for a fee
119166.e: In the green route, researchers also put their article on a university server or a subject repository. This makes it readable even without a subscription.

a: Fees paid for the open access publication of an article
119167.e: In gold open access, the journal is often funded through APCs instead of subscriptions. These are paid by authors, universities or funders.
119167.m: APCs are publication fees in open access.

a: Neither readers nor authors pay fees
119168.e: Diamond journals are supported by institutions or learned societies. Neither readers nor authors pay.
119168.m: In diamond open access nobody pays fees.

119169.q: Which international initiative of 2002 is regarded as one of the founding declarations of the open access movement?
119169.e: In 2002 the Budapest Open Access Initiative defined open access and named two strategies: self-archiving and freely accessible journals. The Berlin Declaration followed in 2003.
119169.m: The Budapest initiative of 2002 helped to found open access.

119170.q: Which preprint server was founded in 1991 for physics and is still central today?
119170.e: Paul Ginsparg founded arXiv in 1991 so that physicists could share advance versions of their articles. Today arXiv also covers mathematics, computer science and other subjects.
119170.m: arXiv is the best-known preprint server.

119171.q: Which licence is used especially often for open access articles?
119171.e: CC BY allows any use and redistribution, as long as the authors are credited. Many funders require this licence.
119171.m: CC BY allows reuse with attribution.

119172.q: What does the SNSF require of the results of the research it funds?
a: That publications are freely accessible (open access)
That they appear only in print
That they appear only in German
119172.e: The SNSF obliges those it funds to make their publications accessible in open access. Under certain conditions it also covers publication costs.
119172.m: The SNSF requires open access for funded publications.

119173.q: Who developed the idea of the impact factor for journals?
119173.e: Eugene Garfield founded the Institute for Scientific Information and the Science Citation Index. The Journal Impact Factor arose from this.
119173.m: Eugene Garfield invented the impact factor.

119174.q: What does the Journal Impact Factor of a given year measure?
a: The average number of citations per article from the two previous years
The number of subscribers to a journal
The number of pages per issue
119174.e: You count the citations in year X to articles from years X-1 and X-2. This number is divided by the number of citable articles from those two years.
119174.m: The impact factor is a journal’s citation average.

119175.q: A journal published 200 articles over two years, which were cited 900 times in the following year. What is the impact factor?
119175.e: 900 citations divided by 200 articles gives 4.5. On average, each article was therefore cited 4.5 times.
119175.m: Impact factor is citations divided by number of articles.

119176.q: In which annual database are impact factors published?
119176.e: The Journal Citation Reports are now published by the company Clarivate. They list the impact factor of many journals.
119176.m: Impact factors are in the Journal Citation Reports.

119177.q: Why is the impact factor unsuitable for assessing individual researchers?
a: Because a few highly cited articles shape the average
Because it stays the same every year
Because it applies only to schools
119177.e: Citations are very unevenly distributed: many articles in a journal are hardly cited at all. A high average therefore says little about an individual article.
119177.m: The impact factor describes journals, not people.

119178.q: Which declaration of 2012 calls for research not to be assessed by the impact factor of the journal?
a: The San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA)
119178.e: DORA was drawn up in 2012 at a conference in San Francisco. Many funders, including the SNSF, have signed it.
119178.m: DORA criticises the impact factor as a yardstick for assessment.

119179.q: A researcher has 5 articles with 12, 8, 5, 3 and 1 citations. What is her h-index?
119179.e: The h-index is the largest number h for which h articles each have at least h citations. At least 3 articles have 3 or more citations, but only three articles have 4 or more. So h equals 3.
119179.m: The h-index combines the number of articles and how often they are cited.

119180.q: Why are impact factors of different fields hard to compare?
a: Because citing habits differ greatly from field to field
Because all fields have the same value
119180.e: In cell biology there is a lot of fast citing, in mathematics clearly less. Absolute values therefore say little across field boundaries.
119180.m: Impact factors are comparable only within a single field.

119181.q: What does the “Plan S” initiative, launched by funding organisations in 2018, demand?
a: Immediate open access for publications from publicly funded research
The abolition of all academic journals
119181.e: Plan S was launched by the cOAlition S alliance of European research funders. From 2021, funded publications were to be freely accessible without a waiting period.
119181.m: Plan S demands immediate open access.

119182.q: What characterises a structured doctoral programme?
a: Accompanying courses and supervision by several people
A doctorate only by distance learning
A doctorate straight after the Bachelor’s without research
119182.e: In structured programmes or graduate schools, doctoral students attend courses and are often supervised by a committee. This complements the classic supervision by one individual.
119182.m: Structured doctoral programmes offer courses and multiple supervision.

119183.q: Which measures in Horizon Europe especially promote the mobility and training of researchers, for example in doctoral networks?
119183.e: The Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) fund doctoral and postdoc positions with a stay abroad. They are named after the physicist and chemist Marie Curie.
119183.m: The MSCA promote the mobility of researchers.

119184.q: What can an SME use an Innosuisse innovation cheque for?
a: For an initial preliminary assessment of an innovation idea with a research partner
119184.e: With the innovation cheque, small and medium-sized enterprises have a research institution examine an idea. This can prepare a later, larger innovation project.
119184.m: The innovation cheque helps SMEs get started with innovation.

119185.q: What is a glomerulus in the kidney?
a: A tangle of fine blood vessels
A hormone gland on the kidney
119185.e: The glomerulus is a tangle of capillaries at the start of each nephron. This is where primary urine is filtered out of the blood.
119185.m: The glomerulus is the filter tangle of the kidney.

119186.q: What is formed when fluid from the blood is filtered in the glomerulus?
119186.e: In the glomerulus, water and small dissolved substances are pressed out of the blood. This primary urine is then greatly concentrated in the kidney tubules.
119186.m: Primary urine is formed in the glomerulus.

119187.q: What are the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule called together?
119187.e: The glomerulus and Bowman's capsule together form the renal corpuscle, also called the Malpighian corpuscle. It is the start of every nephron.
119187.m: Every nephron begins with a renal corpuscle.

119188.q: What is the smallest working unit of the kidney, which begins with the glomerulus, called?
119188.e: Each kidney contains around a million nephrons. A nephron consists of the renal corpuscle and a long kidney tubule.
119188.m: The nephron is the working unit of the kidney.

119189.q: Why do red blood cells not normally get into the primary urine?
a: They are too big for the kidney filter
They are dissolved in the glomerulus
They get stuck in the bladder
119189.e: The filter in the glomerulus only lets water and small particles through. Blood cells and large proteins stay in the blood.
119189.m: The kidney filter holds back blood cells and large proteins.

119190.q: What mainly drives filtration in the glomerulus?
a: The blood pressure in the capillaries
The muscle work of Bowman's capsule
The pressure in the renal pelvis
119190.e: The hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries presses water and small particles into the inside of the capsule. The colloid osmotic pressure of the plasma proteins works against it.
119190.m: Blood pressure pushes the filtrate out of the glomerulus.

119191.q: Roughly how many glomeruli does a human kidney have?
119191.e: Each kidney has about a million nephrons, each with its own glomerulus. Together this gives a very large filter surface.
119191.m: Each kidney has around a million filter tangles.

119192.q: What is an inflammation of the glomeruli called?
119192.e: In glomerulonephritis, the filter tangles are inflamed, often because the immune system reacts wrongly. Blood and protein in the urine are typical.
119192.m: Glomerulonephritis is an inflammation of the kidney filters.

119193.q: A lot of protein is found in a urine sample. What can this point to?
a: You have drunk too much water
The liver is working especially well
119193.e: A healthy glomerulus keeps large proteins in the blood. A lot of protein in the urine therefore suggests a damaged kidney filter.
119193.m: Protein in the urine can be a sign of a damaged kidney filter.

119194.q: Roughly what percentage of primary urine is taken back into the blood?
119194.e: Of around 180 litres of primary urine, only about 1.5 litres of final urine remain. So about 99 per cent is reabsorbed.
119194.m: Almost all primary urine returns to the blood.

119195.q: What is primary urine most similar to in its make-up?
119195.e: Primary urine contains water, salts, glucose, amino acids and urea in almost the same concentration as plasma. Blood cells and large proteins are missing.
119195.m: Primary urine is blood plasma almost without protein.

119196.q: Which substance in primary urine is reabsorbed almost completely in healthy people?
119196.e: Glucose is taken back into the blood almost completely in the proximal tubule. Healthy final urine therefore contains hardly any sugar.
119196.m: Healthy urine contains practically no glucose.

119197.q: Why is sugar often found in the urine in untreated diabetes?
a: The kidneys can no longer take back all the glucose
The liver releases sugar directly into the bladder
Primary urine normally contains no sugar
119197.e: The transporters in the tubule can only take back a certain amount of glucose. If blood sugar is too high, they are overloaded and the rest ends up in the urine.
119197.m: When blood sugar is too high, sugar ends up in the urine.

119198.q: In which section of the nephron is most of the primary urine reabsorbed?
119198.e: The proximal tubule takes back about two thirds of the water and sodium. Its cells carry a brush border that enlarges the surface.
119198.m: The proximal tubule does the main work of reabsorption.

119199.q: What is the process called in which substances from primary urine return to the blood?
119199.e: In reabsorption, tubule cells take up substances from the urine and pass them to the blood. Secretion is the opposite route, from blood into urine.
119199.m: Reabsorption takes valuable substances back from the urine.

119200.q: How is glucose taken up from primary urine in the proximal tubule?
119200.e: Sodium-glucose cotransporters (SGLT) use the sodium gradient to take glucose along. The gradient is created by the sodium-potassium pump, which is why it is called secondary active transport.
119200.m: In the tubule, glucose travels together with sodium.

119201.q: How does primary urine compare osmotically with blood plasma?
a: It is four times more concentrated
119201.e: Water and small dissolved particles are filtered in the same proportion. That is why primary urine has almost the same osmolarity as plasma, around 290 mosmol/l.
119201.m: At first, primary urine is just as concentrated as plasma.

119202.q: Which principle does the loop of Henle use to concentrate urine?
119202.e: The descending and ascending limbs lie side by side and fluid flows through them in opposite directions. This builds up a strong concentration gradient in the kidney medulla.
119202.m: The loop of Henle works on the countercurrent principle.

119203.q: Which part of the loop of Henle is practically impermeable to water?
119203.e: The ascending limb pumps salt into the tissue but does not let water follow. This makes the kidney medulla salty.
119203.m: The ascending limb releases salt, but no water.

119204.q: What happens in the descending limb of the loop of Henle?
a: Water leaves into the kidney medulla by osmosis
Glucose is released into the urine
119204.e: The descending limb lets water through easily. Because the surrounding medulla is salty, water flows out and the urine becomes more concentrated.
119204.m: In the descending limb, water leaves the urine.

119205.q: What does the ascending limb of the loop of Henle release into the surrounding kidney medulla?
119205.e: The ascending limb actively transports salt out of the urine into the tissue. This creates a high salt concentration in the kidney medulla.
119205.m: The ascending limb makes the kidney medulla salty.

119206.q: What do water tablets that block salt transport in the loop of Henle do?
a: The amount of urine rises sharply
The amount of urine falls sharply
119206.e: If more salt stays in the urine, it pulls water with it. As a result, more urine is passed and the body loses water.
119206.m: Water tablets acting on the loop of Henle increase the amount of urine.

119207.q: In which part of the kidney are the loops of Henle mainly found?
119207.e: The loops dip from the cortex down into the medulla, especially deep in the nephrons close to the medulla. There they build up the concentration gradient.
119207.m: The loops of Henle reach deep into the kidney medulla.

119208.q: What use is the loop of Henle to the body?
a: It helps save water and make concentrated urine
It stores urine until it is passed
119208.e: Thanks to the loop of Henle, the kidney can remove a lot of water from the urine. That way the body loses little fluid even when you are thirsty.
119208.m: The loop of Henle helps the body save water.

119209.q: How is the loop of Henle in the kidney built?
a: As a U-shaped loop with a descending and an ascending limb
As a spiral around the renal artery
119209.e: The loop of Henle is a hairpin-shaped section of the kidney tubule. It dips down into the kidney medulla and comes back up again.
119209.m: The loop of Henle is a hairpin-shaped loop of the kidney tubule.

119210.q: At the end of the ascending limb, how does the tubular fluid compare with blood plasma?
a: The same as final urine when thirsty
119210.e: Because the ascending limb removes salt but not water, the fluid afterwards is more dilute than plasma. That is why it is also called the diluting segment.
119210.m: The ascending limb dilutes the urine.

119211.q: Which hormone makes the collecting ducts of the kidney more permeable to water?
119211.e: When water is short, the pituitary gland releases ADH. It makes water channels be built into the collecting duct cells, so more water returns to the body.
119211.m: ADH helps the kidney save water.

119212.q: Which hormone from the adrenal cortex promotes the recovery of sodium in the kidney?
119212.e: Aldosterone acts on the collecting duct. It lets more sodium return to the blood and more potassium be excreted. In this way it also affects blood pressure.
119212.m: Aldosterone keeps salt in the body.

119213.q: Besides water balance, what other job does the kidney have?
a: It helps set the pH of the blood
It makes the red blood cells
It stores glycogen for the muscles
119213.e: The kidney can excrete acid or hold back bases. Part of this fine regulation takes place in the collecting ducts.
119213.m: The kidney also regulates the acid-base balance.

119214.q: What happens to the urine in the collecting duct when the body needs to save water?
119214.e: When water is short, the collecting duct becomes permeable to water. Water flows into the salty medulla, and the urine becomes dark and concentrated.
119214.m: When you are thirsty, the collecting duct concentrates the urine.

119215.q: Where does urine flow after it has left the collecting ducts?
119215.e: The collecting ducts open into the renal pelvis. From there, urine flows through the ureter into the bladder.
119215.m: From the collecting ducts, urine reaches the renal pelvis.

119216.q: Which section passes into the collecting duct through a connecting tubule?
119216.e: After the loop of Henle comes the distal tubule. Through the connecting tubule, several nephrons open into a shared collecting duct.
119216.m: Several nephrons share one collecting duct.

119217.q: Roughly how many nephrons does a human kidney contain?
119217.e: Each kidney has about a million nephrons. Several of them open into a shared collecting duct.
119217.m: A kidney has around a million nephrons.

119218.q: How do medicines that make you pass more urine, so-called diuretics, work?
a: They make the kidney excrete more salt and water
119218.e: Diuretics block the recovery of sodium in the kidney. More water is excreted along with the salt. They are used, for example, for high blood pressure.
119218.m: Diuretics flush out salt and water.

119219.e: ADH is made by nerve cells in the hypothalamus. It travels along their nerve fibres into the pituitary gland.
119219.m: ADH is made in the hypothalamus.

119220.q: Where is ADH released into the blood?
119220.e: The posterior pituitary stores ADH and releases it into the blood when needed. It does not make the hormone itself.
119220.m: The posterior pituitary releases ADH into the blood.

119221.q: What is the second name of antidiuretic hormone?
119221.e: ADH is also called vasopressin because in high concentrations it narrows blood vessels. “Antidiuretic” means that it reduces the amount of urine.
119221.m: ADH and vasopressin are the same hormone.

119222.q: Which stimulus mainly triggers the release of ADH?
a: A drop in the potassium level
119222.e: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus report when the blood becomes too concentrated. A sharp fall in blood volume also promotes the release.
119222.m: Concentrated blood calls ADH into action.

119223.q: How does alcohol affect the release of ADH?
a: It blocks it, so you have to pass more urine
It increases it, so you pass less urine
It has no effect on it at all
119223.e: Alcohol slows the release of ADH. The kidneys then excrete more water, which can contribute to fluid loss and thirst.
119223.m: Alcohol blocks ADH and makes you pass more urine.

119224.q: Which disease arises when too little ADH is made?
119224.e: Without ADH, the kidney cannot concentrate urine; people affected pass many litres of dilute urine and are very thirsty. Since 2022, an international expert group has proposed a new name that directly names the hormone deficiency.
119224.m: If ADH is missing, a great deal of dilute urine flows.

119225.q: How does ADH make sure more water is recovered in the collecting ducts of the kidney?
a: It makes water channels be built into the cell walls
It turns urine into blood plasma
119225.e: ADH makes the cells of the collecting ducts build water channels, called aquaporins, into their membrane. As a result, more water flows from the urine back into the blood.
119225.m: ADH opens water channels in the kidney.

119226.q: Which class of substances does ADH belong to?
a: Peptide hormone made of nine amino acids
119226.e: ADH is a short peptide of nine amino acids. It is closely related to oxytocin, which also consists of nine amino acids.
119226.m: ADH is a small peptide hormone.

119227.q: Which group of hormones does aldosterone belong to?
119227.e: Aldosterone is a steroid hormone that controls the mineral balance. That is why it counts as a mineralocorticoid.
119227.m: Aldosterone is the most important mineralocorticoid.

119228.q: Which rise in the blood directly stimulates the adrenal gland to make aldosterone?
119228.e: Besides angiotensin II, a high potassium level is the strongest direct stimulus. Aldosterone then makes sure that more potassium is excreted.
119228.m: A lot of potassium in the blood increases aldosterone production.

119229.q: In which organ does aldosterone mainly act?
119229.e: In the kidney, aldosterone makes sure more sodium is recovered and more potassium is excreted. Water stays in the body along with the sodium.
119229.m: Aldosterone mainly acts in the kidney.

119230.q: Through which type of receptor does aldosterone act?
a: Through a receptor inside the cell
Through a G protein receptor in the membrane
119230.e: As a fat-soluble steroid, aldosterone enters the cell and binds to a receptor in the cytoplasm. This moves into the nucleus and acts there on reading the genes.
119230.m: Aldosterone changes how genes are read in the nucleus.

119231.q: Which gland makes the hormone aldosterone?
119231.e: Aldosterone is made in the outer layer of the adrenal gland, the cortex. Other steroid hormones such as cortisol are also made there.
119231.m: Aldosterone comes from the adrenal cortex.

119232.q: How does blood pressure typically change with too much aldosterone over a long time?
119232.e: Water stays in the body along with the retained sodium. Blood volume increases, and blood pressure rises.
119232.m: Too much aldosterone raises blood pressure.

119233.q: What happens to the aldosterone level if you eat a lot of table salt for a long time?
119233.e: A lot of salt increases blood volume, so less renin and angiotensin II is made. As a result, the adrenal gland releases less aldosterone.
119233.m: With a lot of salt, the body cuts back on aldosterone.

119234.q: Which blood values are typical of a lack of aldosterone, for example in Addison's disease?
a: Sodium too low, potassium too high
Sodium too high, potassium too low
Calcium too low, phosphate too high
Glucose too high, potassium too low
119234.e: Without aldosterone, the kidney loses sodium and holds on to potassium. People affected often have low blood pressure and crave salt.
119234.m: Without aldosterone, sodium is lost and potassium builds up.

119235.q: From which basic substance is aldosterone made, like all steroid hormones?
119235.e: All steroid hormones have the same ring framework and are made from cholesterol. In the adrenal cortex, aldosterone is formed from it in several enzyme steps.
119235.m: Steroid hormones are built from cholesterol.

119236.q: Why is creatinine well suited to estimating kidney function?
a: It is made at a steady rate and filtered freely
It is made only in the liver
119236.e: Creatinine is made at a fairly constant rate and is filtered freely in the glomerulus, but not reabsorbed. If its blood level rises, the kidney is filtering less.
119236.m: A high creatinine level points to weaker filtering.

119237.q: When does serum creatinine typically first rise above the normal range?
a: When filtering has fallen by about half
With just 5 per cent less filtering
119237.e: Because the blood level and filtering are not linked in a straight line, creatinine stays normal at first. This range is called the creatinine-blind range.
119237.m: Creatinine only reveals weak kidneys late.

119238.q: Apart from kidney function, what does the creatinine level in the blood strongly depend on?
119238.e: People with a lot of muscle make more creatinine. With very little muscle, a normal value can hide weak kidneys.
119238.m: Muscular people have more creatinine in their blood.

119239.q: In whom can a normal creatinine value hide weak kidneys?
a: In people with very little muscle mass
In people with high blood pressure
119239.e: People with little muscle make little creatinine. The value then stays normal despite weak kidneys; as an addition, cystatin C is measured, which hardly depends on muscle mass.
119239.m: With little muscle mass, creatinine can hide weak kidneys.

119240.q: Apart from the creatinine value, what information do you need to estimate kidney filtering (eGFR)?
119240.e: The CKD-EPI formula used most often today calculates an estimated glomerular filtration rate from creatinine, age and sex. Age and sex are linked to muscle mass.
119240.m: The eGFR is estimated from creatinine, age and sex.

119241.q: Urine creatinine 8000 µmol/l, urine flow 1 ml/min, plasma creatinine 80 µmol/l. What is the creatinine clearance?
119241.e: Clearance is urine concentration times urine flow divided by plasma concentration: 8000 times 1 divided by 80 gives 100 ml/min.
119241.m: Clearance is urine flow times urine concentration divided by plasma concentration.

119242.q: Why does creatinine clearance slightly overestimate the true filtration rate?
a: Part of the creatinine is also secreted
Creatinine is broken down in the urine
119242.e: A small share also reaches the urine through tubular secretion. As a result, more creatinine appears in the urine than was filtered.
119242.m: Tubular secretion makes creatinine clearance come out slightly too high.

119243.q: How can serum creatinine change after a big meal of cooked meat?
a: It can rise for a short time
It is sure to stay unchanged
119243.e: When meat is cooked, creatine in it already turns into creatinine. After eating, the blood level can therefore be raised for a short time.
119243.m: Do not eat a big meat meal before a creatinine test.

119244.q: Roughly how much primary urine do an adult's kidneys make per day?
119244.e: The kidneys filter about 180 litres of primary urine every day. About 99 per cent of it is recovered; only about 1.5 litres of urine is passed.
119244.m: About 180 litres of primary urine become only about 1.5 litres of urine.

119245.q: What does the glomerular filtration rate tell you?
a: How much fluid the kidneys filter from the blood per minute
How much urine is stored in the bladder per day
How fast the heart pumps blood to the kidneys
How much sugar the kidneys break down per day
119245.e: The glomerular filtration rate measures how much plasma all the glomeruli together filter per minute. It is the most important measure of kidney function.
119245.m: The filtration rate shows how well the kidneys filter.

119246.q: How does the kidneys' filtration rate normally change with increasing age?
a: It stays the same all your life
119246.e: Over the years, nephrons are lost and the filtration rate slowly falls. That is why some medicines have to be given in lower doses to older people.
119246.m: Kidney function slowly declines with age.

119247.q: What happens to most of the primary urine?
a: It is taken back into the blood
It is stored in the kidney
119247.e: The kidney tubules take water, salts and sugar back into the blood. So of about 180 litres of primary urine, only about 1 per cent is left as urine.
119247.m: Almost all primary urine is taken back into the blood.

119248.q: 600 ml of plasma flows through the kidneys per minute, and 120 ml of it is filtered. What share of the plasma is filtered?
119248.e: 120 divided by 600 gives 0.2, so 20 per cent. This share is called the filtration fraction.
119248.m: About a fifth of the kidney plasma is filtered.

119249.q: The blood pressure in the glomerulus pushes outwards with 50 mmHg. Two opposing forces push back with 40 mmHg together. What is the net pressure that filters?
119249.e: You subtract the opposing forces from the outward pressure: 50 minus 40 gives 10 mmHg. This small surplus drives filtration.
119249.m: The effective filtration pressure is only a small surplus.

119250.q: What happens to the filtration rate when the vessel leading into a glomerulus narrows?
119250.e: A narrowing before the glomerulus lowers the pressure in the capillaries. Less pressure means less filtration.
119250.m: Narrow before the filter means less filtrate.

119251.q: What does autoregulation of kidney blood flow achieve?
a: The filtration rate stays roughly constant when blood pressure varies
The filtration rate follows every blood pressure value exactly
The kidney stops filtering during exertion
The kidney greatly increases filtering at night
119251.e: The kidney's vessels narrow when pressure is high and widen when it is low. That way filtration stays stable over a wide range of blood pressure.
119251.m: The kidney keeps its filtering stable by itself.

119252.q: In which range is the normal pH of arterial blood?
119252.e: The pH of blood is kept tightly around 7.4, so blood is slightly alkaline. Lower values are called acidosis, higher ones alkalosis.
119252.m: Healthy blood has a pH of about 7.4.

119253.q: Which is the most important buffer in blood plasma?
119253.e: The bicarbonate buffer is especially effective because the lungs can control CO2 and the kidneys bicarbonate independently of each other. That is why it is called an open buffer system.
119253.m: Bicarbonate is the main buffer of the blood.

119254.q: Which two organs mainly regulate the body's acid-base balance?
119254.e: The lungs can quickly breathe out more or less CO2. The kidneys work more slowly, but excrete acid in a targeted way and hold on to bicarbonate.
119254.m: The lungs and kidneys keep blood pH stable.

119255.q: How do the lungs partly compensate for metabolic acidosis?
119255.e: Breathing more blows off more CO2, so the pH rises again. The deep breathing in severe acidosis is called Kussmaul breathing.
119255.m: When the body is too acidic, it breathes more deeply.

119256.q: Bicarbonate 24 mmol/l, CO2 partial pressure 40 mmHg (times 0.03 gives 1.2 mmol/l), pKa 6.1. What pH results?
119256.e: According to Henderson-Hasselbalch, pH equals 6.1 plus log(24 divided by 1.2). That is 6.1 plus log 20, so 6.1 plus 1.3, which is 7.4.
119256.m: In blood, a ratio of 20 to 1 gives a pH of 7.4.

119257.q: Which disorder is present in diabetic ketoacidosis?
119257.e: When insulin is lacking, many ketone bodies form, and they are acids. The acid comes from metabolism, hence metabolic.
119257.m: Ketone bodies make the blood acidic through metabolism.

119258.q: Which disorder arises when someone hyperventilates heavily in a panic?
119258.e: The heavy breathing breathes out too much CO2. The blood becomes more alkaline, which can cause tingling and muscle cramps.
119258.m: Breathing too much makes the blood alkaline.

119259.q: Which enzyme speeds up the formation of carbonic acid from CO2 and water?
119259.e: Carbonic anhydrase is found, for example, in red blood cells and in tubule cells. It makes the conversion many times faster.
119259.m: Carbonic anhydrase combines CO2 and water lightning fast.

119260.q: What is an electrolyte in the chemical sense?
a: A substance that breaks up into ions in solution
A substance that contains only electrons
A substance that always blocks electric current
119260.e: Electrolytes such as table salt break up into charged particles in water. That is why their solutions conduct electric current.

119261.q: Which cation is most common in the extracellular space?
119261.e: Sodium largely determines the osmolarity outside the cells. In this way it also controls how much water is held there.
119261.m: Sodium is the main cation outside the cells.

119262.q: Which cation is most common inside cells?
119262.e: In the cells, the potassium concentration is about 30 times higher than in the blood. This is important for the resting membrane potential.
119262.m: Potassium is the main cation inside cells.

119263.q: Why must the sodium level in the blood be regulated very tightly?
a: It determines how water is shared between cells and their surroundings
It provides most of the cells' energy
119263.e: Sodium holds water outside the cells. Too much or too little sodium makes cells shrink or swell, which harms the brain in particular.
119263.m: Sodium controls how water is spread around the body.

119264.q: Which organ is especially at risk when the potassium level in the blood is far off?
119264.e: Potassium is crucial for the electrical excitation of muscle and nerve cells. Even small deviations can trigger dangerous heart rhythm disorders.
119264.m: Too much or too little potassium endangers the heart rhythm.

119265.q: Which extracellular anion is the most important in terms of amount?
119265.e: Chloride accompanies sodium as its counter-ion and is present in plasma at about 100 mmol/l. Bicarbonate follows at about 24 mmol/l.
119265.m: Chloride is sodium's main partner in the blood.

119266.q: How many sodium and potassium ions does the sodium-potassium pump move per cycle?
119266.e: Per cycle, the pump uses one ATP and moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in. In this way it maintains the concentration differences.
119266.m: The sodium-potassium pump swaps three sodium for two potassium.

119267.q: What can happen if someone drinks an extreme amount of plain water in a short time?
a: The sodium level in the blood falls dangerously
The potassium level in the blood rises sharply
119267.e: A great deal of water without salt dilutes the blood. A sodium level that is too low makes brain cells swell and can be life-threatening, for example in marathon runners.
119267.m: Too much water at once can dangerously dilute the sodium in the blood.

119268.q: About 99 per cent of which electrolyte is stored in the skeleton?
119268.e: Calcium is found almost entirely as hydroxyapatite in bones and teeth. The small remainder in the blood is essential for clotting, muscles and nerves.
119268.m: Almost all the body's calcium is in the bones.

119269.q: Which diseases are the most common causes of chronic kidney failure?
119269.e: High blood sugar and high blood pressure damage the small kidney vessels and the glomeruli over years. In many countries they are the main reasons people need dialysis.
119269.m: Diabetes and high blood pressure harm the kidneys most.

119270.q: What does the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) tell you?
a: How much blood the kidneys filter per minute
How much urine you drink per day
How much sugar is in the blood
119270.e: The GFR measures the kidneys' filtering in millilitres per minute. If it falls sharply, this is called kidney failure.
119270.m: The GFR shows how well the kidneys filter.

119271.q: What does the term uraemia mean?
a: Waste substances that should be passed in urine build up in the blood
There is blood in the urine
There is sugar in the urine
119271.e: In uraemia, waste substances such as urea stay in the body. The results include nausea, itching and confusion.
119271.m: Uraemia is poisoning by the body's own waste substances.

119272.q: Why can heavy fluid loss, for example from severe diarrhoea, lead to acute kidney failure?
a: The kidneys get too little blood
The kidneys are attacked by bacteria
119272.e: When fluid is lacking, blood pressure falls and the kidneys get too little blood to filter. Doctors call this prerenal kidney failure.
119272.m: Too little blood for the kidneys can make them fail.

119273.q: Which mineral rises in the blood in advanced kidney failure and can trigger dangerous heart rhythm disorders?
119273.e: The diseased kidney no longer excretes enough potassium. A potassium level that is too high disturbs the electrical excitation of the heart.
119273.m: In kidney failure, potassium in the blood rises.

119274.q: What does permanently raised albumin in the urine show?
a: A harmless, meaningless effect of sport
119274.e: Healthy glomeruli let hardly any albumin through. If it can be detected in the urine permanently, this is considered an early sign of kidney damage.
119274.m: Albumin in the urine is a warning sign for the kidney.

119275.q: Which treatments replace the function of the kidneys in the final stage?
a: A blood transfusion or a plaster cast
119275.e: In end-stage kidney failure, kidney replacement therapy is needed. The best long-term solution is usually a transplant.
119275.m: Without kidney function, only dialysis or a new kidney can help.

119276.q: Why does chronic kidney disease often damage the bones too?
a: The kidney activates too little vitamin D
The kidney makes too much bone marrow
The kidney burns the calcium in the bones
119276.e: The diseased kidney activates too little vitamin D and excretes too little phosphate. The calcium-phosphate balance is thrown off, and the bone is damaged.
119276.m: Diseased kidneys also weaken the bones.

119277.q: Which physical principle does haemodialysis mainly use to remove toxins?
119277.e: Blood and dialysis fluid are separated by a semi-permeable membrane. Small substances such as urea move along their concentration gradient into the dialysate.
119277.m: In dialysis, toxins pass through a membrane.

119278.q: How often is haemodialysis typically carried out for kidney failure?
119278.e: Three sessions a week of about four to five hours each are usual. In between, patients have to be careful with drinking and with foods rich in potassium.
119278.m: Haemodialysis usually takes place three times a week.

119279.q: Which vascular access is often created by surgery on the arm for haemodialysis?
a: An access into the spinal cord
119279.e: In an arteriovenous fistula, often called a Cimino shunt, an artery is joined to a vein. This makes the vein strong and easy to puncture.
119279.m: The shunt vein in the arm is the lifeline of dialysis patients.

119280.q: How is excess water removed during haemodialysis?
a: By ultrafiltration with a pressure gradient
119280.e: A pressure difference across the membrane presses water out of the blood into the dialysate. This ultrafiltration replaces the missing urine production.
119280.m: Ultrafiltration removes excess water from the blood.

119281.q: Which substance usually stops the blood from clotting in the dialysis machine?
119281.e: Heparin blocks clotting while the blood flows outside the body through tubes and filters. Vitamin K, fibrinogen and thrombin, on the other hand, promote clotting.
119281.m: Heparin keeps the blood liquid in the dialysis circuit.

119282.q: Which dialysis method uses the patient's own peritoneum as the membrane?
119282.e: In peritoneal dialysis, dialysis solution is filled into the abdominal cavity and changed after a few hours. It can be done at home.
119282.m: In peritoneal dialysis, your own peritoneum does the filtering.

119283.q: How do blood and dialysis fluid usually flow relative to each other in the dialyser?
a: Not at all, they stand still
119283.e: With countercurrent flow, the concentration gradient is kept along the whole length of the filter. That way more waste substances are removed.
119283.m: In the dialyser, blood and dialysate flow against each other.

119284.q: Which waste product of protein breakdown is removed from the blood in large amounts during dialysis?
119284.e: Urea is produced when proteins are broken down and is normally excreted through the kidneys. How much it decreases is also used to measure how effective a dialysis is.
119284.m: The dialysis dose is measured by urea.

119285.q: Which assumption is part of the ideal gas model?
a: The particles have no volume of their own and do not attract each other
The particles strongly attract each other
The particles rest at fixed places
The particles are bigger than the distances between them
119285.e: In an ideal gas the particles are point-like and interact only through elastic collisions. Forces of attraction and the particles' own volume are ignored.
119285.m: Ideal gas particles are tiny spheres that do not attract each other.

119286.q: Under which conditions does a real gas behave most like an ideal gas?
a: High temperature and very high pressure
119286.e: At low pressure the particles are far apart, so their own volume hardly matters. At high temperature the forces of attraction hardly count compared with the kinetic energy.
119286.m: Hot and thin, gases behave almost ideally.

119287.q: Which equation describes real gases with corrections for the particles' own volume and attraction?
119287.e: Johannes Diderik van der Waals added an internal pressure for attraction and a co-volume for the particles' own volume to the gas equation. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this in 1910.
119287.m: The van der Waals equation describes real gases.

119288.q: Which gas behaves especially close to an ideal gas at room temperature?
119288.e: Helium atoms are small and hardly attract each other. Gases such as water vapour or ammonia, by contrast, have strong forces of attraction between their molecules.
119288.m: Helium is almost an ideal gas.

119289.q: What is the value of the universal gas constant R?
119289.e: The gas constant is about 8.314 joules per mole and kelvin. It links pressure, volume, amount of substance and temperature.
119289.m: The gas constant R is about 8.3 joules per mole and kelvin.

119290.q: What is the value of the compressibility factor p·V/(n·R·T) for an ideal gas?
119290.e: For an ideal gas the equation of state applies exactly, so the ratio is 1. For real gases, the difference from 1 shows how far they depart from the ideal.
119290.m: For an ideal gas the compressibility factor is exactly one.

119291.q: What can happen to a real gas, but never to an ideal gas, if you cool it strongly and compress it?
119291.e: Liquefying needs forces of attraction between the particles. These are missing in the ideal gas model, so it can never condense.

119292.q: Air at 100 kPa contains about 21 per cent oxygen. What is the partial pressure of the oxygen?
119292.e: In a mixture of ideal gases, each gas contributes to the total pressure according to its mole fraction. 0.21 times 100 kPa gives 21 kPa.
119292.m: Each gas in a mixture has its own partial pressure.

119293.q: What is the ideal gas equation with the amount of substance n?
119293.e: Pressure times volume is proportional to amount of substance and temperature. The constant of proportionality is the gas constant R.
119293.m: Pressure times volume grows with amount of substance and temperature.

119294.q: What is the pressure of 2 mol of ideal gas at 300 K in a volume of 0.05 m³?
119294.e: p is nRT divided by V: 2 times 8.314 times 300 divided by 0.05 gives 99,768 Pa. That is about 100 kPa.
119294.m: For the pressure, divide nRT by the volume.

119295.q: How many moles of air does 1 m³ contain at 20 °C and 100 kPa?
119295.e: n is pV divided by RT: 100,000 times 1 divided by 8.314 times 293.15. That gives about 41 mol.
119295.m: One cubic metre of air contains about 41 moles of particles.

119296.q: A gas is at 2 bar, 10 litres and 300 K. What is its volume at 1 bar and 450 K?
119296.e: From p1V1/T1 = p2V2/T2 it follows that V2 = 2 times 10 times 450 divided by 300 times 1. That gives 30 litres.
119296.m: For a fixed amount of gas, pV divided by T stays constant.

119297.q: What is the mass of 1 m³ of helium (M = 4 g/mol) at 0 °C and 101,325 Pa?
119297.e: n is 101,325 divided by 8.314 times 273.15, so about 44.6 mol. Times 4 g/mol, that gives about 178 g.
119297.m: Helium is about seven times lighter than air.

119298.q: 0.513 g of a gas takes up exactly 0.4 litres at 300 K and 100 kPa. Which gas is it?
119298.e: n is pV divided by RT, so 100,000 times 0.0004 divided by 8.314 times 300, about 0.016 mol. The molar mass, 0.513 g divided by 0.016 mol, gives 32 g/mol, which matches O₂.
119298.m: You can use the gas equation to find the molar mass of a gas.

119299.q: What is the law called which says that equal volumes of ideal gases at the same pressure and temperature contain the same number of particles?
119299.e: Amedeo Avogadro put forward this hypothesis in 1811. It follows directly from the equation of state, because the type of gas does not appear in it.
119299.m: Equal volumes of gas contain the same number of particles.
